chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: In the single-sample t-test, a sample mean is compared against a known or hypothesized population mean (mu).
old_anchor: The t-test for a single sample is used to compare an obtained sample mean to a known population mean.
testable_fact: The single-sample t-test compares an obtained sample mean to a known or hypothesized population mean (mu).
passage:
A health psychologist collects blood pressure data from a sample of 50 hospital employees and wants to determine whether their average blood pressure differs significantly from the known national average. She has one sample mean to compare against one known population mean. This straightforward comparison calls for the simplest parametric test in the inferential statistics toolkit.

The **t-test for a single sample** (also called the **one-sample t-test**) is used to compare an obtained sample mean to a known population mean to determine whether the sample was likely drawn from that population. In this scenario, the psychologist compares the mean blood pressure of her 50 employees against the national population mean to determine whether hospital employees have significantly different blood pressure than the general population.

The test statistic is calculated as: t = (sample mean minus population mean) divided by the standard error of the mean. The **standard error of the mean** (SEM) is the standard deviation of the sample divided by the square root of n (the sample size). The resulting t value is compared to the critical value from the t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom (in this case, 49). If the obtained t exceeds the critical value, the null hypothesis (that the sample mean equals the population mean) is rejected.

The single-sample t-test differs from the **z-test for a single sample** in one crucial way: the t-test uses the sample standard deviation to estimate the standard error, while the z-test requires the population standard deviation to be known. In most psychological research, the population standard deviation is unknown, making the t-test the appropriate choice. The t-distribution is wider and has heavier tails than the normal (z) distribution, reflecting the additional uncertainty introduced by estimating the population standard deviation from sample data. As sample size increases, the t-distribution approaches the z-distribution.

The single-sample t-test should be distinguished from the **independent-samples t-test** (which compares the means of two separate groups) and the **correlated-samples t-test** (which compares the means of two related sets of scores). The defining feature of the single-sample t-test is that there is only one group of participants, and their mean is compared against a known population value rather than against another sample.

Assumptions include that the dependent variable is measured on an interval or ratio scale, the sample was randomly drawn from the population, and the population distribution of scores is approximately normal. The normality assumption becomes less critical with larger samples (typically n > 30) due to the **central limit theorem**, which ensures that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality regardless of the population distribution shape.

On the EPPP, the single-sample t-test appears in scenarios describing one group compared to a known population value. The defining feature is one sample mean versus one population mean. A common trap is selecting the independent-samples t-test when there is no second group, or selecting the z-test when the population standard deviation is not specified.

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Steckler, A. & McLeroy, K.R. (2008). The importance of external validity. American Journal of Public Health, 98(1), 9-10: External validity concerns "whether causal relationships can be generalized to different measures, persons, settings, and times." External validity refers to the degree to which research findings can be generalized beyond the specific conditions of the study.
old_anchor: External validity in research design refers to the generalizability of the results.
testable_fact: External validity refers to the degree to which research findings can be generalized to different people, settings, measures, and times beyond the original study conditions.
passage:
A psychologist conducts a laboratory study demonstrating that cognitive behavioral techniques significantly reduce anxiety in college students. The study was tightly controlled, with random assignment, standardized procedures, and validated outcome measures. However, a colleague asks whether these results would hold for older adults in community settings rather than college students in a laboratory. This question addresses one of the most critical considerations in research design.

**External validity** refers to the **generalizability** of research results -- the extent to which findings from a specific study can be extended to other populations, settings, times, and conditions beyond those in the original investigation. While internal validity asks whether the independent variable caused the observed effect, external validity asks whether that effect would replicate under different circumstances.

Several factors affect external validity. **Population validity** concerns whether results generalize to people who differ from the study sample in age, gender, ethnicity, clinical severity, socioeconomic status, or other demographic characteristics. College student samples, which dominate psychological research, raise questions about whether findings apply to the broader population. **Ecological validity** concerns whether results generalize to settings different from the study environment. Laboratory settings allow tight experimental control but may not reflect the complexity, distractions, and social pressures of real-world environments.

Specific threats to external validity have been categorized in the research methods literature. **Reactivity** (also called the **Hawthorne effect**) occurs when participants alter their behavior because they know they are being observed. **Demand characteristics** arise when cues in the research setting signal to participants how they are expected to respond. **Experimenter expectancy effects** occur when the researcher's expectations unconsciously influence participant behavior or data recording. **Order effects** in within-subjects designs may limit generalizability to situations where the same sequence of conditions is experienced.

External validity often exists in tension with **internal validity**. Increasing experimental control (random assignment, standardized protocols, homogeneous samples) strengthens internal validity but may reduce the naturalness and representativeness of the study, weakening external validity. Field experiments and quasi-experimental designs conducted in naturalistic settings often have stronger external validity but weaker internal validity. The optimal balance depends on the research question and stage of investigation.

Replication is the primary strategy for establishing external validity. When a finding replicates across different samples, settings, and time periods, confidence in its generalizability increases. Systematic replication -- varying one feature at a time while maintaining the core design -- is particularly informative for identifying the boundary conditions of an effect.

On the EPPP, external validity questions ask about generalizability. The defining feature is whether results extend beyond the specific study conditions. A common trap is confusing external validity with internal validity; remember that internal validity concerns causation within the study, while external validity concerns applicability outside the study.

old_anchor: A multiple-sample chi-square test would be used to compare the number of adults living in rural, urban, or suburban communities who have received a diagnosis of a bipolar disorder, depressive disorder, or anxiety disorder.
testable_fact: The chi-square test for independence determines whether two nominal variables are related or independent in data collected from independent groups.
passage:
When a researcher wants to determine whether the distribution of categorical outcomes differs across categorical groups, no mean or variance can be computed. The data consist entirely of frequency counts within categories, and the appropriate statistical test must work with those counts rather than with means or standard deviations.

A **multiple-sample chi-square test** (also called the chi-square test of independence or chi-square test of association) would be used to compare the number of adults living in rural, urban, or suburban communities who have received a diagnosis of a bipolar disorder, depressive disorder, or anxiety disorder. Both variables in this analysis, community type and diagnostic category, are measured on a **nominal scale**, consisting of unordered categories. The chi-square test evaluates whether the observed frequency distribution across the cells of the resulting contingency table differs significantly from what would be expected if the two variables were independent.

The multiple-sample chi-square test is called "multiple-sample" because it compares the frequency distributions of two or more groups (in this case, three community types) across the categories of another variable (three diagnostic categories). The data are organized in a contingency table (here, a 3 x 3 matrix) where each cell contains the observed frequency count for that combination of categories. The test statistic compares these observed frequencies to the expected frequencies that would occur if community type and diagnosis were unrelated.

The chi-square statistic is computed by summing the squared differences between observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequencies, across all cells. A large chi-square value indicates that the observed distribution departs substantially from what independence would predict, leading to rejection of the null hypothesis. The degrees of freedom equal (rows minus 1) times (columns minus 1), which for a 3 x 3 table is 4.

The chi-square test makes several assumptions: observations must be independent, each participant contributes to only one cell, and expected frequencies should be sufficiently large (typically at least 5 per cell, though some sources allow a minimum of 1 with no more than 20% of cells below 5). When expected frequencies are too small, Fisher's exact test or collapsing categories may be appropriate.

For the EPPP, candidates should recognize that chi-square is the appropriate test when both variables are categorical (nominal). The key decision point is identifying the measurement scale: when neither variable is continuous, parametric tests like t-tests and ANOVAs are inappropriate, and the chi-square test is the correct choice.

chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: "Paired t tests can be categorized as a type of t test for a single sample because they test the difference between two paired results." A t-test for correlated (paired) samples is used to compare the scores that subjects in two groups receive on a measure (such as symptom severity) after they receive treatment, when the subjects in the two groups have been matched on relevant variables prior to the study.
old_anchor: To compare the scores subjects in two groups receive on a measure of symptom severity after they receive treatment, a t-test for correlated samples will be used.
testable_fact: A paired (correlated) t-test is used to compare scores from two groups matched on relevant variables prior to the study, functioning statistically as a single-sample test of difference scores.
passage:
A researcher designs an experiment to evaluate whether a new stress-management intervention reduces symptom severity. She recruits 60 participants with elevated stress, randomly assigns 30 to the intervention group and 30 to a waitlist control group, administers the intervention over six weeks, and then measures symptom severity in both groups. To determine whether the two groups differ on the outcome measure, she needs to compare two independent group means.

To compare the scores subjects in two groups receive on a measure of symptom severity after treatment, a **t-test for independent samples** (also called the **independent-samples t-test** or **between-subjects t-test**) is the appropriate analysis. This test evaluates whether the means of two unrelated groups differ significantly on a continuous dependent variable. In this study, the two groups are the intervention group and the waitlist control group, and the dependent variable is post-treatment symptom severity.

The test statistic is: t = (mean of Group 1 minus mean of Group 2) / standard error of the difference between means. The standard error of the difference is calculated from the pooled variance of both groups and their sample sizes. The obtained t value is compared to the critical value from the t-distribution with degrees of freedom equal to n1 + n2 - 2 (in this case, 58). A significant result indicates that the group means differ by more than would be expected from sampling error alone.

The independent-samples t-test differs from the **correlated-samples t-test** in a critical way: the two sets of scores come from **different, unrelated individuals**. No participant appears in both groups, and there is no matching or pairing between participants across groups. When the same participants provide both sets of scores (as in a pre-post design), or when participants have been matched on a relevant variable, the correlated-samples t-test is appropriate instead.

Key assumptions include: the dependent variable is measured on an interval or ratio scale, the scores in each group are independent, the populations from which the samples were drawn are normally distributed, and the two populations have equal variances (**homogeneity of variance**). The equal variance assumption can be tested using Levene's test. When variances are unequal, a modified t-test (such as Welch's t-test) that adjusts the degrees of freedom is recommended.

The independent-samples t-test is limited to comparing exactly two groups. When a study includes three or more groups, a one-way ANOVA should be used instead to control the **experimentwise error rate** -- the probability of making at least one Type I error across multiple comparisons. Conducting multiple t-tests instead of a single ANOVA inflates this error rate.

On the EPPP, the independent-samples t-test appears in scenarios describing two separate groups compared on one continuous measure. The defining features are two independent groups and one DV. A common trap is selecting the correlated-samples t-test when the groups are clearly composed of different individuals.

verbatim_anchor: Gueorguieva, R. & Krystal, J.H. (2004). Move over ANOVA. Archives of General Psychiatry, 61(3), 310-317: MANOVA analyzes group differences when there are multiple dependent variables measured at the interval/ratio level.
old_anchor: The multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) is used when a study includes one or more independent variables and two or more dependent variables that are each measured on an interval or ratio scale.
testable_fact: MANOVA is used when a study includes one or more independent variables and two or more dependent variables each measured on an interval or ratio scale.
passage:
A researcher is studying the effects of three types of therapy on clients' outcomes, but she is measuring outcome on two different dimensions: symptom reduction and quality of life improvement. Using separate ANOVAs for each dependent variable would inflate the Type I error rate. She needs a single test that can handle multiple dependent variables simultaneously.

The **multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA)** is the appropriate statistical technique when a study includes one or more independent variables and **two or more dependent variables** that are each measured on an interval or ratio scale. MANOVA tests whether the groups defined by the independent variable(s) differ significantly on the **combination** of dependent variables, providing a single omnibus test that controls the overall Type I error rate.

In the therapy study, the independent variable is therapy type (three levels), and the two dependent variables are symptom reduction and quality of life improvement. MANOVA evaluates whether the three therapy groups differ on the linear combination of these two outcome measures. If the MANOVA produces a significant result, follow-up analyses (such as individual ANOVAs for each dependent variable or discriminant analysis) can be conducted to determine which variables or group comparisons are driving the overall effect.

MANOVA offers two key advantages over conducting separate ANOVAs. First, it **controls the experimentwise Type I error rate** -- the probability of falsely rejecting at least one null hypothesis across multiple tests. Running two separate ANOVAs at alpha = .05 each produces a combined Type I error rate greater than .05. MANOVA maintains the error rate at the nominal level. Second, MANOVA can detect **multivariate effects** that individual ANOVAs would miss. Two dependent variables might each show small, non-significant differences individually, but their combined pattern might reveal a significant multivariate effect when their correlation is taken into account.

Several multivariate test statistics are available for MANOVA, including **Wilks' lambda**, **Pillai's trace**, **Hotelling's trace**, and **Roy's largest root**. Wilks' lambda is the most commonly reported. Each statistic is converted to an approximate F value for significance testing. Pillai's trace is generally considered the most robust to violations of assumptions.

Assumptions of MANOVA include multivariate normality of the dependent variables within each group, homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices across groups (tested by Box's M test), and independence of observations. The dependent variables should be correlated but not so highly correlated as to be redundant; if they are essentially measuring the same thing, MANOVA loses its advantage over univariate ANOVA.

On the EPPP, MANOVA questions describe studies with multiple continuous dependent variables. The defining feature is two or more DVs with one or more IVs. A common trap is selecting a factorial ANOVA, which handles multiple IVs but only one DV, or selecting multiple regression, which has multiple predictors but one continuous criterion.

chapter_title: Advanced Statistical Tests: Chi-Square, MANOVA, Effect Sizes, and Clinical Significance
verbatim_anchor: Keselman, H.J. et al. (2001). The analysis of repeated measures designs. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 54(1), 1-20: "The simplest of the between-by within-subjects RM designs involves a single between-subjects grouping factor and a single within-subjects RM factor." A mixed-design (split-plot) ANOVA combines at least one between-subjects factor and one within-subjects factor.
old_anchor: The split-plot ANOVA is used to analyze data collected from a research study that included one between-subjects independent variable and one within-subjects independent variable.
testable_fact: A split-plot (mixed-design) ANOVA is used when a study includes at least one between-subjects independent variable and at least one within-subjects independent variable.
passage:
A researcher investigates whether the effect of a study technique (highlighting versus summarizing) on test performance differs between morning and evening study sessions. Half the participants are assigned to highlighting and half to summarizing (a between-subjects factor), and every participant is tested under both morning and evening conditions (a within-subjects factor). This hybrid design requires a specialized ANOVA.

The **split-plot ANOVA** (also called the **mixed-design ANOVA** or **mixed-model ANOVA**) is used to analyze data from a study that includes at least one **between-subjects** independent variable and at least one **within-subjects** independent variable. In this design, some factors vary between different groups of participants, while other factors vary within the same participants across conditions or time points.

In the study described, study technique is the between-subjects factor (each participant uses only one technique), and session time is the within-subjects factor (each participant is tested at both morning and evening sessions). The split-plot ANOVA simultaneously tests three effects: the main effect of study technique (between-subjects), the main effect of session time (within-subjects), and the interaction between study technique and session time.

The term "split-plot" originates from agricultural research where plots of land were divided (split) into subplots receiving different treatments. In psychological research, participants are "split" into groups based on the between-subjects factor, and then each participant within a group receives all levels of the within-subjects factor. This design is efficient because it requires fewer participants than a fully between-subjects design while still allowing examination of between-group differences.

The split-plot ANOVA has different error terms for the between-subjects and within-subjects effects. The between-subjects effect is tested against the between-subjects error term (variability among participants within groups). The within-subjects effects (including the interaction) are tested against the within-subjects error term (variability in how participants respond across conditions). This distinction is important because within-subjects error is typically smaller, giving within-subjects effects more statistical power.

A key assumption specific to the within-subjects component is **sphericity** -- the requirement that the variances of the differences between all pairs of within-subjects conditions are equal. Violations of sphericity inflate Type I error. Mauchly's test assesses sphericity, and corrections such as **Greenhouse-Geisser** or **Huynh-Feldt** adjust the degrees of freedom when sphericity is violated.

On the EPPP, split-plot ANOVA questions describe a study with at least one between-subjects and one within-subjects factor. The defining feature is the mixed design. A common trap is selecting a two-way between-subjects ANOVA, which would not account for the repeated measures on the within-subjects factor. Another trap is selecting a repeated-measures ANOVA, which handles only within-subjects factors.

chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Armstrong, R.A. (2014). When to use the Bonferroni correction. Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics, 34(5), 502-508: "As the number of tests increases, so does the likelihood of a type I error." ANOVA evaluates all mean differences simultaneously, avoiding inflated experimentwise alpha from multiple comparisons.
old_anchor: The advantage of conducting a single one-way ANOVA rather than separate t-tests when a study includes one independent variable with three or more levels is that the ANOVA controls the experimentwise error rate.
testable_fact: A one-way ANOVA controls the experimentwise error rate by evaluating all group mean differences simultaneously, avoiding the inflated Type I error risk of conducting multiple separate t-tests.
passage:
A researcher wants to compare the effectiveness of three different memory strategies on recall performance. She could run three separate t-tests (Strategy 1 vs. 2, Strategy 1 vs. 3, Strategy 2 vs. 3), but her statistics consultant warns that this approach carries a hidden cost. The consultant recommends a single one-way ANOVA instead.

The advantage of conducting a single **one-way ANOVA** rather than separate t-tests when a study includes one independent variable with three or more levels is that the ANOVA **controls the experimentwise error rate** (also called the **familywise error rate**). The experimentwise error rate is the probability of making at least one **Type I error** across a set of statistical comparisons. Each individual t-test carries its own alpha level (typically .05), but when multiple tests are conducted, the cumulative probability of at least one false positive increases substantially.

For example, with three groups and three pairwise comparisons, each at alpha = .05, the experimentwise error rate is approximately 1 - (1 - .05)^3 = .143. This means there is about a 14.3% chance of making at least one Type I error, nearly three times the nominal 5% level. With four groups and six comparisons, the rate climbs to approximately 26.5%. The more comparisons conducted, the greater the inflation.

The one-way ANOVA solves this problem by providing a single **omnibus F-test** that evaluates whether any of the group means differ significantly from each other, maintaining the experimentwise error rate at the specified alpha level. The null hypothesis tested by the ANOVA is that all population means are equal. Rejecting this null hypothesis indicates that at least one pair of means differs significantly, but it does not specify which pair(s).

When the omnibus F-test is significant, **post-hoc comparison** tests are used to identify which specific group means differ. These tests, such as **Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD)**, **Scheffe's test**, or **Bonferroni correction**, apply adjustments to maintain the experimentwise error rate at the nominal level while conducting pairwise comparisons. Tukey's HSD is the most commonly used when comparing all possible pairs of means.

The relationship between the ANOVA F-test and the t-test is mathematically precise: when there are exactly two groups, the F-ratio equals the square of the t-value (F = t-squared), and the two tests produce identical p-values. The ANOVA is thus a generalization of the t-test to three or more groups. However, the ANOVA should always be used with three or more groups; using multiple t-tests is never appropriate because it forfeits error rate control.

On the EPPP, questions about ANOVA versus multiple t-tests ask why ANOVA is preferred. The correct answer is that ANOVA controls the experimentwise (familywise) error rate. A common trap is stating that ANOVA is more powerful than t-tests -- the advantage is error rate control, not necessarily greater power for any single comparison.

chapter_title: Advanced Statistical Tests: Chi-Square, MANOVA, Effect Sizes, and Clinical Significance
verbatim_anchor: Gueorguieva, R. & Krystal, J.H. (2004). Move over ANOVA. Archives of General Psychiatry, 61(3), 310-317: MANOVA (multivariate analysis of variance) is used to analyze data from studies with one or more independent variables and two or more dependent variables measured on an interval or ratio scale. By making a single multivariate comparison rather than multiple separate ANOVAs, MANOVA reduces the probability of making a Type I error (familywise error rate).
old_anchor: The MANOVA can be used to analyze data collected in a study that has one independent variable and two or more dependent variables measured on an interval or ratio scale, as it reduces the probability of making a Type I error.
testable_fact: MANOVA reduces the probability of a Type I error by making a single multivariate comparison rather than multiple separate ANOVAs when two or more interval/ratio dependent variables are analyzed simultaneously.
passage:
A sports psychologist measures both competitive anxiety and self-confidence in athletes assigned to three different mental training programs. Running separate ANOVAs on each dependent variable would inflate the Type I error rate. She needs a test that evaluates group differences on both dependent variables simultaneously while maintaining statistical rigor.

The **MANOVA** (multivariate analysis of variance) can be used to analyze data from a study with one independent variable and **two or more dependent variables** measured on an interval or ratio scale. The primary advantage of using MANOVA rather than conducting separate univariate ANOVAs is that MANOVA **reduces the probability of making a Type I error** by testing the combined dependent variables in a single omnibus analysis.

When a researcher conducts separate ANOVAs -- one for competitive anxiety and one for self-confidence -- each test carries its own alpha level. With two tests at alpha = .05, the experimentwise error rate rises above .05, meaning the researcher is more likely to find at least one spurious significant effect. MANOVA addresses this by producing a single multivariate test statistic that evaluates whether groups differ on the **linear combination** of all dependent variables simultaneously, maintaining the Type I error rate at the specified level.

Beyond error rate control, MANOVA offers a second advantage: it can detect **multivariate patterns** that individual ANOVAs would miss. Two dependent variables might each show only small differences between groups when analyzed separately, but their joint pattern might reveal a significant multivariate effect when the correlation between the variables is taken into account. For example, one training program might produce slightly lower anxiety and slightly higher confidence, and while neither difference alone is significant, the combined pattern is.

The MANOVA procedure first tests the overall multivariate effect using statistics such as **Wilks' lambda** or **Pillai's trace**. If this omnibus test is significant, follow-up procedures are used to determine which dependent variables and which group comparisons are responsible. Follow-up options include individual ANOVAs (with Bonferroni correction for multiple tests), discriminant function analysis (to identify the linear combination of DVs that best separates the groups), or simultaneous confidence intervals.

Assumptions of MANOVA include multivariate normality, homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices across groups, independence of observations, and interval or ratio measurement of all dependent variables. The dependent variables should be theoretically related but not redundant. If two dependent variables correlate above .90, they are providing essentially the same information and MANOVA's advantage is diminished.

On the EPPP, MANOVA questions describe studies with one or more IVs and multiple continuous DVs, often asking why MANOVA is preferred over separate ANOVAs. The correct answer emphasizes Type I error control and multivariate detection. A common trap is selecting ANCOVA, which statistically controls for covariates rather than analyzing multiple dependent variables.

verbatim_anchor: Sawyer, S.F. (2009). Analysis of variance: The fundamental concepts. Journal of Manual & Manipulative Therapy, 17(2), 27E-38E: "F = Mean Squares_Between Groups / Mean Squares_Within Groups (Error)." "The MS_Between Groups term is an indirect measure of differences in group means" and reflects "the effects of the independent variable, or treatment, plus error." The numerator of the F-ratio (mean square between) estimates variability in dependent variable scores due to treatment effects plus error.
old_anchor: The numerator of the F-ratio produced by a one-way ANOVA is a measure of variability in dependent variable scores that's due to treatment effects plus error.
testable_fact: The numerator of the F-ratio (mean square between groups) estimates variability in dependent variable scores attributable to treatment effects plus error.
passage:
A researcher conducts a one-way ANOVA comparing four therapy groups on a measure of depression severity. Before interpreting the F-ratio, she needs to understand what the numerator and denominator of this ratio actually represent in terms of sources of variability. This understanding is essential for grasping why the F-ratio serves as a test of treatment effects.

The numerator of the F-ratio produced by a one-way ANOVA is the **mean square between** (MSbetween), which provides a measure of variability in dependent variable scores that is due to **treatment effects plus error**. The denominator is the **mean square within** (MSwithin), which provides a measure of variability due to **error alone** -- random individual differences and measurement imprecision within each treatment group.

MSbetween is calculated by dividing the **sum of squares between** (SSbetween) by its degrees of freedom (k - 1, where k is the number of groups). SSbetween captures the variability of group means around the grand mean, weighted by group size. This variability can arise from two sources: actual differences between groups produced by the treatment (the treatment effect) and random sampling variability (error). Because MSbetween contains both components, it is never purely a measure of treatment effects.

MSwithin is calculated by dividing the **sum of squares within** (SSwithin) by its degrees of freedom (N - k, where N is the total sample size). SSwithin captures the variability of individual scores around their respective group means. Because all individuals within a group received the same treatment, differences among them can only reflect individual differences and random error. MSwithin therefore provides a pure estimate of error variance.

The logic of the F-test follows directly from these definitions. If the null hypothesis is true (all treatments are equally effective), then MSbetween reflects only error variance -- the same quantity estimated by MSwithin. The expected F-ratio is approximately 1.0. If the treatment has an effect, MSbetween is inflated by the treatment effect component, producing an F-ratio greater than 1.0. The larger the treatment effect relative to the error variance, the larger the F-ratio and the more likely it is to exceed the critical value for statistical significance.

This logic also explains why increasing error variance (through poor experimental control, unreliable measures, or heterogeneous samples) reduces the power of the ANOVA: a larger MSwithin denominator produces a smaller F-ratio, making it harder to detect a true treatment effect. Conversely, reducing error variance through careful experimental design increases power.

On the EPPP, questions about the F-ratio ask what the numerator and denominator estimate. The numerator (MSbetween) estimates treatment effects plus error; the denominator (MSwithin) estimates error only. A common trap states that the numerator estimates treatment effects alone -- it always includes error. Another trap confuses MSbetween with SSbetween; remember that mean squares are sums of squares divided by their degrees of freedom.

passage:
A researcher at a large university wants to know whether men and women are accepted into graduate programs at different rates across departments. The data consist of frequency counts: how many men and how many women were accepted into each of six departments. What statistical test should be used to analyze these data?

The researcher will use a **multiple-sample chi-square test** (chi-square test of independence) to analyze the data and determine if there are gender differences in acceptance as a graduate student into the six largest departments at a university. Gender (male/female) is a **nominal variable** with two categories, and department (six departments) is also a **nominal variable** with six categories. Since both variables are categorical and the data consist of frequency counts, the chi-square test of independence is the appropriate analysis.

The data would be organized in a 2 x 6 **contingency table**, with rows representing gender (male, female) and columns representing the six departments. Each cell contains the number of accepted students for that gender-department combination. The chi-square test evaluates whether the pattern of acceptance across departments differs between men and women, or equivalently, whether gender and department are independent with respect to acceptance.

The null hypothesis states that the proportion of accepted students who are male (or female) is the same across all six departments, meaning gender and department are independent. The alternative hypothesis states that the proportions differ across at least some departments, indicating a relationship between gender and department in acceptance decisions. The degrees of freedom for this test would be (2 - 1)(6 - 1) = 5.

This research design parallels a famous real-world case: the Berkeley admissions study, which demonstrated **Simpson's paradox**. The aggregate data showed an apparent bias against women in admissions, but department-level analysis revealed that women were applying disproportionately to more competitive departments. This example illustrates why examining contingency tables at the appropriate level of analysis is important and why a significant chi-square result requires careful interpretation of the pattern of frequencies to understand the nature of the association.

For the EPPP, candidates should recognize that the chi-square test of independence is used whenever the research question involves the association between two categorical variables measured by frequency counts. The key indicators are: both variables are nominal, the data are counts (not means or proportions), and the question asks whether the distribution of one variable depends on the other. Candidates should also know the formula for degrees of freedom in a contingency table: (rows - 1)(columns - 1).

chapter_title: Advanced Statistical Tests: Chi-Square, MANOVA, Effect Sizes, and Clinical Significance
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: For the t test of independent means, "d = (m_A - m_B) / sigma" with conventional benchmarks of Small = .20, Medium = .50, Large = .80. A Cohen's d of .60 falls in the medium range and is interpreted in terms of standard deviation units -- meaning the two group means differ by .60 standard deviations.
old_anchor: A Cohen's d of .60 indicates a medium effect, which is interpreted in terms of standard deviation units.
testable_fact: Cohen's d of .60 represents a medium effect size, indicating the two group means differ by .60 standard deviations.
passage:
When a researcher finds a statistically significant difference between two groups, how large is that difference in practical terms? Statistical significance alone does not convey the magnitude of an effect, and a separate class of statistics is needed to quantify the size of the difference in a standardized, interpretable metric.

A **Cohen's d** of .60 indicates a **medium effect**, and this measure is interpreted in terms of **standard deviation units**. Cohen's d quantifies the difference between two group means divided by the pooled standard deviation, expressing how far apart the means are in standardized terms. A value of .60 means that the two group means are separated by six-tenths of a standard deviation, which falls within the range that Jacob Cohen designated as a medium effect.

Cohen established widely used benchmarks for interpreting d values: a **small effect** is approximately .20 (one-fifth of a standard deviation), a **medium effect** is approximately .50 (one-half of a standard deviation), and a **large effect** is approximately .80 (four-fifths of a standard deviation). These conventions provide general guidelines, but the practical significance of any particular effect size depends on the context of the research question. In some fields, a small d may represent a meaningful and important finding, while in others, only large effects may have practical relevance.

Cohen's d belongs to a broader family of **effect size measures** that serve several purposes in research. First, they complement significance tests by providing information about the magnitude of an effect that p-values alone cannot convey. A significant p-value indicates that the difference is unlikely to have occurred by chance, but it says nothing about whether the difference is large enough to matter. Second, effect sizes are essential for **meta-analysis**, where results from multiple studies are combined, because they provide a common metric that is not influenced by sample size. Third, effect sizes are used in **power analysis** to determine the sample size needed to detect an effect of a given magnitude.

Other common effect size measures include **eta squared** and **partial eta squared** for ANOVA designs (indicating the proportion of variance accounted for), **omega squared** (a less biased alternative to eta squared), and **r** or **r-squared** for correlational analyses. Each serves the same general purpose of quantifying effect magnitude but is suited to different research designs.

For the EPPP, candidates must know Cohen's benchmarks (.20 small, .50 medium, .80 large), understand that d is expressed in standard deviation units, and recognize that a d of .60 falls in the medium range. Questions may present a d value and ask for its interpretation, or they may ask candidates to distinguish effect size from statistical significance.

The multivariate analysis of variance simultaneously tests the effects of one or more independent variables on two or more dependent variables, controlling the experimentwise Type I error rate.
