testable_fact: MANOVA simultaneously tests the effects of one or more independent variables on two or more interval/ratio-level dependent variables while controlling the experimentwise Type I error rate.
passage:
When a study involves multiple outcome measures that are theoretically related, analyzing each one separately with individual ANOVAs inflates the risk of Type I error and ignores the correlations among the dependent variables. A more appropriate approach addresses all outcomes simultaneously within a single analysis.

The **multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA)** is used to simultaneously analyze the effects of one or more **independent variables** on two or more **dependent variables** that are each measured on an **interval or ratio scale**. By combining the dependent variables into a linear composite and testing whether group means on this composite differ significantly, MANOVA provides a single omnibus test that accounts for the intercorrelations among the outcome measures while controlling the overall Type I error rate.

MANOVA extends the logic of ANOVA to multiple dependent variables. Where a one-way ANOVA tests whether group means differ on a single dependent variable, a one-way MANOVA tests whether group **mean vectors** (the sets of means across all dependent variables) differ. The test statistics used in MANOVA, including **Wilks' lambda**, **Pillai's trace**, **Hotelling's trace**, and **Roy's largest root**, each evaluate the multivariate null hypothesis through somewhat different mathematical approaches. Wilks' lambda is the most commonly reported and represents the proportion of variance in the discriminant functions that is not accounted for by group differences.

MANOVA offers several advantages over running separate ANOVAs. It controls the familywise Type I error rate that would inflate if each dependent variable were tested separately. It can detect effects that emerge only when dependent variables are considered jointly rather than individually. And it uses the covariance structure among dependent variables, which can increase statistical power when the dependent variables are moderately correlated.

However, MANOVA requires several assumptions: multivariate normality of the dependent variables within each group, homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices across groups (tested by Box's M test), independence of observations, and adequate sample size relative to the number of dependent variables.

For the EPPP, candidates should recognize MANOVA as the appropriate test when there are two or more continuous dependent variables and one or more categorical independent variables. The key decision trigger is multiple dependent variables measured on interval or ratio scales. If there is only one dependent variable, ANOVA is sufficient. Candidates should also know that a significant MANOVA is typically followed by individual ANOVAs or discriminant function analysis to identify which dependent variables contribute to the group differences.

chapter_title: Advanced Statistical Tests: Chi-Square, MANOVA, Effect Sizes, and Clinical Significance
verbatim_anchor: Jacobson & Truax (1991): "A reliable change index (RC) is also proposed to determine whether the magnitude of change for a given client is statistically reliable." "RC tells us whether change reflects more than the fluctuations of an imprecise measuring instrument."
old_anchor: The reliable change index is used to determine if a difference in pre- and post-treatment scores on an outcome measure is reliable - i.e., if it is due to real improvement or deterioration in a person's clinical condition or to measurement error.
testable_fact: The reliable change index (RCI) determines whether the difference between pre- and post-treatment scores reflects genuine clinical change rather than measurement error.
passage:
A clinician measures a client's depression severity before and after a twelve-week intervention. The pre-treatment score was 28 and the post-treatment score was 19 on a standardized depression inventory. While the nine-point decrease looks promising, the clinician needs to determine whether this change reflects genuine clinical improvement or simply measurement error -- the kind of fluctuation that could occur even without any real change in the client's condition.

The **reliable change index** (RCI), developed by Jacobson and Truax, is used to determine whether a difference between pre- and post-treatment scores on an outcome measure is **statistically reliable** -- that is, whether the change exceeds what would be expected from measurement error alone. If the RCI value exceeds 1.96 (for a 95% confidence level), the change is considered reliable, meaning it is unlikely to be due to measurement imprecision.

The RCI is calculated as: RCI = (post-test score minus pre-test score) / standard error of the difference. The standard error of the difference (Sdiff) is calculated as: Sdiff = square root of (2 times SEM-squared), where SEM is the standard error of measurement. The SEM, in turn, depends on the test's standard deviation and reliability: SEM = SD times the square root of (1 - reliability). By chaining these formulas, the RCI incorporates information about the test's measurement precision into the evaluation of individual score changes.

The RCI is a critical tool in clinical research and practice because it distinguishes between **statistically reliable change** and **clinically significant change**. Reliable change tells us whether the change is real (not just measurement noise); clinical significance tells us whether the change moves the client from a dysfunctional range to a normative range. Jacobson and Truax proposed that both criteria should be met before a client is classified as "recovered." A client who shows reliable change but remains in the clinical range has "improved" but not "recovered."

In treatment outcome research, the RCI provides a more meaningful analysis than group-level statistics alone. An intervention might produce a statistically significant group mean difference (via a t-test) while failing to produce reliable change for many individual participants. The RCI allows clinicians and researchers to evaluate outcomes at the individual level, which is more relevant to clinical decision-making.

The RCI can also identify reliable deterioration: if a client's score increases by more than the Sdiff threshold in the direction of greater pathology, the worsening is considered reliable. This bidirectional sensitivity makes the RCI valuable for monitoring both improvement and deterioration during treatment.

On the EPPP, the RCI appears in questions about determining whether individual score changes are meaningful. The key concept is that it separates real change from measurement error. A common trap is confusing the RCI with effect size measures (such as Cohen's d), which summarize group-level differences rather than individual-level reliability of change.

chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Lee, S. & Lee, D.K. (2018). What is the proper way to apply the multiple comparison test? Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 71(5), 353-360: "When the null hypothesis (H0) is rejected after ANOVA... we do not know how one group differs from a certain group." Post-hoc tests are conducted after a significant omnibus F to determine which specific pairs of means differ significantly, and are applicable when the independent variable has three or more levels.
old_anchor: When a one-way ANOVA produces a statistically significant F-ratio, a post-hoc test would be considered if the independent variable has three or more levels.
testable_fact: Post-hoc tests are conducted after a statistically significant omnibus F-ratio to identify which specific pairs of group means differ significantly, and are necessary when the independent variable has three or more levels.
passage:
A researcher conducts a one-way ANOVA comparing four different study strategies on exam performance. The F-test is statistically significant, confirming that at least one group mean differs from the others. But she wants to know specifically which strategies outperform which. She needs to conduct additional analyses, but only under certain conditions.

When a one-way ANOVA produces a statistically significant F-ratio, a **post-hoc test** (also called a **follow-up test** or **multiple comparison procedure**) would be considered if the independent variable has **three or more levels**. The omnibus F-test tells the researcher only that at least one pair of means differs -- it does not identify which specific pairs. Post-hoc tests make these pairwise comparisons while controlling the experimentwise (familywise) Type I error rate.

If the independent variable has only two levels, post-hoc tests are unnecessary because a significant F-test already identifies the only possible comparison: the two groups differ. With three or more levels, however, multiple pairwise comparisons are possible, and post-hoc tests systematically evaluate each while adjusting for the inflation in Type I error that comes from multiple testing.

Several post-hoc procedures are available, each balancing Type I error control against statistical power differently. **Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD)** is the most commonly used when all pairwise comparisons are of interest and group sizes are equal. It maintains the experimentwise error rate at alpha while providing good power. **Scheffe's test** is the most conservative, controlling Type I error even for complex contrasts (not just pairwise comparisons), but it sacrifices considerable power. The **Bonferroni correction** divides alpha by the number of comparisons, and is straightforward but becomes very conservative with many groups. **Newman-Keuls** and **Duncan's** tests are more powerful but do not fully control the experimentwise error rate.

Post-hoc tests should be distinguished from **planned comparisons** (also called **a priori contrasts** or **orthogonal contrasts**). Planned comparisons are specified before the data are collected, based on theoretical predictions, and do not require a significant omnibus F-test. Post-hoc tests are conducted only after a significant F-test and involve examining all possible comparisons in an exploratory fashion. Planned comparisons are generally more powerful because they focus statistical resources on specific, theory-driven questions.

The choice of post-hoc procedure depends on the research context. When the consequences of a Type I error are severe, conservative tests like Scheffe are preferred. When power is a priority and the number of groups is moderate, Tukey's HSD is typically recommended.

On the EPPP, post-hoc test questions ask when they are appropriate or which test to use. The key condition is a significant omnibus F with three or more groups. A common trap is stating that post-hoc tests are needed whenever F is significant, regardless of the number of groups. With only two groups, no post-hoc test is needed.

chapter_title: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
verbatim_anchor: Steckler, A. & McLeroy, K.R. (2008). The importance of external validity. American Journal of Public Health, 98(1), 9-10: External validity concerns "whether causal relationships can be generalized to different measures, persons, settings, and times."
old_anchor: External validity refers to the extent to which research results are generalizable to other people, settings, and times.
testable_fact: External validity refers to the degree to which research findings can be generalized to different persons, settings, and times.
passage:
A team of researchers demonstrates that a brief mindfulness exercise significantly reduces test anxiety among undergraduate psychology students in a controlled laboratory setting. The finding is robust and well-replicated within the university sample. But a school administrator asks whether the same technique would work for high school students preparing for standardized tests in a noisy classroom environment. This question gets at one of the most fundamental concerns in research methodology.

**External validity** refers to the extent to which research results are **generalizable** to other people, settings, and times beyond those involved in the original study. It asks whether the findings from a particular sample and context will hold up when applied more broadly. In the mindfulness example, the question is whether a result obtained with college undergraduates in a quiet laboratory would replicate with younger students in a different, less controlled environment.

External validity encompasses several dimensions. **Population validity** addresses whether results generalize to individuals who differ from the study sample in demographics, clinical characteristics, or other relevant attributes. A study conducted exclusively with college-aged women may not generalize to middle-aged men or to clinical populations. **Ecological validity** addresses whether results generalize to different settings, particularly from laboratory to real-world environments. The controlled conditions that strengthen internal validity may create an artificial context that does not represent how phenomena operate in everyday life.

Several specific threats compromise external validity. The **Hawthorne effect** (reactivity) occurs when participants change behavior simply because they know they are being observed. **Selection-treatment interaction** occurs when the treatment effect depends on specific characteristics of the sample that would not be present in the target population. **Setting-treatment interaction** occurs when the effect depends on specific features of the research environment. **History-treatment interaction** occurs when the effect depends on the particular historical moment in which the study was conducted.

External validity exists in inherent tension with **internal validity**. Increasing experimental control (random assignment, standardized procedures, restricted samples) strengthens internal validity but may create conditions that do not mirror the real world, weakening external validity. This is sometimes called the **laboratory-to-field** problem. Conversely, conducting research in naturalistic settings enhances external validity but introduces confounds that threaten internal validity.

The primary strategy for establishing external validity is **replication** across diverse samples, settings, and time periods. A single study has limited external validity; a finding that replicates consistently across varied conditions has strong external validity.

On the EPPP, external validity questions focus on generalizability. The defining feature is whether results apply beyond the original study. A common trap is confusing external validity with internal validity (which concerns causation within the study) or with construct validity (which concerns whether the study measures the intended construct).

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: "The sampling distribution shows normal distribution with mean of mu and variance of sigma-squared/n." The standard error formula SE = sigma/sqrt(n) shows the standard error is directly proportional to the population standard deviation and inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.
old_anchor: The standard error of the mean increases in size as the population standard deviation increases and sample size decreases.
testable_fact: The standard error of the mean is directly proportional to population standard deviation and inversely proportional to the square root of sample size (SE = σ/√n).
passage:
A researcher is designing a study to estimate the average response time of emergency room physicians. She knows that the precision of her estimate will depend on two factors: the natural variability among physicians and the number of physicians she can include in her sample. Understanding how these factors affect the precision of her estimate requires knowledge of the standard error of the mean.

The **standard error of the mean** (SEM) is the standard deviation of the **sampling distribution of means** -- the theoretical distribution of all possible sample means that could be drawn from a population. It quantifies how much sample means are expected to vary from sample to sample due to random sampling variability. The SEM is calculated as: SEM = population standard deviation / square root of n, where n is the sample size.

The SEM **increases in size** as the **population standard deviation increases** and as **sample size decreases**. This relationship is directly captured by the formula. A larger population standard deviation means there is more variability among individual scores in the population, which translates to more variability among sample means. A smaller sample size means each sample provides less information about the population, making the sample mean a less stable estimate.

Conversely, the SEM decreases when the population standard deviation is small (scores are clustered closely around the population mean) or when the sample size is large (each sample contains enough cases to stabilize the mean estimate). Note that the relationship between sample size and SEM follows a square root function: to halve the SEM, one must quadruple the sample size. This diminishing returns property means that very large sample sizes are required to achieve very small improvements in precision.

The SEM has critical practical applications. It is used to construct **confidence intervals** around the sample mean, providing a range of plausible values for the population mean. A 95% confidence interval is the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 times the SEM. It is also used in **hypothesis testing**: the t-test and z-test both divide the difference between observed and expected means by the SEM (or its estimate) to determine statistical significance.

The SEM should be carefully distinguished from the **standard deviation** (which describes the spread of individual scores in a sample or population) and from the **standard error of measurement** (which describes the precision of individual test scores based on test reliability). All three quantities involve variability, but they describe different aspects of different distributions.

On the EPPP, SEM questions typically ask about the factors that influence its size. The correct answer involves population standard deviation (positive relationship) and sample size (inverse relationship). A common trap reverses the relationship with sample size, stating that larger samples produce larger SEMs. Remember: larger samples always produce smaller standard errors, leading to more precise estimates.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: "The risk of mistakenly rejecting the null hypothesis (H_0) and thus of committing a Type I error, alpha, represents a policy: the maximum risk of a false rejection." Alpha and beta are inversely related: raising alpha increases Type I error risk but decreases beta (Type II error probability).
old_anchor: Increasing the level of significance (alpha) from .05 to .10 increases the probability of making a Type I error and decreases the probability of making a Type II error.
testable_fact: Increasing alpha (e.g., from .05 to .10) increases the probability of a Type I error and simultaneously decreases the probability of a Type II error (beta).
passage:
A biomedical researcher is studying whether a new exercise program reduces blood pressure. She initially planned to use an alpha level of .05 but is considering changing it to .10 to increase her chances of finding a significant result. Before making this change, she needs to understand the full consequences of altering the significance level on both Type I and Type II error rates.

Increasing the level of significance (alpha) from .05 to .10 **increases the probability of making a Type I error** and **decreases the probability of making a Type II error**. These two error types exist in an inverse relationship: actions that reduce one tend to increase the other, and changing the alpha level directly manipulates this trade-off.

A **Type I error** (also called a **false positive** or **alpha error**) occurs when the researcher rejects a true null hypothesis -- concluding that an effect exists when it actually does not. The probability of a Type I error is set directly by the alpha level. When alpha = .05, there is a 5% chance of incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis. When alpha is increased to .10, this probability doubles to 10%. The researcher has widened the "rejection region" of the sampling distribution, making it easier to reject the null hypothesis but also easier to reject it incorrectly.

A **Type II error** (also called a **false negative** or **beta error**) occurs when the researcher fails to reject a false null hypothesis -- concluding that no effect exists when one actually does. The probability of a Type II error (beta) decreases when alpha increases because the wider rejection region captures more of the alternative distribution. With a more lenient criterion for significance, the researcher is less likely to miss a real effect.

**Statistical power** is defined as 1 - beta: the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. Because increasing alpha decreases beta, it simultaneously increases power. However, this power gain comes at the cost of increased Type I error risk. Researchers must balance the relative costs of the two errors. In exploratory research, a higher alpha (more Type I error risk) may be acceptable because the consequences of a false positive (pursuing a non-existent effect in future research) are less severe. In confirmatory or high-stakes research, a lower alpha is warranted.

Other factors that affect the Type I/Type II trade-off include sample size (larger samples increase power without affecting alpha), effect size (larger effects are easier to detect), and the directionality of the test (one-tailed tests are more powerful than two-tailed tests for detecting effects in the predicted direction).

On the EPPP, questions about changing alpha ask about the consequences for error rates. Increasing alpha increases Type I error probability and decreases Type II error probability (increases power). A common trap states that increasing alpha increases both error types -- in reality, they move in opposite directions.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Bridge, P.D. & Sawilowsky, S.S. (1999). Increasing physicians' awareness of the impact of statistics on research outcomes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 52(3), 229-235: "The t-test is one of the most prevalent tests used in the medical field and is the uniformly most powerful unbiased test (UMPU) under normal curve theory." Parametric tests are generally more powerful than nonparametric counterparts when assumptions are met.
old_anchor: Parametric statistical tests are more powerful than nonparametric tests, meaning that when using a parametric test, you're more likely to reject a false null hypothesis.
testable_fact: Parametric statistical tests are more powerful than nonparametric tests when their assumptions are met, meaning they have a greater probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.
passage:
A researcher is deciding between a parametric and a nonparametric test for her data. Her colleague advises using the parametric version whenever the assumptions are reasonably met, citing the parametric test's greater statistical power. She wants to understand what this power advantage means in practical terms.

**Parametric statistical tests** (such as the t-test and ANOVA) are generally **more powerful** than their **nonparametric** counterparts (such as the Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests). Statistical **power** is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis -- that is, detecting a real effect when one exists. Higher power means a lower probability of making a **Type II error** (failing to detect a real effect).

The power advantage of parametric tests stems from their use of all available quantitative information in the data. Parametric tests operate on the actual numerical values of scores, preserving the information contained in the distances between scores. Nonparametric tests typically convert scores to ranks or categories, discarding information about the magnitude of differences. This information loss reduces the test's ability to detect differences, lowering power.

For example, consider three anxiety scores: 12, 15, and 42. A parametric test uses all three values and recognizes that 42 is much further from the others. A nonparametric test converts these to ranks (1, 2, 3), treating the gap between 15 and 42 the same as the gap between 12 and 15. The parametric test has more information to work with, giving it a better chance of detecting a true effect.

The power advantage of parametric tests comes with conditions, however. Parametric tests make specific **assumptions** about the data: the dependent variable should be measured on an interval or ratio scale, the population distribution should be approximately normal, and (for tests comparing groups) the variances should be approximately equal across groups. When these assumptions are met, parametric tests are optimal. When assumptions are severely violated -- particularly with small samples, extreme skewness, or ordinal data -- nonparametric tests may actually perform better because they do not require these assumptions.

In practice, parametric tests are fairly **robust** to moderate violations of normality, especially with larger samples (thanks to the central limit theorem). The equal variance assumption is more critical, particularly when group sizes are unequal. Researchers should assess assumption violations before choosing between parametric and nonparametric approaches, recognizing that the power advantage of parametric tests holds only when assumptions are reasonably satisfied.

On the EPPP, questions about parametric versus nonparametric tests typically ask about the advantage of parametric tests. The correct answer is greater power (higher probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis). A common trap confuses power with alpha level or effect size. Remember: power is about detecting real effects, and parametric tests are better at this when their assumptions are met.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Neyman & Pearson (1933): "We fail to reject H_0 when some alternative hypothesis is true." They called these "errors of the second kind" -- concluding there is no difference when one actually exists.
old_anchor: A Type II error occurs when a researcher retains a false null hypothesis.
testable_fact: A Type II error (beta) occurs when a researcher fails to reject a false null hypothesis, concluding no difference exists when one actually does.
passage:
A pharmaceutical company conducts a clinical trial comparing a new compound to a placebo. The study finds no statistically significant difference between groups, and the company concludes that the compound has no effect. However, a subsequent large-scale study reveals that the compound does, in fact, produce meaningful improvement. The original study made a specific type of statistical error that every researcher must understand.

A **Type II error** (also called a **false negative** or **beta error**) occurs when a researcher **retains a false null hypothesis** -- concluding that there is no significant effect or difference when one actually exists in the population. In the pharmaceutical example, the null hypothesis stated that the compound and placebo produce equal outcomes. The reality was that the compound was superior, but the study failed to detect this difference, leading to the erroneous conclusion that no effect existed.

The probability of making a Type II error is denoted by **beta**. Statistical **power**, defined as 1 - beta, is the complement: the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false. A study with power of .80 (the conventional minimum) has a 20% probability of committing a Type II error. Factors that reduce power -- small sample sizes, high variability, small effect sizes, and overly stringent alpha levels -- increase the probability of Type II errors.

Type II errors should be distinguished from **Type I errors** (false positives), which occur when a researcher rejects a true null hypothesis. The two error types have an inverse relationship: holding everything else constant, decreasing the probability of one increases the probability of the other. Lowering alpha from .05 to .01 reduces the Type I error rate but increases the Type II error rate (reduces power), making it harder to detect real effects.

The consequences of a Type II error depend on the research context. In medical research, failing to detect an effective treatment means that patients continue to suffer unnecessarily. In educational research, failing to identify an effective teaching method means lost opportunities for student improvement. In basic research, Type II errors can stall scientific progress by leading researchers to abandon promising lines of investigation based on false negative results.

Several strategies reduce the risk of Type II errors: increasing sample size (the most direct method), using more reliable measures, choosing the appropriate statistical test, using one-tailed tests when directional hypotheses are justified, and accepting a somewhat higher alpha level when Type II errors are particularly costly.

On the EPPP, Type II error questions ask candidates to identify the error from a scenario description. The defining feature is retaining (failing to reject) a null hypothesis that is actually false. A common trap is confusing Type II with Type I errors: Type I is rejecting a true null hypothesis (finding an effect that is not there), while Type II is retaining a false null hypothesis (missing an effect that is there). Remember: Type II = miss.

chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: "The statistical power of a significance test is the long-term probability, given the population ES, alpha, and N, of rejecting H_0. Power is thus 1 - beta." Power increases with larger alpha, larger effect size, larger sample size, and use of parametric tests.
old_anchor: Increasing the size of alpha, increasing the effect size, and using a parametric test when appropriate are methods for increasing the statistical power, which is the ability to reject a false null hypothesis, in designing and conducting a research study.
testable_fact: Statistical power (1 − beta) increases with larger alpha, larger effect size, larger sample size, and use of parametric rather than nonparametric tests.
passage:
A researcher designs a study hoping to detect a real effect if one exists. What factors determine whether the study will have enough sensitivity to find that effect? This question addresses one of the most fundamental concerns in research methodology: the ability to avoid missing real effects when they are present.

**Statistical power** is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, meaning it is the likelihood of detecting a real effect when one truly exists. Power is mathematically defined as 1 minus beta, where beta is the probability of making a **Type II error** (failing to reject a false null hypothesis). Researchers can increase statistical power through several methods, including increasing the size of **alpha**, increasing the **effect size**, and using a **parametric test** when its assumptions are met.

Increasing the alpha level (for example, from .01 to .05) directly increases power because a larger alpha makes the critical region for rejecting the null hypothesis more inclusive. With a more lenient threshold, smaller observed effects can achieve statistical significance. However, this increase in power comes at a cost: the probability of making a **Type I error** (incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis) also increases. This tradeoff between Type I and Type II error rates is a fundamental tension in hypothesis testing.

Increasing the effect size increases power because larger effects are easier to detect. While the true effect size in the population is fixed, researchers can increase the observed effect size by strengthening the experimental manipulation, reducing measurement error through more reliable instruments, or using more homogeneous samples that reduce within-group variability.

Using a parametric test (such as a t-test or ANOVA) rather than a nonparametric alternative (such as the Mann-Whitney U or Kruskal-Wallis) increases power when the parametric assumptions are met, because parametric tests extract more information from the data by utilizing the actual values rather than just their ranks.

Other factors that affect power include **sample size** (larger samples increase power), the use of a **one-tailed versus two-tailed test** (one-tailed tests have greater power when the direction of the effect is correctly specified), and the variability within groups (less variability increases power).

For the EPPP, candidates must know the definition of power (1 - beta) and the methods for increasing it. Exam questions may ask which design modification will increase power, or they may present a scenario and ask candidates to evaluate the power implications of specific methodological choices.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: "When samples are drawn from population N (mu, sigma-squared) with a sample size of n, the distribution of the sample mean should be a normal distribution." The distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as n increases, regardless of the population distribution's shape.
old_anchor: The central limit theorem predicts that the sampling distribution of means increasingly approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution of scores.
testable_fact: The central limit theorem states that the sampling distribution of means approaches normality as sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution.
passage:
A statistics instructor asks her class what would happen to the shape of the distribution of sample means if she drew thousands of samples of increasing size from a population with a highly skewed distribution. Students who understand the central limit theorem know the surprising answer: regardless of the population shape, the distribution of means will approximate a normal curve.

The **central limit theorem** (CLT) predicts that the **sampling distribution of means** increasingly approaches a **normal distribution** as the **sample size increases**, regardless of the shape of the population distribution of individual scores. This theorem is one of the most important results in statistics because it justifies the use of normal-distribution-based inferential techniques (z-tests, t-tests, confidence intervals) even when the underlying population is not normally distributed.

The sampling distribution of means is the theoretical distribution of all possible sample means that could be drawn from a population. If you drew an infinite number of samples of size n, calculated the mean of each, and plotted these means, you would have the sampling distribution of means. The CLT states that this distribution will be approximately normal when n is sufficiently large, with a mean equal to the population mean (mu) and a standard deviation equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n (the standard error of the mean).

The key qualifier is "sufficiently large." For populations that are already normally distributed, the sampling distribution of means is exactly normal for any sample size. For populations that are moderately non-normal (mildly skewed or kurtotic), samples of n = 25 to 30 are generally sufficient for the sampling distribution to be approximately normal. For populations with extreme skewness or heavy tails, larger samples may be needed. There is no single universal threshold, but the convention of n = 30 is commonly cited as a practical guideline.

The CLT explains why parametric statistical tests are robust to violations of normality with larger samples. Even if individual scores in a population are highly skewed, the means of samples drawn from that population will be approximately normally distributed when samples are large enough. Since parametric tests operate on sample means (and their associated sampling distributions), the normality assumption is satisfied at the sampling distribution level even when violated at the individual score level.

The CLT also has implications for the precision of estimation. As sample size increases, the standard error of the mean decreases, meaning sample means cluster more tightly around the population mean. Larger samples yield more precise estimates, and the CLT guarantees that the distributional framework for constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests is valid.

On the EPPP, CLT questions ask what happens to the sampling distribution as sample size increases. The correct answer is that it approaches normality regardless of the population shape. A common trap states that the population distribution itself becomes normal -- it does not. Only the sampling distribution of means normalizes.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: "The statistical power of a significance test is the long-term probability, given the population ES, alpha, and N, of rejecting H_0. Power is thus 1 - beta." Increasing alpha from .01 to .05 increases both statistical power (1 - beta) and the probability of making a Type I error, because alpha and beta are inversely related.
old_anchor: Increasing alpha from .01 to .05 increases both statistical power and the probability of making a Type I error.
testable_fact: Increasing alpha from .01 to .05 simultaneously increases statistical power (1 − beta) and the probability of a Type I error, because alpha and beta are inversely related.
passage:
When a researcher loosens the criterion for statistical significance, what are the consequences for the two types of decision errors? This question captures one of the most important tradeoffs in hypothesis testing, and understanding it requires clarity about the inverse relationship between these error types.

Increasing alpha from .01 to .05 simultaneously increases both **statistical power** and the probability of making a **Type I error**. These two consequences follow directly from the same mathematical change: expanding the rejection region of the sampling distribution. A larger alpha means that a wider range of sample outcomes will lead to rejection of the null hypothesis, which increases the chance of detecting a real effect (power) but also increases the chance of falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type I error).

Alpha is defined as the probability of making a Type I error, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. When alpha is set at .01, there is a 1% chance of incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis. When alpha is increased to .05, that probability rises to 5%. The researcher has directly accepted a higher risk of a false positive in exchange for other benefits.

The corresponding increase in power occurs because power and alpha are positively related. **Power** equals 1 minus beta, where beta is the probability of a Type II error (failing to reject a false null hypothesis). When the rejection region expands (larger alpha), it becomes easier for a true effect to produce a test statistic that falls in the rejection region, thereby reducing beta and increasing power. In other words, the study becomes more sensitive to detecting real effects.

This tradeoff between Type I and Type II errors is not symmetrical in all research contexts. In some situations, the consequences of a Type I error are more severe (such as approving an ineffective treatment), and a conservative alpha is preferred. In other situations, the consequences of a Type II error are more concerning (such as missing a genuine safety hazard), and a more liberal alpha is warranted. The researcher's task is to balance these risks based on the practical and scientific context of the study.

For the EPPP, candidates must understand that alpha and power are directly related: increasing alpha increases both the Type I error rate and statistical power, while decreasing alpha reduces both. Exam questions often present a scenario where alpha is changed and ask candidates to identify all consequences, requiring them to recognize both effects simultaneously.

verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: "The sampling distribution shows normal distribution with mean of mu and variance of sigma-squared/n." From the formula SE = sigma / sqrt(n), the standard error of the mean decreases as the population standard deviation decreases and as the sample size increases.
old_anchor: The standard error of the mean decreases in magnitude as the population standard deviation decreases and the sample size increases.
testable_fact: The standard error of the mean (SE = sigma/√n) decreases as population standard deviation decreases and as sample size increases.
passage:
How precisely does a sample mean estimate the population mean? The answer depends on a statistic that captures the expected variability of sample means across repeated sampling, and understanding the factors that influence this statistic is essential for grasping the logic of inferential statistics.

The **standard error of the mean** decreases in magnitude as the **population standard deviation** decreases and the **sample size** increases. The standard error of the mean quantifies how much sample means would be expected to vary from sample to sample if the same study were repeated many times. A smaller standard error indicates that sample means cluster tightly around the population mean, providing more precise estimates.

Mathematically, the standard error of the mean equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size (SE = sigma / square root of N). This formula reveals the two factors that determine its magnitude. First, the population standard deviation (sigma) appears in the numerator. When the population is more variable, individual scores are more dispersed, and sample means drawn from that population will also be more dispersed. Reducing population variability directly reduces the standard error. Second, the sample size (N) appears in the denominator under the square root. As sample size increases, the denominator grows, and the standard error shrinks. Larger samples produce more stable and precise estimates because individual extreme scores are diluted by the greater number of observations.

The standard error of the mean is foundational to inferential statistics because it provides the basis for constructing **confidence intervals** and conducting **hypothesis tests**. Confidence intervals are constructed by taking the sample mean plus or minus a multiple of the standard error (the multiple determined by the desired confidence level and the relevant sampling distribution). Hypothesis tests use the standard error to standardize the difference between the sample mean and the hypothesized population mean, producing a test statistic (such as a z-score or t-score) that indicates how many standard errors the sample mean falls from the hypothesized value.

The standard error is conceptually linked to the **central limit theorem**, which states that the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. This theorem guarantees that the standard error accurately describes the spread of sampling distribution for sufficiently large samples.

For the EPPP, candidates should know the formula and the directional relationships: standard error decreases with larger samples and with smaller population variability. Exam questions may ask what happens to the standard error when sample size doubles, or they may present scenarios requiring candidates to predict how changes in population variability or sample size affect estimation precision.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: "The risk of mistakenly rejecting the null hypothesis (H_0) and thus of committing a Type I error, alpha, represents a policy: the maximum risk of a false rejection." Alpha and beta are inversely related: changing alpha from .01 to .05 increases the probability of a Type I error (false rejection of a true null hypothesis) and decreases the probability of a Type II error (failure to reject a false null hypothesis), thereby increasing statistical power.
old_anchor: Changing alpha from .01 to .05 increases the probability of making a Type I error when the null hypothesis is true and decreases the probability of making a Type II error when the null hypothesis is false.
testable_fact: Changing alpha from .01 to .05 increases the probability of a Type I error and decreases the probability of a Type II error, thereby increasing statistical power.
passage:
Adjusting the significance criterion has simultaneous consequences for two distinct types of inferential errors. Understanding these consequences requires recognizing that the two error types move in opposite directions when alpha changes, creating a fundamental tradeoff that researchers must navigate.

Changing alpha from .01 to .05 **increases the probability of making a Type I error** when the null hypothesis is true and **decreases the probability of making a Type II error** when the null hypothesis is false. This inverse relationship is one of the most important principles in inferential statistics and reflects the inherent tension between sensitivity and specificity in hypothesis testing.

A **Type I error** occurs when the researcher rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true, concluding that an effect exists when it does not. The probability of a Type I error is directly equal to alpha. When alpha is .01, there is a 1% chance of this error; when alpha is raised to .05, there is a 5% chance. The researcher has expanded the rejection region of the sampling distribution, making it easier for any sample result, including one from a population where the null is true, to fall in the rejection zone.

A **Type II error** (symbolized as beta) occurs when the researcher fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, missing a real effect. When alpha increases from .01 to .05, the expanded rejection region means that more true effects will produce test statistics that reach the significance threshold. This reduces the probability of failing to detect a real effect, thereby decreasing beta. Since **statistical power** equals 1 minus beta, decreasing beta simultaneously increases power.

The inverse relationship between Type I and Type II errors means that researchers cannot minimize both simultaneously by adjusting alpha alone. Making alpha more stringent (smaller) protects against false positives but increases the risk of false negatives. Making alpha more lenient (larger) reduces the risk of false negatives but increases the risk of false positives. The only way to reduce both error types simultaneously is to increase sample size, which improves power without affecting the nominal alpha level.

For the EPPP, candidates must understand the directional effects of changing alpha on both error types. A common exam question describes an alpha change and asks candidates to identify the consequences for Type I error, Type II error, and power. The correct answer recognizes that when alpha increases, Type I error probability increases, Type II error probability decreases, and power increases. All three consequences follow from the same change in the rejection region.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Kim, T.K. (2015). T test as a parametric statistic. Korean Journal of Anesthesiology, 68(6), 540-546: "When samples are drawn from population N (mu, sigma-squared) with a sample size of n, the distribution of the sample mean should be a normal distribution N (mu, sigma-squared/n)." The standard error of the mean (SE = sigma / sqrt(n)) increases as the population standard deviation increases and as the sample size decreases.
old_anchor: The size of the standard error of the mean increases as the population standard deviation increases and the sample size decreases.
testable_fact: The standard error of the mean increases as population standard deviation increases and as sample size decreases.
passage:
How accurately can a sample represent its population? The precision of a sample mean as an estimate of the population mean depends on a statistic that is influenced by two key factors, and understanding these factors is critical for designing studies with adequate precision and for interpreting inferential test results.

The size of the **standard error of the mean** increases as the **population standard deviation** increases and the **sample size** decreases. The standard error of the mean is a measure of how much variability is expected among sample means across repeated sampling from the same population. When the standard error is large, sample means tend to scatter widely around the population mean, yielding less precise estimates. When it is small, sample means cluster tightly, providing more accurate estimates.

The formula for the standard error of the mean is SE = sigma / square root of N, where sigma is the population standard deviation and N is the sample size. This formula reveals the directional influence of each factor. When the population standard deviation (sigma) increases, the numerator grows, producing a larger standard error. A more variable population generates more variable samples, making any single sample mean a less reliable estimate. When the sample size (N) decreases, the denominator shrinks, also producing a larger standard error. Smaller samples provide fewer data points to average, making the sample mean more susceptible to the influence of extreme scores.

These relationships have direct practical implications for research design. Researchers seeking precise population estimates can either select populations (or subpopulations) with less variability or collect larger samples. In many cases, the population standard deviation is beyond the researcher's control, making sample size the primary lever for improving precision. The relationship between sample size and standard error is not linear but follows a square root function: to halve the standard error, the researcher must quadruple the sample size.

The standard error also plays a central role in confidence interval construction. A 95% confidence interval for the mean is calculated as the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 times the standard error (assuming a large sample or known population variance). A larger standard error produces a wider confidence interval, reflecting greater uncertainty about the population mean.

For the EPPP, candidates should understand both the formula and the directional relationships. Exam questions may present a scenario where population variability increases or sample size decreases and ask how the standard error is affected. The correct answer is that both changes increase the standard error, reducing the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean.

chapter_title: Choosing the Right Test: t-Tests, ANOVA, and Post-Hoc Comparisons
verbatim_anchor: Cohen, J. (1992). A power primer. Psychological Bulletin, 112(1), 155-159: Cohen's effect size index d = (m_A - m_B) / sigma. Because d is inversely related to sigma, greater population variability (heterogeneity) inflates sigma, shrinks d, and thereby reduces statistical power rather than increasing it.
old_anchor: Statistical power is increased by all factors except population heterogeneity on the dependent variable.
testable_fact: Greater population heterogeneity (variability) on the dependent variable reduces statistical power by inflating the population standard deviation and thereby shrinking Cohen's d effect size.
passage:
A researcher planning a study on the effects of exercise on cognitive performance wants to maximize her statistical power -- the probability of detecting a real effect. She reviews the factors known to influence power and finds that most of them can be optimized through good study design. However, one factor actually decreases power, and she needs to understand which one it is.

**Statistical power** is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis -- that is, detecting a real effect when one exists. Power = 1 - beta, where beta is the probability of a Type II error. Researchers aim for power of at least .80, meaning an 80% chance of detecting a true effect. Power is increased by several factors, but **population heterogeneity** on the dependent variable is **not** among them -- in fact, increased variability generally reduces power.

The factors that increase power include: **larger sample size** (more participants provide more information and reduce the standard error), **larger effect size** (bigger differences or stronger associations are easier to detect), **higher alpha level** (a more lenient significance criterion widens the rejection region), **one-tailed rather than two-tailed tests** (concentrating the rejection region in one direction increases power for effects in that direction), and **more reliable measures** (less measurement error reduces noise and increases the signal-to-noise ratio).

Population heterogeneity -- greater variability among individuals on the dependent variable -- works against power. When there is more variability in the population, the within-group error variance is larger, which inflates the denominator of test statistics like the t-value or F-ratio. A larger denominator produces a smaller test statistic, making it harder to reach statistical significance. In practical terms, the more variable the population, the harder it is to detect a treatment effect against the background noise of individual differences.

Researchers can partially offset the negative effect of population heterogeneity through study design choices. Using a within-subjects design (where each participant serves as their own control) removes between-subject variability from the error term. Restricting the sample to a more homogeneous population reduces variability but may limit external validity. Using ANCOVA to statistically control for sources of extraneous variability can also increase power.

The distinction between controllable and uncontrollable factors is important. Researchers can choose their sample size, alpha level, and measurement instruments. They can select appropriate statistical tests and research designs. But they typically cannot control the population's inherent variability on the dependent variable, making it a factor that influences power but cannot be directly optimized.

On the EPPP, power questions typically present a list of factors and ask which one does not increase power, or which factor is related to power in a specific direction. Population heterogeneity (increased variability) is the factor that reduces rather than increases power. A common trap is stating that a larger alpha decreases power -- in fact, a more lenient alpha increases power at the cost of a higher Type I error rate.

chapter_title: Testing Ideas: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Testing, and Statistical Power
verbatim_anchor: Kruschke, J.K. (2010). Bayesian data analysis. Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Cognitive Science, 1(5), 658-676: "Bayesian analysis uses Bayes' rule to combine the prior distribution with the likelihood function, yielding the posterior distribution." Bayes' theorem updates the prior probability distribution with observed data (the likelihood function) to produce a posterior (updated) probability distribution for the parameter of interest.
old_anchor: Bayes' theorem combines the prior probability distribution and the likelihood function to obtain a posterior (updated) probability distribution for the parameter.
testable_fact: Bayes' theorem combines a prior probability distribution with the likelihood function derived from observed data to produce a posterior (updated) probability distribution for the parameter of interest.
passage:
A clinical researcher wants to estimate the probability that a patient has a particular condition, given a positive test result. She knows the condition's base rate in the population (the prior probability) and the test's sensitivity and specificity (which determine the likelihood of the data). Rather than relying on the test result alone, she wants to update the prior probability in light of the new evidence. The mathematical framework for this updating process is Bayes' theorem.

**Bayes' theorem** provides a formal method for combining the **prior probability distribution** (what was known or believed before new data were collected) with the **likelihood function** (the probability of the observed data given each possible parameter value) to obtain a **posterior probability distribution** (the updated belief after incorporating the new data). In formula form: P(H|D) = P(D|H) times P(H) / P(D), where H is the hypothesis and D is the observed data.

In the clinical example, the prior probability is the base rate of the condition in the population. The likelihood function incorporates the test's sensitivity (probability of a positive result given the condition is present) and specificity (probability of a negative result given the condition is absent). The posterior probability is the updated probability that the patient has the condition given the positive test result. This posterior probability is often substantially different from both the raw base rate and the test's apparent accuracy, especially when the condition is rare.

Bayesian reasoning contrasts with traditional **frequentist** statistical inference in several important ways. Frequentist methods (t-tests, ANOVA, significance testing) evaluate the probability of the data given the null hypothesis -- P(D|H0). Bayesian methods directly evaluate the probability of the hypothesis given the data -- P(H|D), which is typically the question researchers actually want to answer. Frequentist methods use fixed parameters and random data; Bayesian methods treat parameters as having probability distributions that are updated by data.

A key practical insight from Bayesian reasoning is the profound effect of base rates on posterior probabilities. Even a highly accurate test (high sensitivity and specificity) will produce a large proportion of false positives when the base rate of the condition is very low. This is because the small number of true positives is overwhelmed by the false positives generated from the much larger group of non-affected individuals. Ignoring base rates -- a common reasoning error called the **base rate fallacy** -- leads to substantially overestimating the probability that a positive test result represents a true case.

On the EPPP, Bayes' theorem questions ask about updating probabilities using prior information and new data. The key concept is combining prior probability with likelihood to obtain posterior probability. A common trap is ignoring the base rate when interpreting test results. Remember: the posterior probability depends critically on both the test's accuracy and the prior probability of the condition.

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Slack, M.K. & Draugalis, J.R. (2001). Establishing the internal and external validity of experimental studies. American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy, 58(22), 2173-2181: "History becomes a threat when other factors external to the subjects (in addition to the treatment variable) occur by virtue of the passage of time." In a study examining the effects of an anti-drug program on middle school students' attitudes toward drug use, history would be the biggest threat to internal validity, as external events during the study period (e.g., media campaigns, community events) may systematically affect the students' attitudes independent of the program.
old_anchor: The biggest threat to the internal validity of Dr. Osprey's study on the effects of an anti-drug program on middle school students' attitudes toward drug use is history, as external events during the study period may have systematically affected the students' attitudes.
testable_fact: History is a threat to internal validity when external events occurring during a study's timeframe, independent of the treatment, may systematically affect the dependent variable.
passage:
Dr. Osprey is studying the impact of an anti-drug educational program on middle school students' attitudes toward drug use. She uses a one-group pretest-posttest design, measuring attitudes before and after the eight-week program. Although post-test attitudes are significantly more anti-drug, a major drug-related news event occurred during the same period. This external event creates an alternative explanation for the observed change, threatening the study's ability to establish causation.

The biggest threat to the **internal validity** of this study is **history**. The history threat occurs when events external to the study happen between the pretest and posttest and plausibly affect the dependent variable. In Dr. Osprey's study, the drug-related news event could have shifted students' attitudes independently of the educational program, making it impossible to determine whether the observed attitude change was caused by the program, the news event, or both.

**Internal validity** is the extent to which a study can demonstrate a causal relationship between the independent variable and the dependent variable. When threats to internal validity are present, alternative explanations for the observed results exist, and the causal inference is weakened. The one-group pretest-posttest design is particularly vulnerable to threats like history because there is no control group to distinguish treatment effects from effects of extraneous events.

Campbell and Stanley's classic taxonomy identifies several threats to internal validity beyond history. **Maturation** involves biological or psychological changes within participants over time (aging, fatigue, practice). **Testing** involves the pretest influencing posttest responses. **Instrumentation** involves changes in the measurement device or scoring criteria. **Statistical regression** affects extreme scorers who tend to regress toward the mean on retesting. **Selection** involves pre-existing differences between groups in multi-group designs. **Attrition** (mortality) involves differential dropout between groups.

History differs from these other threats in that it specifically involves external events occurring during the study period. The threat increases with longer study durations because more events have the opportunity to occur. In Dr. Osprey's eight-week study, many external events could influence students' attitudes -- media coverage, family conversations, school assemblies, or peer interactions unrelated to the program.

The most effective control for history is the inclusion of a control group. In a randomized pretest-posttest control group design, both groups experience the same external events, so any difference in attitude change between groups can be attributed to the treatment rather than to history.

On the EPPP, history threat questions present a pre-post design with a concurrent external event. The key identifier is an outside event during the study period. A common trap is maturation, which involves internal participant changes, or testing, which involves the pretest influencing the posttest. History is always about external events.

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Brooks, J.L. (2012). Counterbalancing for serial order carryover effects in experimental condition orders. Psychological Methods, 17(4), 600-614: "Each condition appears in each serial position equally often." A Latin square ensures each treatment appears in every ordinal position an equal number of times, controlling for order and sequence effects.
old_anchor: The Latin square is a type of counterbalanced design that ensures each level of the independent variable appears an equal number of times in each ordinal position.
testable_fact: A Latin square is a counterbalanced design ensuring each level of the independent variable appears equally often in each ordinal position, controlling for order and sequence effects.
passage:
A researcher studying the effects of three different teaching methods wants to counterbalance the order in which participants experience each condition. With three conditions and limited resources, she needs a systematic approach that ensures each condition appears equally often in each ordinal position without requiring every possible order. The Latin square design provides exactly this structure.

The **Latin square** is a type of **counterbalanced design** that ensures each level of the independent variable appears an equal number of times in **each ordinal position** across the sequence of conditions. In a Latin square with three conditions (A, B, C), three different orders are created, such that each condition appears once in the first position, once in the second, and once in the third. For example: Order 1 = A, B, C; Order 2 = B, C, A; Order 3 = C, A, B. Participants are then divided into three groups, each receiving one of these orders.

The Latin square controls for **order effects** (also called **sequence effects** or **carryover effects**) that arise in within-subjects designs. When every participant experiences all conditions, the order in which conditions are presented can influence performance. Participants may improve due to practice, deteriorate due to fatigue, or carry the effects of one condition into the next. By counterbalancing the order, the Latin square distributes these order effects evenly across conditions, preventing them from confounding the treatment effects.

The key advantage of the Latin square over complete counterbalancing is efficiency. Complete counterbalancing requires all possible orderings of conditions (k! orders, where k is the number of conditions). For three conditions, that is 6 orders; for four conditions, 24 orders; for five conditions, 120 orders. The Latin square requires only k orders, making it practical for studies with many conditions or limited participants. However, this efficiency comes at a cost: the Latin square controls for the position of each condition in the sequence but does not control for every possible pairwise carryover effect.

The Latin square is distinct from other counterbalancing strategies. A **randomized block design** assigns participants to blocks based on a relevant characteristic. A **crossover design** is a two-condition Latin square. **Balanced Latin squares** add the additional constraint that each condition follows every other condition equally often, providing better control over first-order carryover effects.

On the EPPP, Latin square questions describe a within-subjects design with multiple conditions and ask about the counterbalancing method used. The defining feature is that each condition appears in each ordinal position an equal number of times. A common trap is confusing the Latin square with complete counterbalancing (all possible orders) or with random assignment to conditions (which characterizes between-subjects designs).

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Braver, M.W. & Braver, S.L. (1988). Statistical treatment of the Solomon four-group design. Psychological Bulletin, 104(1), 150-154: The design is "the only one of the three able to assess the presence of pretest sensitization" because it includes groups without pretesting. Controls for pretest sensitization by including pretested and non-pretested versions of both treatment and control groups.
old_anchor: The Solomon four-group design is used to control for the threat to internal validity known as pretest sensitization.
testable_fact: The Solomon four-group design controls for pretest sensitization by including both pretested and non-pretested versions of treatment and control groups.
passage:
A researcher is concerned that administering a pretest might sensitize participants to the purpose of her study, causing them to respond differently on the posttest than they would have without the pretest. She needs a research design that can detect whether the pretest itself is influencing the results, while still maintaining a rigorous experimental framework.

The **Solomon four-group design** is used to control for the threat to internal validity known as **pretest sensitization** (also called **testing effects**). This design extends the standard pretest-posttest control group design by adding two additional groups that do not receive a pretest, creating a total of four groups: (1) pretest, treatment, posttest; (2) pretest, no treatment, posttest; (3) no pretest, treatment, posttest; (4) no pretest, no treatment, posttest.

Pretest sensitization occurs when the act of taking a pretest **changes** how participants respond to the treatment or to the posttest. For example, a pretest measuring racial attitudes might make participants more aware of their biases, causing them to respond differently to a subsequent diversity training program than they would have without the pretest. The pretest does not just measure the dependent variable -- it actively influences it. This creates a confound: observed posttest differences might reflect the treatment effect, the pretest sensitization effect, or their interaction.

The Solomon design detects pretest sensitization by comparing groups that received the pretest with groups that did not. If the treatment effect is present only in the pretested groups (Group 1 vs. Group 2) but not in the non-pretested groups (Group 3 vs. Group 4), pretest sensitization is likely interacting with the treatment. If the treatment effect is consistent across pretested and non-pretested groups, pretest sensitization is not a significant confound.

The design also provides information about the main effect of pretesting (comparing pretested vs. non-pretested groups) and the main effect of treatment (comparing treated vs. untreated groups). This rich set of comparisons makes the Solomon four-group design the most internally valid experimental design available, as it controls for history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, and regression simultaneously.

The primary disadvantage is practical: the Solomon design requires four groups, doubling the sample size needed compared to a simple two-group design. This makes it expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to implement in settings with limited participant availability.

On the EPPP, Solomon four-group design questions typically describe a concern about pretest sensitization and ask which design addresses it. The defining feature is the addition of two non-pretested groups. A common trap is selecting the pretest-posttest control group design, which controls for history and maturation but cannot detect pretest sensitization because all groups receive the pretest.

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Day, S.J. & Altman, D.G. (2000). Blinding in clinical trials and other studies. BMJ, 321(7259), 504: "In a double blind trial neither the patient nor the caregivers are aware of the treatment assignment." Controls for both participant expectancy effects and experimenter bias.
old_anchor: The double-blind technique reduces experimenter expectancy when designing a research study.
testable_fact: The double-blind technique controls for both participant expectancy effects and experimenter bias by keeping both participants and caregivers unaware of treatment assignment.
passage:
How can researchers prevent their own expectations from unconsciously influencing the outcomes of a study? When experimenters know which participants are in the treatment group and which are in the control group, this knowledge can subtly shape how they interact with participants, administer procedures, or record data. A specific research design technique addresses this threat directly.

The **double-blind technique** reduces **experimenter expectancy** (also known as experimenter bias or the Rosenthal effect) when designing a research study. In a double-blind design, neither the participants nor the researchers who interact with them and collect data know which condition each participant has been assigned to. By keeping both parties blind to group assignment, the design eliminates the possibility that the experimenter's knowledge of a participant's condition will influence how the participant is treated, observed, or evaluated.

**Experimenter expectancy** refers to the tendency for researchers' hypotheses or expectations about the study outcome to influence the results in the direction of those expectations. Robert Rosenthal's research demonstrated that experimenters who expected certain results from their subjects obtained those results more often than experimenters who held different expectations, even when the procedures were ostensibly standardized. The mechanism operates through subtle, often unconscious channels: differential tone of voice, facial expressions, body language, selective attention to certain behaviors, or biased recording of ambiguous data.

In a double-blind design, a third party (such as a pharmacist or project coordinator) handles the randomization and condition assignments, coding them in a way that conceals the information from both the experimenter and the participant until data collection is complete. This arrangement differs from a **single-blind design**, in which only the participants are kept unaware of their condition assignment while the experimenters know.

The double-blind technique also controls for **demand characteristics**, which are cues in the experimental setting that communicate to participants what behavior is expected of them. When participants do not know their group assignment, they cannot adjust their behavior to confirm or disconfirm the hypothesis.

For the EPPP, candidates should recognize that the double-blind design is the primary method for controlling experimenter expectancy effects. Exam questions may describe a study where the researcher's behavior could influence results and ask which technique would address this threat. The answer is the double-blind procedure, and candidates should distinguish it from random assignment (which controls for selection bias), counterbalancing (which controls for order effects), and single-blind designs (which control only participant expectations).

chapter_title: Threats from Within and Without: Research Design and Validity
verbatim_anchor: Barnett, A.G. et al. (2005). Regression to the mean: What it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology, 34(1), 215-220: "Relatively high (or relatively low) observations are likely to be followed by less extreme ones nearer the subject's true mean." When participants are selected for a study because they obtained extreme scores (e.g., high test anxiety), statistical regression is the biggest threat to internal validity because their scores will naturally move toward the mean on retesting, regardless of treatment.
old_anchor: The biggest threat to the internal validity of a study evaluating the effectiveness of a stress reduction technique for alleviating test anxiety is statistical regression.
testable_fact: When participants are selected based on extreme scores, statistical regression is the primary threat to internal validity because scores naturally move toward the mean on retesting.
passage:
When participants are selected for a study because they scored at the extreme end of a distribution, a predictable statistical artifact can masquerade as a treatment effect. Identifying this threat requires understanding how extreme scores behave when measured a second time, regardless of any intervention.

The biggest threat to the internal validity of a study evaluating the effectiveness of a stress reduction technique for alleviating test anxiety is **statistical regression** (also called regression to the mean). When participants are selected because they obtained extreme scores on a pretest, their scores on a subsequent posttest will tend to move toward the mean of the distribution, not because of the treatment but because of the natural unreliability of measurement. This regression effect can create the illusion that the intervention caused the improvement.

**Statistical regression** occurs because extreme scores contain a disproportionate amount of measurement error. Any test score is a composite of the individual's true score and random error. Individuals who score extremely high on a pretest likely benefited from positive measurement error (their true scores are probably somewhat lower), while individuals who score extremely low likely suffered from negative measurement error (their true scores are probably somewhat higher). On retesting, the error component is expected to be random and independent of the first testing, so the scores migrate toward the population mean.

In the context of this study, participants were presumably selected because they reported extremely high levels of test anxiety on a pretest measure. After receiving the stress reduction technique, their posttest anxiety scores would likely decrease. While this decrease might be partly attributable to the treatment, it is confounded by statistical regression: even without any treatment, the extreme pretest scores would be expected to decline on retesting. Without a control group of equally extreme scorers who do not receive the treatment, it is impossible to separate the treatment effect from regression to the mean.

This threat is particularly insidious because it operates in the same direction as the expected treatment effect. The treatment is designed to reduce anxiety, and regression also reduces extreme anxiety scores.
