chapter_title: When Chromosomes Carry Consequences: Prenatal Development, Genetic Disorders, and Environmental Threats
verbatim_anchor: Dollard, Grosse, & Ross (2007): "CMV is the most common infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss in infants."
old_anchor: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) during prenatal development is most likely to cause sensorineural hearing loss in infants.
testable_fact: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss in infants.
passage:
An audiologist evaluates a two-year-old who has failed a hearing screening. Testing reveals significant sensorineural hearing loss in both ears. The child's medical records indicate that her mother tested positive for cytomegalovirus during pregnancy, and the infant was diagnosed with congenital CMV at birth. The audiologist recognizes this as one of the most common infectious causes of childhood hearing impairment.

**Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV)** infection during prenatal development is **most likely to cause sensorineural hearing loss** in affected infants. CMV is a member of the herpes virus family and is one of the most common congenital infections worldwide, affecting approximately 0.5-1% of all live births in developed countries. While many infants with congenital CMV are asymptomatic at birth, the virus can cause serious and lasting damage to the developing fetus, with **sensorineural hearing loss** being the single most common long-term consequence.

**Sensorineural hearing loss** involves damage to the inner ear (specifically the cochlea) or the auditory nerve, resulting in reduced ability to detect and process sound. Unlike conductive hearing loss (which involves problems with the outer or middle ear and is often treatable), sensorineural hearing loss is typically permanent. In congenital CMV, the virus directly infects and damages the sensory hair cells of the cochlea and the stria vascularis (the structure that maintains the electrochemical environment of the inner ear), leading to hearing impairment that may be present at birth or may develop progressively during the first years of life.

A particularly challenging feature of CMV-related hearing loss is its **delayed and progressive** nature. Some infants with congenital CMV pass their newborn hearing screening but develop hearing loss later in infancy or early childhood, sometimes with a fluctuating course. This means that a single hearing screening at birth is insufficient to detect all cases of CMV-related hearing impairment, and ongoing audiological monitoring is recommended for infants known to have congenital CMV.

The severity of CMV-related hearing loss ranges from mild to profound and may affect one ear (unilateral) or both ears (bilateral). Approximately 10-15% of infants with congenital CMV who are symptomatic at birth develop sensorineural hearing loss, and approximately 10-15% of those who are asymptomatic at birth also develop hearing loss, making CMV the leading nongenetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children.

Congenital CMV can also cause other developmental problems in addition to hearing loss, including vision impairment, intellectual disability, seizures, and motor deficits. However, hearing loss is by far the most common sequel and may occur in isolation, without other obvious signs of congenital infection. This makes CMV-related hearing loss particularly important for developmental screening, as the hearing impairment can significantly affect language acquisition, academic achievement, and social development if not identified and addressed early.

Early identification of CMV-related hearing loss allows for timely intervention with hearing aids, cochlear implants, and speech-language therapy, which can substantially improve language outcomes. Universal newborn CMV screening has been proposed as a public health measure to improve early detection, though it is not yet standard practice in most jurisdictions.

For the EPPP, the key fact is that congenital CMV is most likely to cause sensorineural hearing loss. Questions may present a prenatal infection scenario and ask which developmental outcome is most associated with CMV. The common trap is selecting intellectual disability or vision impairmentâ€”while CMV can cause these, hearing loss is the most common and characteristic sequel.

verbatim_anchor: Cassidy & Driscoll (2009): "Prader-Willi syndrome — characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, small hands/feet, and obesity — results from a chromosomal deletion on paternal chromosome 15."
old_anchor: Prader-Willi syndrome, characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, small hands and feet, and obesity, is the only disorder in the list caused by a chromosomal deletion.
testable_fact: Prader-Willi syndrome, characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, small hands and feet, and obesity, results from a chromosomal deletion on paternal chromosome 15.
passage:
A pediatrician evaluates a three-year-old boy who presents with intellectual disability, unusually short stature, small hands and feet, and a pattern of insatiable appetite and food-seeking behavior that has led to rapid weight gain. The child's parents describe constant battles over food access and report that the boy will eat anything available, including items from the garbage. Genetic testing reveals a deletion on chromosome 15. The pediatrician recognizes this presentation as a classic case of a specific genetic syndrome.

**Prader-Willi syndrome** is a genetic condition characterized by **intellectual disability, short stature, small hands and feet, and obesity** (due to an insatiable appetite called hyperphagia). It is the **only disorder** among commonly tested genetic conditions on the EPPP that is caused by a **chromosomal deletion**â€”specifically, a deletion of a segment on **chromosome 15**.

The genetics of Prader-Willi syndrome involve a phenomenon called **genomic imprinting**, which means that the expression of certain genes depends on which parent contributed them. Prader-Willi syndrome most commonly results from the deletion of a specific region on the **paternal** copy of chromosome 15 (the copy inherited from the father). The corresponding region on the maternal copy of chromosome 15 is normally silenced through imprinting, so when the paternal copy is deleted, there is no functional copy of the affected genes. This absence of gene expression produces the syndrome's characteristic features.

The clinical presentation of Prader-Willi syndrome changes across development. In infancy, the most prominent features are **hypotonia** (low muscle tone), **feeding difficulties**, and a weak cry. Paradoxically, the insatiable appetite that becomes the defining feature of the syndrome is not present in infancyâ€”instead, infants with Prader-Willi often have difficulty feeding and may require special assistance to obtain adequate nutrition. The switch from feeding difficulty to hyperphagia typically occurs between ages 2 and 6.

**Hyperphagia** is the most challenging management issue in Prader-Willi syndrome. The hypothalamic dysfunction that underlies the condition impairs the satiety signaling system, so individuals with Prader-Willi rarely feel full. Without strict environmental controls on food access, individuals with the syndrome will eat continuously and can develop life-threatening obesity. Management requires locked food storage, constant supervision around food, and structured meal plans.

Other features of Prader-Willi syndrome include **intellectual disability** (typically in the mild to moderate range, with IQ scores averaging 60-70), **behavioral problems** (including temper tantrums, stubbornness, and compulsive behaviors), **hypogonadism** (incomplete sexual development due to reduced production of sex hormones), **sleep disturbances** (including excessive daytime sleepiness), and a characteristic behavioral profile that includes skin-picking and difficulty with transitions.

Prader-Willi syndrome should be distinguished from other genetic conditions tested on the EPPP. **Angelman syndrome** also involves chromosome 15 but results from a deletion on the maternal (not paternal) copy and presents with a very different phenotype: severe intellectual disability, absent speech, a happy demeanor with frequent laughter, and seizures. **Down syndrome** involves an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy), not a deletion. **Klinefelter syndrome** involves an extra X chromosome in males.

For the EPPP, the key facts are that Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by a chromosomal deletion (on paternal chromosome 15) and is characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, small hands and feet, and obesity due to hyperphagia. The most common trap is confusing Prader-Willi with Angelman syndromeâ€”both involve chromosome 15, but they result from deletions on different parental copies and have very different clinical presentations.

verbatim_anchor: Amir et al. (1999): "Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene located on the X chromosome. It primarily affects females because affected males rarely survive to birth." Characterized by normal early development followed by regression in motor and language skills, stereotypic hand movements, and intellectual disability.
old_anchor: Rett syndrome primarily affects females and is caused by a mutation in an X-linked gene.
testable_fact: Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome, primarily affecting females, and is characterized by normal early development followed by regression in motor and language skills and stereotypic hand movements.
passage:
A mother brings her 18-month-old daughter to the pediatrician, alarmed by changes she has noticed over the past few months. Her daughter had been developing normallyâ€”babbling, reaching for toys, beginning to walkâ€”but has recently lost the ability to use her hands purposefully, has stopped babbling, has become less socially engaged, and has developed repetitive hand-wringing movements. The regression is heartbreaking and confusing. The pediatrician, recognizing the pattern of early normal development followed by regression, orders genetic testing that confirms the diagnosis.

**Rett syndrome** is a neurodevelopmental condition that **primarily affects females** and is caused by a **mutation in an X-linked gene**â€”specifically, the **MECP2 gene** located on the X chromosome. It is one of the few genetic conditions that demonstrates both X-linked inheritance and a striking sex difference in prevalence, and understanding why it predominantly affects females requires knowledge of basic genetic principles.

Rett syndrome occurs almost exclusively in females because the MECP2 gene is located on the X chromosome. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), so a female with a MECP2 mutation on one X chromosome still has a normal copy of the gene on her other X chromosome. This normal copy provides enough MECP2 protein for survival, though not enough to prevent the neurological symptoms of the syndrome. Males have only one X chromosome (XY), and a MECP2 mutation on that single X chromosome typically results in such severe loss of MECP2 function that the condition is lethal in utero or in early infancy. This is why Rett syndrome is seen predominantly in girls.

The clinical course of Rett syndrome follows a characteristic pattern. Development appears normal for the first **6 to 18 months** of life. Then, a period of **regression** begins, during which the child loses previously acquired skills, including purposeful hand use and spoken language. The hallmark feature of Rett syndrome is the development of **stereotypic hand movements**â€”most commonly hand-wringing, hand-washing, or hand-squeezing movements that replace purposeful hand use. Other features include gait abnormalities, breathing irregularities (including hyperventilation and breath-holding), seizures, scoliosis, and slowed head growth (acquired microcephaly).

After the regression period, the condition typically stabilizes, and some individuals may show partial recovery of certain skills. However, Rett syndrome is a lifelong condition with significant intellectual disability and motor impairment. Most affected individuals require full-time care and support throughout their lives.

Rett syndrome should be distinguished from other conditions that involve early regression. **Autism spectrum disorder** can also involve regression of social and language skills, but the characteristic hand stereotypies, breathing abnormalities, and specific genetic basis of Rett syndrome differentiate the two conditions. Prior to the publication of the DSM-5, Rett syndrome was classified as a pervasive developmental disorder alongside autism, but it was removed from this category in the DSM-5 because its genetic basis was identified, and it is now classified as a distinct genetic condition.

The MECP2 protein plays a critical role in brain development and function, regulating the expression of many other genes. The loss or dysfunction of MECP2 leads to widespread abnormalities in neuronal maturation, synapse formation, and neurotransmitter systems, which accounts for the broad range of neurological symptoms.

For the EPPP, the key facts are that Rett syndrome primarily affects females, is caused by a mutation in an X-linked gene (MECP2), and is characterized by a period of normal development followed by regression with loss of hand skills and development of hand stereotypies. A common trap is stating that Rett syndrome affects males equally or confusing it with Angelman syndrome or autism.

verbatim_anchor: Tyson, Parikh, Langer, Green, & Higgins (2008) / Berk (2018): "The age of viability — the earliest point at which the fetus can survive outside the womb — is generally considered to be between 22 and 26 weeks of gestation." Survival depends on lung maturity and medical intervention; outcomes improve substantially with each additional week of gestation.
old_anchor: The earliest age at which a baby can survive outside the womb is referred to as the age of viability, which is between 22 and 26 weeks after conception.
testable_fact: The age of viability — the earliest point at which a fetus can survive outside the womb — is generally between 22 and 26 weeks of gestation, with survival improving substantially with each additional week.
passage:
A couple facing an extremely premature delivery at 23 weeks sits down with a neonatologist to discuss what to expect. The doctor explains that their baby is at the very edge of the developmental threshold at which survival outside the womb becomes possible. The lungs and brain have reached a level of maturation that makes life-sustaining medical intervention potentially effective, but the risks remain extraordinarily high. The couple wants to understand what makes this particular moment in fetal development so critical.

The **age of viability** is defined as the **earliest age at which a baby can survive outside the womb**, and it is generally placed **between 22 and 26 weeks after conception**. This developmental window represents the point at which the fetus's vital organ systemsâ€”most critically the respiratory and neurological systemsâ€”have matured to a degree that life can be sustained with intensive medical support.

The respiratory system is the primary determinant of viability because the ability to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide is essential for independent life. The fetal lungs undergo several stages of development. During the **canalicular stage** (approximately 16-26 weeks), the airways branch further and the future gas-exchanging structures begin to form. During the **saccular stage** (approximately 24-38 weeks), primitive air sacs develop, and **type II alveolar cells** begin producing **surfactant**â€”a critical substance that reduces surface tension within the air sacs and prevents them from collapsing during exhalation. Without adequate surfactant, the lungs cannot maintain inflation, and the infant develops **respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)**, which was historically the leading cause of death in premature infants.

The introduction of **exogenous surfactant therapy** in the 1990s was a breakthrough in neonatal medicine that significantly improved survival rates at the edge of viability. Additional advancesâ€”including **antenatal corticosteroids** (given to the mother before delivery to accelerate fetal lung maturation), improved mechanical ventilation techniques, and specialized neonatal intensive careâ€”have collectively pushed the practical limits of viability earlier than would be possible based on natural lung development alone.

The neurological system also places constraints on viability. Before 22-24 weeks, the brain's cortical structures and neural networks have not matured sufficiently to support the coordinated physiological functions necessary for life, even with respiratory support. The brainstem centers that control breathing, heart rate, temperature regulation, and feeding reflexes are still developing, and their immaturity contributes to the instability and complications seen in extremely premature infants.

Outcomes at the edge of viability remain highly variable and depend on multiple factors. Gestational age is the strongest predictor, but birth weight, sex (female infants have slightly better outcomes), singleton versus multiple birth, and access to a Level III or IV neonatal intensive care unit all influence survival and long-term outcomes. At 22 weeks, survival is possible but uncommon, and survivors face very high rates of severe impairment. By 26 weeks, the majority of infants survive with modern neonatal care, and the rates of severe disability are substantially lower.

The age of viability is not a fixed boundary but a gradient of increasing probability of survival and decreasing probability of severe complications. It has shifted earlier over the past several decades with advances in neonatal medicine, but a biological floor exists below which organ systems are simply too immature to sustain life regardless of medical intervention.

For the EPPP, candidates should know that the age of viability falls between 22 and 26 weeks, that it is primarily determined by lung maturation and surfactant production, and that it represents a gradient rather than a sharp cutoff. The common trap is confusing weeks after conception with trimester boundaries or selecting a single specific week as the definitive age of viability.

verbatim_anchor: Cassidy & Driscoll (2009): "Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of genes on the paternally inherited chromosome 15q11-q13 region, most commonly due to a deletion." Angelman syndrome results from loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene in the same 15q11-q13 region. Both disorders exemplify genomic imprinting, where expression depends on the parent of origin.
old_anchor: Prader-Willi syndrome is most often the result of the deletion of a segment on paternal chromosome 15, while Angelman syndrome is usually the result of the deletion of a segment on maternal chromosome 15.
testable_fact: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function in the paternally inherited chromosome 15q11-q13 region, while Angelman syndrome results from loss of function in the maternally inherited region, exemplifying genomic imprinting.
passage:
A genetics instructor presents two case studies to her class. Case A is a boy with intellectual disability, short stature, small hands and feet, and severe obesity from constant food-seeking. Case B is a girl with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, frequent laughter, and seizures. Both conditions, the instructor explains, involve a deletion on chromosome 15â€”but the parent of origin of the affected chromosome is different, and this difference produces two strikingly different syndromes.

**Prader-Willi syndrome** is most often the result of the **deletion of a segment on paternal chromosome 15** (the copy inherited from the father), while **Angelman syndrome** is usually the result of the **deletion of a segment on maternal chromosome 15** (the copy inherited from the mother). This remarkable findingâ€”that the same chromosomal deletion produces entirely different syndromes depending on which parent contributed the affected chromosomeâ€”is explained by the phenomenon of **genomic imprinting**.

**Genomic imprinting** is an epigenetic process in which certain genes are expressed from only one parental copy while the other parental copy is silenced. For the genes in the critical region of chromosome 15 involved in Prader-Willi syndrome, the maternal copy is normally imprinted (silenced), and only the paternal copy is expressed. If the paternal copy is deleted, there is no active copy of these genes, and Prader-Willi syndrome results. For the genes in the nearby region involved in Angelman syndrome, the paternal copy is normally imprinted, and only the maternal copy is expressed. If the maternal copy is deleted, Angelman syndrome results.

The clinical presentations of the two syndromes are markedly different despite involving the same chromosome. **Prader-Willi syndrome** features intellectual disability (usually mild to moderate), hypotonia in infancy, hyperphagia (insatiable appetite) beginning in early childhood leading to obesity, short stature, small hands and feet, hypogonadism, and behavioral problems. **Angelman syndrome** features severe intellectual disability, absent or minimal speech, frequent laughter and smiling (giving the appearance of a happy disposition), seizures, ataxia (uncoordinated movement), and microcephaly. The "happy puppet" appearance of Angelman syndrome (an older, now-discouraged term) contrasts sharply with the food-obsessed, often irritable presentation of Prader-Willi syndrome.

Both conditions occur in approximately 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 20,000 births. While the most common cause of each is a chromosomal deletion (approximately 70% of cases), both can also result from other genetic mechanisms, including uniparental disomy (inheriting both copies of chromosome 15 from the same parent) and imprinting defects.

The Prader-Willi/Angelman comparison is one of the most elegant demonstrations of genomic imprinting in human genetics. It shows that genes do not simply operate in a dominant/recessive frameworkâ€”the parental origin of a gene can determine whether and how it is expressed. This concept has implications beyond these specific syndromes, as genomic imprinting affects numerous other genes and may contribute to a variety of developmental conditions.

For the EPPP, the essential distinction is that Prader-Willi results from a paternal chromosome 15 deletion and Angelman results from a maternal chromosome 15 deletion. Questions typically present the two syndromes and ask candidates to identify which parent's chromosome is affected. The most common trap is reversing the parent of originâ€”Prader-Willi = paternal, Angelman = maternal.

verbatim_anchor: Moore, Persaud, & Torchia (2016): "The embryonic period (weeks 3-8) is the most critical for teratogenic effects because this is when major organ systems undergo rapid differentiation." Alcohol exposure during the embryonic period produces the most severe structural birth defects; exposure during the fetal period is more likely to cause functional and behavioral impairments.
old_anchor: Consumption of alcohol by pregnant women is most likely to cause major birth defects in their offspring when drinking occurs during the embryonic period (weeks 3 through 8).
testable_fact: Alcohol exposure during the embryonic period (weeks 3–8) causes the most severe structural birth defects, while fetal-period exposure more likely causes functional and behavioral impairments.
passage:
A pregnant woman who did not realize she was pregnant consumed several alcoholic beverages during weeks four through seven of her pregnancy. She is now deeply worried about the potential effects on her developing baby. Her obstetrician explains that the timing of her alcohol consumption places it during the most sensitive window for certain types of birth defects.

**Consumption of alcohol by pregnant women is most likely to cause major birth defects in their offspring when drinking occurs during the embryonic period (weeks 3 through 8)**. The embryonic period is the stage of prenatal development when the major organ systems and body structures are formingâ€”a process called **organogenesis**â€”and it is during this window that the developing organism is most vulnerable to structural damage from teratogenic exposures.

Prenatal development is divided into three major stages: the **germinal period** (conception through approximately week 2), the **embryonic period** (approximately weeks 3 through 8), and the **fetal period** (approximately week 9 through birth). Each period has distinct developmental characteristics and different vulnerabilities to environmental insults.

During the **germinal period**, the fertilized egg undergoes rapid cell division and implants in the uterine wall. At this stage, a teratogenic exposure typically has an all-or-nothing effect: either it destroys the embryo (resulting in miscarriage) or it has no lasting effect because the undifferentiated cells can compensate for damaged cells.

The **embryonic period** is the critical window for major structural birth defects. During weeks 3 through 8, the basic structures of all major organ systems are established: the heart, brain, limbs, eyes, ears, and other organs develop from undifferentiated tissue into recognizable forms. Because each organ system has a specific **critical period** during which it is undergoing rapid formation, exposure to teratogens during this time can disrupt normal development and produce structural malformations. Alcohol exposure during this period is associated with the characteristic facial abnormalities of fetal alcohol syndrome (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures), as well as heart defects, skeletal abnormalities, and brain malformations.

During the **fetal period** (weeks 9 through birth), the major structures have already formed and the primary developmental activities are growth and functional maturation. Teratogenic exposure during the fetal period is less likely to cause major structural defects but can still affect growth (causing growth restriction), brain development (causing cognitive and behavioral effects), and the maturation of organ systems. Alcohol exposure during the fetal period is more likely to affect brain function and growth than to cause the structural facial anomalies associated with embryonic period exposure.

This timing principle applies not only to alcohol but to teratogenic exposure in general. The specific effects of any teratogen depend on **when during development the exposure occurs**, **how much of the substance the organism is exposed to** (dose), and the **genetic susceptibility** of the individual. The embryonic period is universally recognized as the period of greatest vulnerability to structural birth defects across all teratogenic agents.

For the EPPP, the key testable fact is that alcohol causes the most severe birth defects when consumed during the embryonic period (weeks 3-8). A common exam trap is selecting the fetal period as the most sensitive window, or failing to distinguish between the embryonic and germinal periods. Remember: germinal = weeks 1-2, embryonic = weeks 3-8, fetal = week 9 to birth.

subdomain: Early Influences on Development - Prenatal Development
chapter_title: Where Biology Meets Biography: Gene-Environment Interplay and the Roots of Individual Differences
verbatim_anchor: Scriver (2007): "PKU follows autosomal recessive inheritance — it occurs only in individuals homozygous for the recessive allele."
old_anchor: Phenylketonuria (PKU) occurs in individuals who are homozygous for a recessive allele.
testable_fact: Phenylketonuria (PKU) follows autosomal recessive inheritance, occurring only in individuals who are homozygous for the recessive allele.
passage:
A genetic counselor explains to prospective parents that they are both carriers of the gene for phenylketonuria. Each parent has one normal allele and one PKU allele, and neither shows any symptoms of the condition. The counselor draws a Punnett square and explains that with each pregnancy, there is a 25% chance their child will inherit the PKU allele from both parents and have the condition, a 50% chance the child will be a carrier like the parents, and a 25% chance the child will inherit two normal alleles.

**Phenylketonuria (PKU)** occurs in individuals who are **homozygous for a recessive allele**â€”meaning the individual has inherited two copies of the recessive allele responsible for PKU, one from each parent. PKU follows an **autosomal recessive** inheritance pattern, which means the gene is located on an autosome (a non-sex chromosome, specifically chromosome 12) and the condition is expressed only when both copies of the gene carry the recessive mutation.

To understand why PKU requires homozygosity, it is necessary to review basic principles of Mendelian genetics. Every person carries two copies (alleles) of each geneâ€”one inherited from the mother and one from the father. When a gene has both a **dominant** allele (which produces a functional version of the gene's protein product) and a **recessive** allele (which produces a nonfunctional or deficient version), the dominant allele typically masks the effect of the recessive allele in **heterozygous** individuals (those who carry one of each). Only **homozygous recessive** individuals (those who carry two copies of the recessive allele) express the recessive phenotype.

In the case of PKU, the gene in question codes for the enzyme **phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)**, which converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine. Individuals with two functional alleles (homozygous dominant) produce full amounts of PAH and metabolize phenylalanine normally. Individuals with one functional allele and one PKU allele (heterozygous carriers) produce approximately half the normal amount of PAH, which is sufficient for normal phenylalanine metabolismâ€”they show no symptoms and are clinically unaffected. Individuals with two PKU alleles (homozygous recessive) produce little or no functional PAH, resulting in dangerous accumulation of phenylalanine.

The autosomal recessive inheritance pattern has several characteristic features. First, affected individuals typically have unaffected parents who are both carriers. Because carriers show no symptoms, PKU can appear unexpectedly in families with no known history of the condition. Second, the condition affects males and females equally (unlike X-linked conditions, which show sex differences in prevalence). Third, there is a 25% probability of an affected child with each pregnancy when both parents are carriers.

PKU occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 15,000 births in the United States. Carrier frequency varies by population, with higher rates in some European and Middle Eastern populations. Newborn screening for PKU is universal in the United States and many other countries, allowing early identification and dietary intervention that can prevent the intellectual disability and other neurological consequences of untreated PKU.

For the EPPP, the critical fact is that PKU is an autosomal recessive condition, meaning it requires homozygosity for the recessive allele. Questions may ask about the inheritance pattern, the probability of affected offspring from carrier parents (25%), or may use PKU as an example of recessive inheritance. A common trap is describing PKU as dominant or X-linked.

subdomain: Early Influences on Development - Prenatal Development
chapter_title: When Chromosomes Carry Consequences: Prenatal Development, Genetic Disorders, and Environmental Threats
verbatim_anchor: Hook (1981) / Berk (2018): "Risk for trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) increases with maternal age, with greatest risk for women 42+."
old_anchor: Women who are 42 years of age or older at the time of conception are at the greatest risk for having a child with standard (nondisjunction) trisomy 21.
testable_fact: Risk for trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) increases with maternal age, with women aged 42 and older at greatest risk for nondisjunction trisomy 21.
passage:
A 43-year-old woman meets with a genetic counselor to discuss the risks associated with her pregnancy. The counselor explains that while women of any age can have a child with Down syndrome, the risk increases substantially with advancing maternal age, and that women in her age group face the highest probability of having a child with the most common form of this chromosomal condition.

**Women who are 42 years of age or older** at the time of conception are at the **greatest risk for having a child with standard (nondisjunction) trisomy 21**, commonly known as **Down syndrome**. The risk increases exponentially with maternal age: at age 20, the risk is approximately 1 in 1,500; at age 30, approximately 1 in 900; at age 35, approximately 1 in 350; at age 40, approximately 1 in 100; and at age 45, approximately 1 in 30.

Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, occurring in approximately 1 in 700 live births overall. The standard form of Down syndromeâ€”**nondisjunction trisomy 21**â€”accounts for about 95% of cases and results from the presence of a complete extra copy of chromosome 21 in every cell. This extra chromosome arises from **nondisjunction**, an error in cell division during the formation of the egg (or, less commonly, the sperm) in which chromosome 21 fails to separate properly, resulting in an egg or sperm cell with two copies of chromosome 21 instead of one.

The link between advancing maternal age and increased risk of nondisjunction is related to the biology of **oogenesis** (egg cell formation). Women are born with all the oocytes (immature egg cells) they will ever have. These oocytes begin the first stage of meiosis (cell division) during fetal development and then remain suspended in an arrested state for decadesâ€”until they resume division just before ovulation. By the time a woman is 42, her oocytes have been arrested in meiosis for over 40 years. During this prolonged suspension, the cellular machinery responsible for proper chromosome separation can deteriorate. The **cohesin proteins** that hold chromosome pairs together weaken over time, increasing the probability that chromosomes will fail to separate correctly during the final stages of meiosis.

It is important to distinguish nondisjunction trisomy 21 from two other, less common forms of Down syndrome. **Translocation Down syndrome** (approximately 3-4% of cases) occurs when a piece of chromosome 21 breaks off and attaches to another chromosome. This form can be inherited from a parent who carries a balanced translocation and is **not** associated with advanced maternal age. **Mosaic Down syndrome** (approximately 1-2% of cases) occurs when nondisjunction happens after fertilization, resulting in some cells with trisomy 21 and others with a normal chromosome complement. This form is also not strongly associated with maternal age.

The clinical features of Down syndrome include characteristic facial features (flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes, small ears), intellectual disability (usually mild to moderate), hypotonia (low muscle tone), congenital heart defects (in approximately 50% of cases), and increased risk for certain health conditions including thyroid disorders, hearing problems, and early-onset Alzheimer-type changes.

For the EPPP, the key facts are that women aged 42 and older are at greatest risk, that the standard form (nondisjunction trisomy 21) is the form most strongly associated with maternal age, and that the mechanism involves errors in chromosome separation during oogenesis. A common trap is stating that all forms of Down syndrome are associated with advanced maternal ageâ€”translocation Down syndrome is not.

subdomain: Early Influences on Development - Prenatal Development
chapter_title: When Chromosomes Carry Consequences: Prenatal Development, Genetic Disorders, and Environmental Threats
verbatim_anchor: Visootsak & Graham (2006) / Berk (2018): "Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is caused by the presence of an extra X chromosome in males — a sex chromosome aneuploidy, not a chromosomal deletion." Males with Klinefelter syndrome typically present with tall stature, small testes, reduced fertility, and may have learning difficulties.
old_anchor: Klinefelter syndrome is not caused by a chromosomal deletion, but rather by the presence of two or more X chromosomes in addition to a single Y chromosome in males.
testable_fact: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from the presence of one or more extra X chromosomes in males, causing tall stature, small testes, reduced fertility, and potential learning difficulties.
passage:
When a baby is born and a chromosomal analysis reveals a 47,XXY karyotype, the child has one of the most common sex-chromosome variations in humans. Understanding how this configuration arises and what it means for development is a foundational topic in the study of prenatal influences on lifespan development.

**Klinefelter syndrome** is not caused by a chromosomal deletion but rather by the presence of two or more X chromosomes in addition to a single Y chromosome in males. The most common karyotype is 47,XXY, although variants such as 48,XXXY and 49,XXXXY also occur. The condition results from **nondisjunction**, a failure of chromosome pairs to separate properly during cell division in either the egg or the sperm. When nondisjunction occurs, one gamete ends up with an extra sex chromosome, and if that gamete participates in fertilization, the resulting embryo carries the additional genetic material.

Because a Y chromosome is present, individuals with Klinefelter syndrome develop as phenotypic males. However, the extra X chromosome influences development in several characteristic ways. Physical features that may become apparent during puberty include taller-than-average stature, broader hips, reduced muscle mass, and incomplete secondary sex characteristic development. These features vary considerably in severity; some individuals are not identified until adulthood, while others show more pronounced differences in childhood.

From a developmental standpoint, Klinefelter syndrome is relevant to the study of how genetic factors shape the trajectory of physical and cognitive growth. Research has documented that children with the 47,XXY karyotype may show subtle differences in **language development**, particularly in expressive language and verbal processing speed. Some studies report mild delays in reaching early language milestones, such as first words and two-word combinations, compared to age-matched peers with typical karyotypes. These differences tend to be modest and variable, and many individuals function well within the normal range with appropriate early support.

Cognitive profiles in Klinefelter syndrome tend to show relative strengths in visual-spatial reasoning and relative weaknesses in verbal and auditory processing. This pattern has been documented across multiple studies and appears to persist across the lifespan, though the magnitude of the difference is often small. Overall intellectual functioning typically falls within the average range.

It is essential to distinguish Klinefelter syndrome from conditions caused by chromosomal deletions, such as **Cri-du-chat syndrome** (a deletion on chromosome 5) or **Williams syndrome** (a microdeletion on chromosome 7). Klinefelter syndrome involves extra chromosomal material, not missing material. It should also be distinguished from **Turner syndrome** (45,X), in which a female has only one X chromosome. Turner syndrome involves a missing sex chromosome, while Klinefelter syndrome involves an additional one.

The incidence of Klinefelter syndrome is estimated at approximately 1 in 500 to 1 in 1,000 live male births, making it one of the most common chromosomal variations. Many cases go undetected because the phenotypic expression can be subtle.

For EPPP preparation, Klinefelter syndrome is tested in the context of chromosomal abnormalities and prenatal development. The most common exam angle is asking candidates to identify the genetic mechanism. The correct answer is the presence of extra X chromosomes in a male, not a deletion. Candidates should also be prepared to distinguish Klinefelter syndrome from Turner syndrome and from autosomal trisomies such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

chapter_title: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
verbatim_anchor: Brown & Bellugi (1964): "At about eighteen months children are likely to begin constructing two-word utterances; such a one, for instance, as Push car." Two-word combinations (telegraphic speech) emerge between 18-24 months, using high-content words in grammatically meaningful order while omitting functors.
old_anchor: Children use two words to create a simple sentence, such as "juice gone," "get toy," and "big doggie," by about 18 to 24 months of age.
testable_fact: Telegraphic speech, emerging between 18–24 months, consists of two-word utterances that preserve meaningful word order while omitting grammatical functors such as articles and prepositions.
passage:
A mother keeps a language diary for her 20-month-old daughter. She records the following utterances over the course of a week: "juice gone," "get toy," "big doggie," "daddy go," "more cookie," and "no bath." Each of these utterances consists of exactly two words, yet they convey a remarkable range of meaningsâ€”the disappearance of an object, a request, a description, a commentary on someone's action, a demand for more, and a refusal. The mother is witnessing a critical milestone in her daughter's language development.

**Children use two words to create simple sentences** such as "juice gone," "get toy," and "big doggie" **by about 18 to 24 months of age**. This stage, known as the **two-word stage** or the stage of **telegraphic speech**, represents a major advance in language development because it marks the child's first systematic use of **syntax**â€”the rules governing the arrangement of words to create meaningful combinations.

Before the two-word stage, children communicate using single words (the **holophrastic stage**, beginning around 12 months). A single word like "milk" might mean "I want milk," "there is milk," or "the milk spilled," depending on context. The child conveys meaning, but the single word must carry the full communicative burden, and the listener must rely heavily on context to interpret the intended message.

The transition to two-word combinations around 18-24 months typically coincides with the **vocabulary spurt** (or "naming explosion"), during which children's productive vocabularies rapidly expand from approximately 50 words to 200 or more. Once children have a sufficient vocabulary base, they begin combining words to express more complex and specific meanings.

Two-word utterances have a distinctive structure that reveals the child's emerging grammatical knowledge. Roger Brown and other researchers identified several **semantic relations** that children consistently express in their two-word combinations across different languages:

- **Agent + action**: "daddy go," "doggie bark"
- **Action + object**: "get toy," "eat cookie"
- **Agent + object**: "mommy sock" (mommy is putting on the sock)
- **Modifier + object**: "big doggie," "pretty flower"
- **Negation + object**: "no bath," "no milk"
- **Recurrence**: "more cookie," "more juice"
- **Disappearance**: "juice gone," "ball allgone"

These combinations follow consistent word order rules that reflect the basic syntactic patterns of the child's native language. English-speaking children overwhelmingly produce subject-verb and verb-object orderings, even though no one explicitly teaches them these rules. This consistent word ordering suggests that children are not simply stringing random words together but are operating according to an implicit grammatical system.

The term "telegraphic speech" reflects the observation that two-word utterances, like old-fashioned telegrams, include only the essential content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and omit grammatical function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliary verbs) and inflections (past tense, plural). "Get toy" instead of "Can you get the toy for me?" conveys the core meaning efficiently, if not grammatically.

For the EPPP, the key facts are the age range (18-24 months), the term "telegraphic speech," and examples of two-word combinations. A common trap is placing two-word combinations too early (12 months, when children are typically in the one-word stage) or too late (after 24 months).

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Brown & Bellugi (1964): Children's speech preserves the word order of adult models but omits functors — inflections, auxiliary verbs, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. Free morphemes can stand alone as words (e.g., 'do'); bound morphemes cannot stand alone and must attach to another morpheme (e.g., 'pre-,' '-ism').
old_anchor: Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units in a language, such as "inter," "er," "ism," "pre," and "post" in English.
testable_fact: Free morphemes can stand alone as words, while bound morphemes must attach to another morpheme; children's telegraphic speech preserves adult word order but omits bound grammatical morphemes and functors.
passage:
Consider the English word "unhappiness." A fluent speaker intuitively recognizes that it is built from three separable parts, each carrying its own meaning: "un-" (negation), "happi" (a state of well-being), and "-ness" (the quality of). This ability to decompose and recombine meaningful units is central to how language works, and the study of these units is a cornerstone of developmental linguistics.

**Morphemes** are the smallest meaningful units in a language. Examples include "inter," "er," "ism," "pre," and "post" in English. Each of these carries a distinct meaning that contributes to the words in which it appears. "Pre-" signals something that comes before; "-er" can indicate a person who performs an action (as in "teacher"); "-ism" denotes a system of beliefs or practices. A morpheme cannot be broken down further without losing its meaning.

Morphemes are classified into two broad categories. **Free morphemes** can stand alone as independent words. "Book," "run," and "happy" are free morphemes because each conveys meaning without being attached to anything else. **Bound morphemes** must be attached to another morpheme to convey meaning. Prefixes such as "un-" and "pre-" and suffixes such as "-ing," "-ed," and "-ness" are bound morphemes. A single word can contain multiple morphemes: "reusable" consists of "re-" (bound), "use" (free), and "-able" (bound).

In the context of language development, the acquisition of morphemes follows a remarkably predictable sequence. Roger Brown's landmark longitudinal research identified 14 **grammatical morphemes** that English-speaking children acquire in a largely consistent order. Among the earliest to appear are the present progressive "-ing" (as in "running"), the prepositions "in" and "on," and the regular plural "-s." Later-acquired morphemes include the contractible copula ("she's happy") and the contractible auxiliary ("he's running"). Brown's ordering has been replicated across multiple samples, suggesting that the sequence reflects underlying cognitive and linguistic complexity rather than the frequency with which children hear these forms.

The number of morphemes a child uses is captured by a metric called **Mean Length of Utterance (MLU)**, calculated by dividing the total number of morphemes in a language sample by the total number of utterances. MLU is one of the most widely used indices of early grammatical development. A child who says "doggy running" has produced an utterance with three morphemes ("doggy" + "run" + "-ing"), yielding an MLU contribution of 3.0 for that utterance. Increases in MLU over time signal that the child is combining morphemes in increasingly complex ways.

It is important to distinguish morphemes from **phonemes**, which are the smallest units of sound in a language. Phonemes do not carry meaning on their own. The sounds /b/ and /p/ are different phonemes in English because substituting one for the other changes meaning ("bat" versus "pat"), but neither /b/ nor /p/ means anything in isolation. Morphemes, by contrast, always carry meaning.

For EPPP preparation, morpheme-related questions typically ask candidates to define the term, to distinguish morphemes from phonemes, or to identify the order in which grammatical morphemes are acquired. The essential point is that morphemes are the smallest units of meaning, not the smallest units of sound. Remembering this distinction and knowing Brown's general acquisition sequence will address the majority of exam items on this topic.

chapter_title: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
verbatim_anchor: Clark (1973): "Overextension occurs when a child applies a word too broadly — using it for objects sharing some perceptual feature with the referent but not belonging to the correct category."
old_anchor: When a child learns the word "dada," she initially applies it to all adult males, which is an example of overextension.
testable_fact: Overextension occurs when a child applies a word too broadly to objects sharing a perceptual feature with the correct referent, as when "dada" is used for all adult males.
passage:
A toddler learns the word "dada" and initially uses it correctly to refer to her father. Within days, however, she begins pointing at the mailman, her uncle, and a man at the grocery store and calling each of them "dada." Her mother finds this amusing but also slightly embarrassing. The child is not confused about who her father isâ€”she is demonstrating a normal and well-studied pattern in early language development.

**Overextension** occurs when a child **applies a word to a broader category of referents than the word actually denotes**. In this example, the child has learned "dada" as a label for one adult male (her father) and then extends it to all adult males, because they share the perceptual features she has associated with the wordâ€”adult, male, upright, walking. The child's internal category for "dada" is too broad; it includes referents that the word does not actually apply to.

Overextension is one of the most common features of early lexical development, typically appearing during the **one-word (holophrastic) stage** and the early part of the **two-word stage**, roughly between **12 and 30 months of age**. Research suggests that approximately one-third of children's early words are overextended at some point during acquisition.

Overextensions are typically based on **perceptual similarity**â€”the child extends a word to new referents that share observable features with the original referent. The most common bases for overextension include shape (calling all round objects "ball"), size (calling all small animals "bug"), movement (calling all moving vehicles "car"), texture (calling all soft things "blankie"), and sound (calling all animals that make noise "doggie"). The child is using the limited vocabulary available to categorize a world full of objects and people, and when the existing vocabulary does not include a word for a new referent, the child stretches the closest available word to cover it.

Overextensions serve an important communicative function. When a toddler calls all four-legged animals "doggie," she may not actually believe they are all dogs. Research has shown that children can often distinguish between the referents in comprehension tasks even when they overextend the label in production. The child may point correctly to a cat when asked "Where's the kitty?" even though she calls it "doggie" in her own speech. This suggests that overextension is partly a production strategyâ€”the child knows more distinctions than she can express with her limited vocabulary, so she uses the closest available word as a communicative approximation.

Overextension should be distinguished from **underextension**, which is the opposite patternâ€”applying a word to a narrower range of referents than appropriate (for example, calling only the family pet "doggie" and refusing to apply the word to any other dog). Underextension is less noticeable than overextension because the child is not making conspicuous errors; rather, the child is failing to generalize a word to all appropriate referents.

As the child's vocabulary expands, overextensions naturally resolve. Once the child learns the word "kitty," she stops calling cats "doggie." Once she learns specific names for other men in her life, she restricts "dada" to her father. The acquisition of new words provides the differentiated labels needed to carve the world into more precise categories.

For the EPPP, the key definition is that overextension involves applying a word too broadly. The classic example is calling all adult males "dada" or all four-legged animals "doggie." A common trap is confusing overextension with overregularization (applying grammatical rules too broadly, like saying "goed" instead of "went"). Overextension concerns word meaning; overregularization concerns grammatical rules.

chapter_title: Words in the World: How Language Meets Social Context
verbatim_anchor: Gumperz (1982) / Berk (2018): "Code-switching is the practice of alternating between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation or utterance." Bilingual and multilingual speakers use code-switching strategically to signal group identity, establish solidarity, convey emphasis, or navigate social contexts.
old_anchor: Code-switching is used by bilingual and multilingual speakers to establish solidarity with listeners belonging to their own minority group.
testable_fact: Code-switching is the practice of alternating between languages or language varieties to signal group identity, establish solidarity, convey emphasis, or navigate social contexts.
passage:
A bilingual teenager speaks English at school with her teachers and classmates but switches seamlessly to Spanish when she joins her family for dinner. At a community event with other Mexican-American families, she moves fluidly between the two languages within a single conversation, using English for some topics and Spanish for others, and sometimes mixing both in the same sentence. This linguistic flexibility is not a sign of confusion or limited proficiencyâ€”it is a sophisticated communicative skill.

**Code-switching** is the practice of alternating between two or more languages or language varieties within a conversation, and it is commonly used by **bilingual and multilingual speakers to establish solidarity with listeners belonging to their own minority group**. Code-switching can occur between sentences (intersentential switching), within a single sentence (intrasentential switching), or even within a single word (using a morpheme from one language attached to a word from another).

Research has established that code-switching is not a sign of linguistic deficiency or an inability to keep languages separate. On the contrary, it requires **high proficiency in both languages** and a sophisticated understanding of the social rules governing when each language is appropriate. Bilingual speakers who code-switch must simultaneously activate both language systems, select the appropriate language for each word or phrase, and monitor the social context to determine which language or combination of languages will be most effective.

One of the primary social functions of code-switching is **establishing group identity and solidarity**. When a bilingual speaker switches from the majority language to the minority language in the presence of fellow minority-group members, the switch signals shared cultural identity and in-group membership. It creates a sense of intimacy and belonging that would not be achieved by speaking only the majority language. The switch communicates, in effect, "We share a language and a culture that connects us."

Code-switching serves additional communicative functions beyond solidarity. It is used for **emphasis** (switching languages to make a point more forcefully), **clarification** (expressing a concept in the language that has a better word for it), **exclusion** (switching to a language that certain listeners do not understand), **quotation** (reporting what someone said in the language they said it in), and **topic marking** (using one language for formal or academic topics and another for personal or emotional topics).

The development of code-switching ability follows a predictable trajectory. Young bilingual children (ages 2-3) occasionally mix languages in ways that appear unsystematic, but by age 4-5, most bilingual children demonstrate sensitivity to the linguistic preferences of their conversational partners, speaking the appropriate language with monolingual and bilingual interlocutors. By middle childhood and adolescence, code-switching becomes a highly refined skill that reflects both linguistic competence and social awareness.

Code-switching has important implications for educational settings. Teachers who are unfamiliar with code-switching may mistakenly interpret it as a language disorder or a sign of limited English proficiency. Understanding that code-switching is a normal, sophisticated bilingual behavior helps educators respond appropriately and avoid pathologizing a healthy linguistic practice.

For the EPPP, the key facts are that code-switching is used by bilingual and multilingual speakers, that one of its primary functions is establishing solidarity with in-group members, and that it reflects linguistic sophistication rather than deficiency. A common trap is describing code-switching as a sign of language confusion or incomplete language acquisition.

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Chomsky (1959): "The fact that all normal children acquire essentially comparable grammars of great complexity with remarkable rapidity suggests that human beings are somehow specially designed to do this." Humans possess an innate capacity for language allowing detection of native language structure from limited input.
old_anchor: Noam Chomsky attributed language acquisition to an innate language acquisition device.
testable_fact: Chomsky proposed that humans possess an innate language acquisition device that enables rapid acquisition of complex grammar from limited input.
passage:
A two-year-old who has never been taught grammar explicitly produces sentences like "I goed to the store" and "She runned fast."â€‹ These errors are actually remarkableâ€”the child is applying grammatical rules (adding "-ed" to form past tense) that no one taught her, and applying them to verbs she has never heard in the past tense form. She has somehow extracted the rule from the language she hears and is applying it systematically, even to irregular verbs where the rule does not apply. How does a toddler accomplish this feat of abstract pattern recognition that would challenge a computer?

**Noam Chomsky** attributed language acquisition to an innate **language acquisition device (LAD)**â€”a hypothetical, biologically based mechanism that all humans are born with that enables them to acquire the grammar of any language to which they are exposed. Chomsky's proposal was revolutionary because it challenged the dominant behaviorist view (associated with B. F. Skinner) that language is learned entirely through reinforcement, imitation, and environmental conditioning.

Chomsky argued that the behaviorist account of language learning was fundamentally inadequate for several reasons. First, children acquire language with remarkable speed and uniformity despite wide variations in the quantity and quality of linguistic input they receive. This suggested that something internal was guiding the process. Second, children produce sentences they have never heard before, including both creative correct sentences and systematic errors (like "goed" and "runned") that reflect the application of abstract rules rather than mere imitation. Third, children's grammatical errors are highly systematicâ€”they overgeneralize regular rules to irregular cases, which they would not do if they were simply imitating adult speech. Fourth, the linguistic input children receive (often called the **"poverty of the stimulus"**) is frequently incomplete, ungrammatical, and fragmented, yet children somehow converge on the correct grammar of their language.

Chomsky proposed that the LAD contains a **Universal Grammar (UG)**â€”a set of innate grammatical principles and parameters that are common to all human languages. These universal principles constrain the possible forms that any human language can take. When a child is exposed to a specific language, the LAD uses the linguistic input to set the parameters of the Universal Grammar to match the particular language being learned. In this view, language acquisition is not so much "learning" as it is "parameter setting"â€”the child comes equipped with the basic grammatical framework and uses experience to specify the details.

Evidence supporting the nativist position includes the universality of language acquisition across cultures, the existence of **critical (or sensitive) periods** for language learning, the observation that children acquire grammar in a predictable sequence regardless of the specific language being learned, and neurological evidence that specific brain regions (Broca's area and Wernicke's area) are specialized for language processing.

Chomsky's nativist theory should be contrasted with competing accounts of language acquisition. **Behaviorist theories** (Skinner) emphasize reinforcement and imitation. **Social interactionist theories** (Bruner, Tomasello) emphasize the role of social interaction and communicative intent. **Connectionist/statistical learning theories** propose that language is acquired through general pattern-recognition mechanisms applied to linguistic input rather than through a language-specific device.

For the EPPP, the key fact is that Chomsky proposed an innate LAD that enables language acquisition. Questions may ask candidates to identify the theorist associated with the LAD, to distinguish the nativist position from the behaviorist position, or to explain the concept of Universal Grammar. A common trap is attributing the LAD to Skinner or Vygotsky.

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Oller (2000): "Babbling emerges between 3–6 months with repetition of vowel-consonant combinations, initially including sounds from multiple languages."
old_anchor: Babbling emerges between 3 and 6 months of age and initially involves the repetition of single vowel-consonant combinations that include sounds from different languages.
testable_fact: Babbling emerges between 3–6 months with repetition of vowel-consonant combinations and initially includes sounds from multiple languages before narrowing to the native language.
passage:
A mother notices that her four-month-old has begun making repetitive sounds that are distinctly different from the cooing and crying of earlier months. The infant produces strings like "babababa" and "mamamama," repeating the same consonant-vowel combination over and over with apparent delight. Interestingly, the sounds include not only those found in the family's native English but also sounds from languages the infant has never heard.

**Babbling** emerges **between 3 and 6 months of age** and initially involves the **repetition of single vowel-consonant combinations that include sounds from different languages**. This early form of babbling is called **canonical babbling** (or **reduplicated babbling**) and is characterized by the rhythmic repetition of consonant-vowel syllablesâ€”such as "bababa," "mamama," and "dadada"â€”that resemble the sound patterns of speech.

Babbling represents a significant advance in vocal development. Before babbling begins, infants communicate primarily through crying (from birth), cooing (around 2-3 months, consisting of vowel-like sounds such as "oooh" and "aaah"), and vocal play (around 3-4 months, involving experimentation with pitch and volume). Babbling differs from these earlier vocalizations because it introduces **consonant sounds** combined with vowels in syllabic patterns that approximate the structure of real words.

One of the most fascinating features of early babbling is its **linguistic universality**. During the initial period of babbling, infants produce sounds from a wide range of human languages, not just the language spoken in their home. A baby in an English-speaking household may produce sounds typical of Mandarin, Swahili, or Hindi, and vice versa. This suggests that babbling is driven by **biological maturation** of the vocal apparatus and the neural systems controlling speech production, rather than by imitation of specific language input. The infant's vocal system is capable of producing the full range of human speech sounds, and early babbling reflects this universal capacity.

The articulatory basis of early babbling involves the maturation of the vocal tract, the jaw, the tongue, and the respiratory system. The rhythmic jaw movements that produce canonical babbling (opening and closing the mouth while vocalizing) emerge as the infant gains voluntary control over these structures. The most common consonant sounds in early babbling are those produced with relatively simple articulatory movements: bilabial stops (/b/, /m/, /p/) and alveolar stops (/d/, /t/, /n/).

Babbling serves several important developmental functions. It provides the infant with auditory feedback that helps calibrate the relationship between motor commands and acoustic outcomesâ€”the infant learns what it sounds like to produce different articulatory movements. It also serves a social-communicative function, as caregivers typically respond to babbling with enthusiastic verbal and nonverbal feedback, creating early conversational turn-taking exchanges that support both language and social development.

The transition from universal babbling to language-specific babbling occurs gradually over the second half of the first year. By approximately 9-10 months, the infant's babbling begins to narrow, increasingly reflecting the sound patterns of the ambient language. This narrowing process, sometimes called **perceptual narrowing** or **phonological attunement**, marks the beginning of the infant's specialization for the native language.

For the EPPP, the key facts are the age of onset (3-6 months), the initial universality of babbling sounds (includes sounds from many languages), and the repetitive consonant-vowel structure. A common trap is stating that babbling consists only of sounds from the native language from the beginningâ€”the narrowing to native language sounds occurs later, around 9-10 months.

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Goldfield & Reznick (1990): "The vocabulary spurt typically begins around 18 months when children have acquired approximately 50 words, with word learning accelerating dramatically."
old_anchor: The vocabulary spurt, when babies use about 50 words, usually begins around 18 months of age.
testable_fact: The vocabulary spurt typically begins around 18 months when children have acquired approximately 50 words, after which word learning accelerates dramatically.
passage:
For months, a toddler's vocabulary grew slowly, adding one or two new words per week. Then, seemingly overnight, the child begins learning new words at a breathtaking paceâ€”five, ten, even fifteen new words per week. Her parents are astonished at how quickly she is labeling everything in sight: "cup," "shoe," "tree," "book," "bird." The child seems to have reached a tipping point in word learning that has dramatically accelerated her pace of vocabulary acquisition.

The **vocabulary spurt** (also called the **naming explosion** or **word spurt**) is a period of rapid vocabulary growth that **usually begins around 18 months of age**, typically when the child has acquired a productive vocabulary of approximately **50 words**. During this period, the rate of new word acquisition increases dramatically, with some children learning several new words per day compared to the slower pace of the preceding months.

Before the vocabulary spurt, word learning during the one-word stage proceeds gradually. Children typically produce their first recognizable word around 12 months of age and add new words slowly over the next several months. By 18 months, the average child has a productive vocabulary of approximately 50 words, though there is considerable individual variation. The vocabulary spurt appears to begin when the child reaches this approximate threshold, suggesting that a critical mass of vocabulary knowledge triggers a qualitative shift in the word-learning process.

Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain why the vocabulary spurt occurs when it does. One account involves the **naming insight**â€”the child's realization that everything has a name. Before this insight, the child may learn words in a relatively unsystematic way. Once the child grasps the principle that every object, action, and quality can be labeled with a word, the child becomes motivated to learn the names for everything encountered. This insight transforms the child from a passive recipient of vocabulary to an active, eager word-learner.

Another account emphasizes **categorization ability**. Around 18 months, children's ability to form categories improves, allowing them to organize new words more efficiently and to use existing category knowledge to constrain the meanings of new words. When a child hears a new word applied to an unfamiliar object, she can use the principle of **mutual exclusivity** (the assumption that each object has only one name) to narrow down the word's meaning, accelerating the learning process.

A third account points to improvements in **memory and processing speed**. As the child's cognitive abilities mature around 18 months, the child can encode, store, and retrieve word-meaning associations more efficiently, enabling faster vocabulary growth.

The vocabulary spurt has important clinical significance. Children who do not show a vocabulary spurt by 24 monthsâ€”sometimes called **late talkers**â€”may be at risk for language delays, although many late talkers catch up to their peers by age 3. Monitoring vocabulary growth and the presence or absence of a vocabulary spurt is a standard component of developmental screening during the toddler period.

For the EPPP, the key facts are the age of onset (approximately 18 months), the vocabulary threshold (approximately 50 words), and the dramatic increase in rate of word learning. A common trap is placing the vocabulary spurt at 12 months (when the first words are appearing but the spurt has not yet begun) or at 24 months (which is later than the typical onset).

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Brown & Bellugi (1964): "In English the order of words in a sentence is an important grammatical signal. Order is used to distinguish among subject, direct object, and indirect object." Phonemes are the smallest units of sound that signal a difference in meaning.
old_anchor: The smallest distinctive units of sound in a language are referred to as phonemes.
testable_fact: Phonemes are the smallest units of sound in a language that signal a difference in meaning.
passage:
Consider the English words "bat" and "pat." They differ by only a single sound at the beginningâ€”the /b/ in "bat" and the /p/ in "pat"â€”yet this tiny acoustic difference changes the meaning entirely. One word refers to a flying mammal or a piece of sports equipment; the other refers to a gentle touch. The fact that a single sound change can alter meaning reveals something fundamental about how language is structured.

The **smallest distinctive units of sound in a language** are referred to as **phonemes**. A phoneme is defined not by its acoustic properties alone but by its ability to **distinguish meaning** between words. The /b/ and /p/ sounds are separate phonemes in English because substituting one for the other produces a different word ("bat" versus "pat," "bill" versus "pill," "big" versus "pig"). Any two sounds that can change the meaning of a word when substituted for each other are considered different phonemes.

The number of phonemes varies across languages. English has approximately **44 phonemes**â€”about 24 consonant phonemes and 20 vowel phonemes (the exact count varies slightly depending on the dialect). Some languages have far fewer: Hawaiian has only about 13 phonemes. Others have far more: some languages in southern Africa include click consonants and may have over 100 phonemes. Despite this variation, all human languages are built from a finite set of phonemes that are combined according to rules (called **phonotactic rules**) to form words.

Phonemes are conventionally written between forward slashes to distinguish them from letters. This is important because the relationship between phonemes and letters is not one-to-one in English. The letter "c" can represent the /k/ phoneme (as in "cat") or the /s/ phoneme (as in "city"). The combination "sh" represents a single phoneme (/sh/). The letter "x" represents two phonemes (/k/ + /s/). This mismatch between spelling and phonemic representation is one reason why English is a particularly challenging language to read and spell.

Phonemes are distinct from **morphemes**, which are the smallest units of **meaning** in a language. A morpheme may consist of one or more phonemes. The word "cat" is a single morpheme made up of three phonemes (/k/, /ae/, /t/). The word "cats" is two morphemes ("cat" + the plural morpheme "-s") made up of four phonemes. Phonemes are the building blocks of sound; morphemes are the building blocks of meaning.

The study of phonemes is relevant to developmental psychology because infants' ability to perceive and categorize phonemes undergoes a dramatic developmental change during the first year of life. Newborns can discriminate phonemic contrasts from any language in the world. By approximately 10-12 months, this universal discriminatory ability narrows, and infants become specialists in the phonemes of their native language while losing the ability to discriminate non-native contrasts. This **perceptual narrowing** is one of the earliest signs of language-specific specialization.

For the EPPP, the key definition is that phonemes are the smallest distinctive units of sound that distinguish meaning in a language. A common trap is confusing phonemes with morphemes or with letters. Another common error is defining a phoneme simply as the smallest unit of sound without specifying its meaning-distinguishing function.

chapter_title: The First Words: How Infants Build a Language from Sound and Meaning
verbatim_anchor: Kuhl (2004): "Infant babbling narrows to primarily native-language phonemes by approximately 9–10 months, reflecting perceptual narrowing."
old_anchor: Infant babbling initially includes sounds from all languages but begins to narrow to the sounds of the infant's native language by about 9 months of age.
testable_fact: By approximately 9–10 months, infant babbling narrows to native-language phonemes through perceptual narrowing, having initially included sounds from all languages.
passage:
A researcher records the babbling of two infantsâ€”one raised in a Japanese-speaking household and one in an English-speaking householdâ€”at 6 months and again at 10 months. At 6 months, the babbling samples are virtually indistinguishable: both infants produce a wide range of consonant-vowel combinations drawn from the universal set of human speech sounds. At 10 months, however, the samples have diverged: the Japanese infant's babbling increasingly features sounds and prosodic patterns characteristic of Japanese, while the English infant's babbling reflects English phonological patterns. Something has changed in the intervening months.

**Infant babbling initially includes sounds from all languages** but **begins to narrow to the sounds of the infant's native language by about 9 months of age**. This process, known as **phonological attunement** or **perceptual narrowing**, represents one of the earliest examples of experience-dependent specialization in language development.

During the first months of babbling (approximately 3-6 months), infants produce a wide variety of consonant-vowel combinations that include phonemes from languages they have never heard. This universal babbling reflects the biological readiness of the human vocal tract and nervous system to produce the full range of speech sounds used in any human language. At this stage, the infant's phonological system is broadly tuned and has not yet been shaped by the specific linguistic environment.

Beginning around 6-8 months and becoming more pronounced by 9-10 months, the infant's babbling begins to reflect the phonological characteristics of the ambient language. Several changes occur simultaneously. First, the **consonant and vowel sounds** that the infant produces increasingly match those of the native language, while sounds not present in the native language become less frequent. Second, the **prosodic contours** (the rhythm, stress, and intonation patterns) of the babbling begin to resemble those of the native language, so that listeners can often identify the language environment of a 10-month-old solely from the sound of the babbling. Third, the infant's **perceptual sensitivity** to phonemic contrasts undergoes a complementary narrowing: the ability to discriminate non-native phonemic contrasts declines, while sensitivity to native-language contrasts is maintained or sharpened.

This perceptual narrowing has been demonstrated in elegant experimental studies. Patricia Kuhl and colleagues showed that at 6 months, American and Japanese infants could equally well discriminate the English /r/-/l/ contrast (which does not exist in Japanese). By 10-12 months, the American infants maintained this ability while the Japanese infants had largely lost it. Conversely, the Japanese infants maintained sensitivity to phonemic contrasts relevant to Japanese that the American infants lost.

The narrowing of babbling and phonemic perception is driven by **statistical learning**â€”the infant's brain tracks the frequency and distribution of speech sounds in the ambient language and adjusts its perceptual and productive systems to match the statistical patterns of the input. Sounds that occur frequently in the language are retained and refined; sounds that are rare or absent gradually drop out.

For the EPPP, the key testable facts are that babbling is initially universal (includes sounds from all languages) and begins to narrow to native language sounds around 9 months.
