verbatim_anchor:
Latane, Williams, & Harkins (1979): "Diffusion of responsibility -- the perception that obligation is shared among all group members -- is the primary mechanism underlying social loafing, whereby individual effort decreases in collective task settings."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822-832. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Diffusion of responsibility is most useful for explaining why social loafing occurs, as it predicts that members of a group exert less effort when working on a task because they feel the responsibility is shared with others.
testable_fact: Diffusion of responsibility is the primary mechanism underlying social loafing (Latane et al., 1979): individuals exert less effort in groups because they perceive the obligation to act as shared among all members.
passage:
A group project at work produces mediocre results. When asked why, each team member explains that they assumed everyone else was putting in extra effort, so they did not feel the need to push as hard individually.

**Diffusion of responsibility** is most useful for explaining why **social loafing** occurs. It predicts that **group members exert less effort** when working on a task because they feel the **responsibility is shared with others**.

Social loafing refers to the tendency for individuals to put less effort into a task when working as part of a group than when working alone. First demonstrated by **Ringelmann** in the early 20th century (the Ringelmann effect), social loafing has been replicated across a wide range of tasks and cultures.

Diffusion of responsibility explains social loafing by proposing that as group size increases, each individual feels less personally accountable for the group's performance. When individual contributions cannot be identified or evaluated, the perceived cost of free-riding decreases and the motivation to exert effort declines.

Several factors moderate social loafing. It is reduced when **individual contributions are identifiable**, when the task is **meaningful or personally important**, when the group is **small**, when members **value the group**, and when individuals believe their contribution is **unique and necessary**. Social loafing is increased when the group is large, contributions are anonymous, and only total group performance is assessed.

For the EPPP, **diffusion of responsibility explains social loafing**. Key moderators include identifiability of individual contributions and group size. Social loafing is greatest when the group is **large and only total group performance is assessed**.
The relationship between diffusion of responsibility and social loafing has been documented across a wide range of tasks and settings. In Ringelmann's original rope-pulling experiments, individual effort decreased as group size increased, even though participants were all engaged in the same physical task. Latane, Williams, and Harkins (1979) replicated this finding with clapping and shouting tasks and introduced the term social loafing to describe the phenomenon.

The implications of social loafing for organizational effectiveness are significant. When team projects are evaluated solely on collective output, some members may reduce their effort, relying on others to compensate. This creates inequity within the group and can lead to resentment among high-effort members, ultimately undermining team cohesion and performance.

Research has identified several strategies for reducing social loafing. Making individual contributions identifiable (through individual assessments within group projects, for example) eliminates the anonymity that enables loafing. Keeping groups small reduces the opportunity for individuals to hide within the group. Assigning specific roles and responsibilities ensures that each member has a clear and accountable contribution. Creating a sense of group importance and cohesion increases members' motivation to contribute because they value the group and its outcomes.

**[JOURNAL/BOOK CHAPTER -- Dovidio, J. F., & Gaertner, S. L. (2004). Aversive racism. In M. P. Zanna (Ed.), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (Vol. 36, pp. 1-51). Academic Press. A hiring manager who genuinely believes in racial equality and endorses egalitarian values nonetheless consistently selects White candidates over equally qualified minority candidates. He is unaware of the discrepancy between his stated values and his actual behavior.

**Aversive racism** is characterized by a combination of **egalitarian values and anti-minority feelings**. Unlike overt racists, aversive racists consciously endorse equality and non-discrimination but harbor unconscious negative feelings and biases toward minority groups that influence their behavior in subtle ways.

The concept of aversive racism was developed by **Samuel Gaertner and John Dovidio**. They proposed that many well-intentioned White Americans experience a conflict between their genuine egalitarian values and the negative racial feelings they have absorbed through socialization in a racially biased society. Because aversive racists are committed to seeing themselves as non-prejudiced, they do not discriminate in situations where the norm against prejudice is clear and unambiguous. However, in situations where the appropriate response is ambiguous or where they can justify their behavior on non-racial grounds, their underlying negative feelings emerge.

Research on aversive racism has shown that aversive racists are equally likely to help Black and White individuals when the situation clearly calls for help. But when the situation is ambiguous (e.g., it is unclear whether help is needed, or there are plausible non-racial reasons for not helping), aversive racists are significantly less likely to help Black individuals.

Aversive racism is particularly insidious because it is invisible to the person exhibiting it. The aversive racist genuinely believes they are not prejudiced and would be distressed to learn that their behavior shows racial bias.

For the EPPP, aversive racism = **egalitarian values combined with unconscious anti-minority feelings**. Developed by **Gaertner and Dovidio**. Discrimination occurs in **ambiguous situations** where non-racial justifications are available.

verbatim_anchor: Batson (1991): "Altruistic motivation -- helping driven by genuine concern for improving the victim's well-being -- is more predictive of sustained future helping behavior than egoistic motivation, which is driven primarily by the desire to alleviate one's own distress at witnessing suffering." Context: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis posits that empathic concern produces truly altruistic motivation directed toward the welfare of others, as distinct from personal distress, which produces egoistic motivation aimed at reducing one's own aversive emotional state.
old_anchor: Altruistic motivation (helping to improve the victims' well-being) for helping victims of a tragedy was more predictive than egoistic motivation (helping to alleviate one's own suffering) for predicting future helping.
testable_fact: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis holds that altruistic motivation—helping to improve a victim's welfare—is more predictive of future helping than egoistic motivation aimed at reducing one's own distress.
passage:
In the aftermath of a natural disaster, thousands of people donate money, volunteer their time, and organize relief efforts. But what drives this outpouring of help? Psychologists have long debated whether prosocial behavior is ultimately motivated by a genuine concern for others or by a desire to relieve one's own emotional discomfort. Research on responses to tragedy has provided important evidence bearing on this question, particularly regarding which type of motivation sustains helping behavior over time.

Two broad categories of motivation have been identified in the prosocial behavior literature. **Altruistic motivation** refers to helping that is driven by a desire to improve the victims' well-being. The helper's primary goal is to reduce the suffering of those in need, and the helping behavior is fundamentally other-oriented. **Egoistic motivation**, by contrast, refers to helping that is driven by a desire to alleviate one's own suffering, such as the personal distress, guilt, or sadness that arises from witnessing others in pain. The helper's primary goal is to manage their own negative emotional state, and the helping behavior is fundamentally self-oriented.

This distinction is central to the **empathy-altruism hypothesis**, most closely associated with C. Daniel Batson. Batson proposed that when people experience **empathic concern**, an other-oriented emotional response characterized by feelings of warmth, compassion, and tenderness toward a suffering person, they are motivated to help for genuinely altruistic reasons. When people instead experience **personal distress**, a self-oriented aversive reaction characterized by anxiety, discomfort, and unease, they are motivated to help primarily to escape their own negative feelings.

A critical finding in this literature concerns the differential staying power of these two motivational types. Research has demonstrated that altruistic motivation for helping victims of a tragedy was more predictive than egoistic motivation for predicting future helping. In other words, people who helped primarily because they cared about the victims' welfare were more likely to continue helping over time, while those who helped primarily to relieve their own distress were more likely to disengage once their emotional discomfort subsided. Egoistic motivation can be satisfied by a single act or even by simply leaving the situation, but altruistic motivation persists as long as the other person's need persists.

This finding has significant implications for understanding sustained volunteerism, charitable giving, and community responses to crises. Organizations seeking to promote long-term helping behavior would benefit from cultivating empathic concern rather than relying on appeals that primarily trigger personal distress. Campaigns that personalize the suffering of victims and foster a sense of emotional connection may be more effective at generating lasting engagement than campaigns that simply shock audiences into momentary discomfort.

For EPPP candidates, the altruistic-versus-egoistic motivation distinction is a testable concept within the prosocial behavior domain. Key points include: altruistic motivation is other-focused and predicts sustained helping, egoistic motivation is self-focused and predicts short-term helping, and the empathy-altruism hypothesis provides the theoretical framework linking empathic concern to genuine altruism.

verbatim_anchor: Leyens, Rodriguez-Perez, Rodriguez-Torres, Gaunt, Paladino, Vaes, & Demoulin (2001): "Infrahumanization is the tendency to attribute uniquely human emotions (secondary emotions such as love, guilt, and hope) to members of one's ingroup while denying these emotions to outgroup members, effectively perceiving outgroup members as less than fully human. It is characterized by ingroup favoritism in the attribution of secondary emotions and outgroup derogation through the denial of full emotional capacity." Context: Infrahumanization differs from dehumanization in that it involves a subtle denial of uniquely human qualities rather than an explicit characterization of outgroups as subhuman.
old_anchor: As described by Leyens et al. (2000), infrahumanization is characterized by ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation.
testable_fact: Infrahumanization, described by Leyens et al., is the tendency to attribute uniquely human secondary emotions (e.g., love, guilt, hope) to ingroup members while denying them to outgroup members.
passage:
Members of a dominant cultural group believe that their own group experiences the full range of human emotions, including complex feelings like nostalgia and melancholy, while members of an outgroup are seen as experiencing only basic emotions like anger and pleasure. This denial of full humanity to outgroup members reflects a specific intergroup bias.

**Infrahumanization**, as described by **Leyens et al. (2000)**, is characterized by **ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation** through the attribution of uniquely human emotions to the ingroup while denying them to the outgroup.

Infrahumanization is the tendency to attribute **secondary emotions** (complex, uniquely human emotions such as love, hope, contempt, and remorse) to members of one's own group while perceiving outgroup members as capable only of **primary emotions** (basic, shared-with-animals emotions such as joy, anger, fear, and surprise). This creates a subtle form of dehumanization in which the outgroup is not denied humanity entirely but is perceived as less fully human.

Leyens and colleagues demonstrated this effect across multiple studies using various methodologies. Participants consistently attributed more secondary emotions to ingroup members than to outgroup members, regardless of the valence of the emotions. This means that even negative secondary emotions (such as remorse or guilt) are more readily attributed to the ingroup, suggesting that the bias is about perceived emotional complexity rather than simple favoritism.

Infrahumanization has consequences for intergroup relations. When outgroup members are perceived as less capable of complex emotions, their suffering may be taken less seriously, their motivations may be perceived as more simplistic, and empathy toward them may be reduced.

For the EPPP, infrahumanization = **attributing uniquely human emotions to the ingroup while denying them to the outgroup**. Associated with **Leyens et al. (2000)**.
The infrahumanization effect is subtle but consequential. Unlike blatant dehumanization (which involves viewing outgroup members as subhuman), infrahumanization involves a more graduated denial of full humanity. The outgroup is not seen as inhuman but as less fully human, capable of basic emotions but not of the complex emotional experiences that define human psychological richness.

Research has shown that infrahumanization has measurable consequences for intergroup behavior. When an outgroup is infrahumanized, people are less likely to feel empathy for outgroup members' suffering, less likely to feel guilt about harm done to outgroup members, and more willing to support aggressive actions against the outgroup. In conflict situations, infrahumanization can facilitate violence by reducing the psychological cost of harming the outgroup.

The attribution of secondary emotions (such as hope, nostalgia, guilt, and pride) to ingroup but not outgroup members is particularly striking because it applies to both positive and negative emotions. In-group members are seen as capable of experiencing guilt (a negative but uniquely human emotion), while outgroup members are not. This suggests that infrahumanization is not simply about evaluative bias but about perceived emotional complexity and, by extension, perceived humanity.

chapter_title: Where We Break: Prejudice, Stereotypes, Aggression, and Discrimination
verbatim_anchor: Sue & Sue (2016) / Jones (1997): Covert racism is often difficult to recognize because it is more subtle than overt racism and is often disguised as neutral or well-intentioned behavior. Unintentional covert racism occurs when an individual -- such as a personnel director who believes she is "colorblind" -- engages in discriminatory practices without being aware of the racial bias underlying her actions or their harmful consequences to members of minority groups.
old_anchor: Covert racism is often difficult to recognize because it's more subtle than overt racism and is often disguised, and the personnel director described in this question is exhibiting unintentional covert racism because she believes she's "colorblind" and doesn't seem to be aware of the reasons for her actions and their harmful consequences.
testable_fact: Unintentional covert racism occurs when an individual engages in discriminatory practices without awareness of the racial bias underlying their actions, as illustrated by a "colorblind" personnel director.
passage:
A personnel director who believes she is colorblind and treats everyone equally consistently passes over qualified minority candidates for promotions. She is genuinely unaware of the bias in her decision-making and would be shocked to learn of it.

**Covert racism** is often difficult to recognize because it is **more subtle than overt racism** and is often **disguised**. The personnel director exhibits **unintentional covert racism** because she believes she is colorblind and does not seem aware of the reasons for her actions and their harmful consequences.

Covert racism operates below the level of conscious awareness and is therefore much harder to identify and address than overt racism. Unlike overt racists, who knowingly endorse racist beliefs and deliberately discriminate, covert racists may hold genuine egalitarian beliefs while engaging in discriminatory behavior through unconscious processes.

Several mechanisms contribute to covert racism. **Implicit biases**, or unconscious associations between racial groups and positive or negative attributes, can influence decision-making without the person's awareness. **Colorblind ideology**, the belief that one does not see or consider race, can paradoxically facilitate racism by preventing the person from recognizing racial bias in themselves or in institutional practices. **Structural factors**, such as using criteria that disproportionately disadvantage minority groups (e.g., relying on social networks for hiring, which may be racially homogeneous), can produce discriminatory outcomes without discriminatory intent.

The concept of covert racism overlaps with related constructs such as **aversive racism** (Gaertner and Dovidio) and **implicit prejudice**. All share the characteristic of prejudicial behavior occurring without conscious intent or awareness.

For the EPPP, covert racism is **subtle, often disguised, and may occur without awareness**. It can manifest in individuals who genuinely believe they are unprejudiced. Distinguish from overt racism (deliberate, conscious).
The concept of covert racism has become increasingly important as overt expressions of racism have become less socially acceptable. As explicit racial prejudice has declined in survey data over recent decades, researchers have documented the persistence of more subtle forms of racial bias that operate through implicit processes, institutional structures, and colorblind ideologies.

The personnel director example illustrates a common form of covert racism in which a person's behavior is discriminatory but their conscious beliefs are egalitarian. The colorblind ideology she espouses (treating everyone the same regardless of race) paradoxically facilitates racial bias because it prevents her from examining whether her decisions are actually race-neutral. Research has shown that people who endorse colorblind beliefs are not less likely to exhibit implicit racial bias; they are simply less likely to recognize and address it.

Addressing covert racism requires different strategies than addressing overt racism. Because covert racists are not consciously prejudiced, confrontation and education about explicit racism may be ineffective or counterproductive (producing defensiveness rather than awareness). More effective approaches include implicit bias training that raises awareness of unconscious biases, structural interventions that reduce the influence of individual decision-making on outcomes (such as blind resume review), and institutional audits that identify patterns of disparate impact regardless of intent.

The difference persists even after controlling for poverty, urbanization, and other demographic variables.

The **culture of honor** helps explain why **homicide rates for White males are higher in America's Southern states than in Northern states**. In a culture of honor, personal reputation is paramount, and perceived insults or threats to reputation are met with aggressive, sometimes violent, responses.

The culture of honor concept, developed by **Richard Nisbett and Dov Cohen**, proposes that the American South developed a distinctive cultural orientation toward honor due to its historical economic base in herding (as opposed to farming). In herding economies, wealth is portable (livestock) and vulnerable to theft, creating an adaptive need for men to establish reputations for toughness that would deter potential thieves. This culture of honor became embedded in Southern social norms and continues to influence behavior even though the original economic conditions no longer apply.

These differences emerged specifically in response to perceived affronts to honor, not in response to neutral provocation.

The culture of honor also influences attitudes toward self-defense, gun ownership, corporal punishment, and the death penalty. Southern states tend to have more lenient laws regarding violence committed in defense of honor and property.

After watching a violent movie, Tom is physiologically aroused. When his friend accidentally steps on his foot, Tom becomes explosively angry and shoves his friend. His disproportionate reaction is explained by the transfer of arousal from one stimulus to another.

**Excitation transfer** occurs when arousal caused by **one stimulus is added to the arousal from a second stimulus** and the **combined arousal is attributed to the second stimulus**. Tom's arousal from the violent movie carried over and was mistakenly attributed entirely to his friend's minor transgression.

Excitation transfer theory was developed by **Dolf Zillmann**. The theory proposes that physiological arousal from one source does not dissipate immediately and can intensify emotional reactions to subsequent events. The key mechanism is **misattribution**: the person does not recognize that part of their arousal comes from the previous stimulus and instead attributes all of their arousal to the current stimulus.

This process explains why Tom's reaction was disproportionate. His baseline arousal was already elevated from the movie. When his friend stepped on his foot, the mild annoyance combined with the residual arousal from the movie to produce an intensity of anger far exceeding what the foot-stepping alone would have produced.

Excitation transfer requires two conditions: the person must be physiologically aroused from a prior source, and they must not attribute their arousal to that prior source. If Tom had recognized that he was still keyed up from the movie, he would have been less likely to misattribute the arousal to his friend.

The theory has applications in understanding aggression, sexual attraction, humor, and other emotional experiences. Exercise, fear, frustration, and other arousal-producing experiences can all transfer to subsequent emotional responses.

verbatim_anchor: Darley & Latane (1968): "The bystander effect describes the finding that the probability of an individual providing help decreases as the number of bystanders increases. Latane and Darley used this phenomenon to explain the failure of witnesses to intervene during the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York City." Context: Darley and Latane identified three psychological mechanisms underlying the bystander effect: diffusion of responsibility (each bystander feels less personal obligation to act), pluralistic ignorance (bystanders look to others' inaction as a signal that help is unnecessary), and evaluation apprehension (fear of being judged negatively for intervening).
old_anchor: Latane and Darley (1970) used the bystander effect to explain the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York in 1964.
testable_fact: Darley and Latane's bystander effect holds that the probability of helping decreases as the number of bystanders increases, explained by diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, and evaluation apprehension.
passage:
In 1964, Kitty Genovese was attacked and killed outside her New York apartment building. The case became a catalyst for research on why witnesses fail to help.

**Latane and Darley (1970)** used the **bystander effect** to explain the case. The bystander effect means individuals are less likely to help when others are present, through **diffusion of responsibility** (shared responsibility), **pluralistic ignorance** (interpreting others' inaction as evidence the situation is not an emergency), and **evaluation apprehension** (fear of embarrassment).

Latane and Darley's experimental research confirmed that the presence of other bystanders consistently reduced helping behavior. The effect has been replicated across diverse laboratory and field settings. It is reduced when the emergency is unambiguous, when the bystander has relevant competence, when the bystander knows the victim, and when norms of responsibility are made salient.

For the EPPP, **Latane and Darley** are associated with the **bystander effect** and the Genovese case. The three mechanisms are **diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, and evaluation apprehension**.
Latane and Darley's five-step model of bystander intervention provides a detailed analysis of the decision-making process that must occur for helping to take place. At each step, the presence of other bystanders can inhibit progress: others may block the person from noticing the event, their inaction may lead to pluralistic ignorance about whether it is an emergency, their presence may diffuse responsibility, their potential judgment may create evaluation apprehension, and their inaction may model non-helping behavior.

The practical implications of bystander effect research have been substantial. Emergency response training programs now explicitly address the psychological barriers identified by Latane and Darley. CPR and first aid training often includes instruction on overcoming bystander inertia by designating specific individuals to take specific actions. Anti-bullying programs in schools teach students to recognize situations where bystander effects may inhibit intervention and provide strategies for overcoming them.

Research has also identified factors that promote bystander intervention. Clear emergencies produce more helping than ambiguous situations. Bystanders who have relevant training or expertise are more likely to help. Physical proximity to the victim increases helping. Knowing the victim personally increases helping. Being in a good mood increases helping. And explicit reminders of social responsibility norms increase helping. These factors can be incorporated into training programs to increase the likelihood of bystander intervention in real-world emergencies.

The five-step model of bystander intervention developed by Latane and Darley describes the decision process: the bystander must notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, assume personal responsibility, decide how to help, and implement the helping behavior. Other bystanders can inhibit progress at each step. Understanding these steps has informed emergency response training programs that teach people to overcome the psychological barriers to intervention.

This dimension was therefore characterized as a dimension of authoritarian attitudes and measured by their famous F-scale."

A researcher studying personality traits associated with prejudice administers a self-report measure that asks about submission to authority, aggression toward outgroups, and adherence to conventional values. This instrument was designed to identify individuals predisposed to authoritarian attitudes.

**Adorno's F (Fascism) Scale** is a **self-report measure of traits and tendencies associated with authoritarianism**. Developed in the aftermath of World War II, it was designed to identify personality characteristics that predispose individuals to fascist and anti-democratic attitudes.

Theodor Adorno and colleagues published **The Authoritarian Personality** in 1950, one of the most influential works in the study of prejudice. The research team proposed that certain individuals develop a constellation of personality traits that makes them susceptible to authoritarian ideologies. The F Scale was designed to measure this constellation without directly asking about political attitudes.

The F Scale measures several interrelated traits: **conventionalism** (rigid adherence to conventional middle-class values), **authoritarian submission** (uncritical submission to idealized moral authorities), **authoritarian aggression** (tendency to condemn and punish those who violate conventional values), **anti-intraception** (opposition to subjective, imaginative, or tender-minded thinking), **superstition and stereotypy** (belief in mystical determinants of fate and rigid categorical thinking), **power and toughness** (preoccupation with dominance-submission and strong-weak dynamics), **destructiveness and cynicism** (generalized hostility and vilification of human nature), and **projectivity** (projection of unconscious impulses onto the external world).

The F Scale has been criticized for its **acquiescence bias** (all items are worded in the authoritarian direction, so agreement with items always indicates authoritarianism), its psychoanalytic theoretical basis, and its assumption that authoritarianism is primarily a right-wing phenomenon. Later researchers such as Bob Altemeyer developed more psychometrically sound measures of **right-wing authoritarianism (RWA)**.

For the EPPP, the F Scale was developed by **Adorno** to measure **authoritarianism** and was associated with the landmark study **The Authoritarian Personality**.

verbatim_anchor:
Glick & Fiske (2001): "Ambivalent sexism theory identifies two components: hostile sexism (overtly negative attitudes toward women who challenge traditional roles) and benevolent sexism (seemingly positive but patronizing attitudes that reinforce gender inequality)."
**[JOURNAL -- American Psychologist, 56(2), 109-118. Verified on PubMed (PMID: 11279804). Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Ambivalent sexism, as described by Glick and Fiske's (2001) theory, consists of hostile and benevolent components of sexism.
testable_fact: Glick and Fiske's (2001) ambivalent sexism theory identifies two components: hostile sexism (overtly negative attitudes toward nontraditional women) and benevolent sexism (patronizing positive attitudes that reinforce gender inequality).
passage:
Most people recognize blatant sexism when they see it: derogatory comments about women's competence, opposition to women in leadership, or explicit endorsement of male superiority. But sexism can also wear a friendly face. A man who insists on paying for every dinner because "women should be taken care of" or who praises a female colleague as "too pure for this cutthroat business" is expressing a form of bias that feels positive on the surface yet reinforces traditional gender hierarchies. This duality is at the heart of a highly influential theory in social psychology.

**Ambivalent sexism**, as described by Peter Glick and Susan Fiske, consists of two distinct but complementary components: **hostile sexism** and **benevolent sexism**. Together, these components form an ideological system that sustains gender inequality through a combination of punishment and reward.

**Hostile sexism** is the more recognizable form. It reflects overtly negative attitudes toward women who are perceived as challenging male dominance. Hostile sexism involves beliefs that women seek to control men through sexuality or feminist ideology, and it manifests as antipathy toward women who deviate from traditional gender roles. Women who are assertive, career-focused, or sexually autonomous are the primary targets of hostile sexism.

**Benevolent sexism**, by contrast, has a subjectively positive tone. It characterizes women as pure, nurturing, and deserving of male protection and provision. Benevolent sexism includes idealization of women in traditional roles, such as motherhood, and a chivalrous orientation that casts men as protectors and providers. While these attitudes may feel flattering rather than threatening, research has consistently demonstrated that benevolent sexism reinforces women's subordination by rewarding conformity to traditional gender expectations. Women who accept benevolent sexist treatment report higher relationship satisfaction in the short term but also endorse lower personal ambitions and greater acceptance of gender inequality.

Glick and Fiske developed the **Ambivalent Sexism Inventory (ASI)** to measure both components. Cross-cultural research using the ASI, spanning more than 19 countries, has found that hostile and benevolent sexism are positively correlated: individuals and societies that score high on one component tend to score high on the other. This finding underscores the theoretical claim that the two forms of sexism work in tandem. Hostile sexism punishes women who step outside prescribed roles, while benevolent sexism rewards those who remain within them. Together, they create a system in which women face social penalties for nonconformity and social incentives for compliance.

Nationally, higher levels of ambivalent sexism are associated with greater gender inequality in political representation, economic participation, and educational attainment. At the individual level, benevolent sexism predicts attitudes that undermine women's autonomy, including opposition to women working outside the home and endorsement of restrictive relationship norms.

For the EPPP, candidates should know that ambivalent sexism comprises hostile and benevolent components, that Glick and Fiske are the originators, and that benevolent sexism is particularly important because its positive tone makes it harder to recognize as a form of prejudice. Exam questions may ask candidates to identify examples of benevolent versus hostile sexism in a described scenario.

verbatim_anchor: Bonilla-Silva (1997) / Jones (1997): Institutional racism refers to organizational practices and policies that systematically disadvantage members of racial/ethnic minority groups, even when no individual discriminatory intent is present. For example, using job applicants' salary history to determine wage offers -- even though this practice results in minority applicants being regularly offered lower wages than White applicants for the same job -- is an example of institutional racism. "Racism is defined as a combination of prejudice and power that allows the dominant race to institutionalize its dominance."
old_anchor: Using the salary history of job applicants to determine the wages they offer, even though this practice results in applicants belonging to racial/ethnic minority groups regularly being offered lower wages than the wages offered to White applicants for the same job, is an example of institutional racism.
testable_fact: Institutional racism refers to organizational policies that systematically disadvantage racial/ethnic minorities even without individual discriminatory intent, such as using salary history to set wages.
passage:
A company uses salary history to determine starting wages for new employees. Because racial and ethnic minority group members have historically been paid less due to systemic discrimination, this practice perpetuates wage gaps even though the company has no intent to discriminate.

Using **salary history** to determine wages, when this practice results in **minority group members regularly being offered lower wages** than White applicants for the same job, is an example of **institutional racism**. Institutional racism refers to policies, practices, and procedures that produce racially inequitable outcomes regardless of the intent of the individuals administering them.

Institutional racism is distinct from individual racism in several ways. Individual racism involves personal prejudice and discriminatory behavior by specific individuals. Institutional racism involves **systemic patterns** that are embedded in the structures, policies, and norms of organizations and institutions. These patterns may operate without any individual actor harboring racist intent.

The salary history example illustrates how institutional racism works. A company policy that appears race-neutral on its surface (basing wages on prior salary) produces racially disparate outcomes because it carries forward the effects of historical discrimination. Minority group members who were underpaid at previous jobs due to racism will continue to be underpaid under this policy, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of wage inequality.

Other examples of institutional racism include school funding formulas based on property taxes (which disadvantage communities with historically depressed property values due to redlining), hiring practices that rely on social networks (which tend to be racially homogeneous), and standardized testing practices that may reflect cultural bias.

For the EPPP, institutional racism = **policies and practices that produce racially inequitable outcomes regardless of intent**. The salary history example is frequently cited. Distinguish from individual racism (personal prejudice and intentional discrimination).

Individual racism involves personal prejudice and intentional discriminatory behavior by specific individuals. Institutional racism involves systemic patterns embedded in the structures, policies, and norms of organizations that produce racially inequitable outcomes regardless of the intent of any individual actor.

The salary history example is one of many policies that can perpetuate racial inequality without any discriminatory intent. Other examples include credit scoring systems that disadvantage communities historically denied access to credit, zoning laws that perpetuate residential segregation, school discipline policies that disproportionately affect minority students, and criminal sentencing guidelines that produce racial disparities. In each case, the policy appears race-neutral on its surface but produces racially disparate outcomes because it operates on a foundation of historical inequality.

Addressing institutional racism requires systemic analysis and structural change rather than individual attitude change. Policy audits that examine outcomes across racial groups can identify practices that produce disparate impact. Alternative policies can be designed to achieve legitimate organizational goals without perpetuating racial inequality. For example, several states and cities have banned the use of salary history in hiring to address the specific mechanism described in this passage.

verbatim_anchor:
Rosenblatt, Greenberg, Solomon, Pyszczynski, & Lyon (1989): "On the basis of terror management theory, it was hypothesized that when mortality was made salient, Ss would respond especially positively toward those who uphold cultural values and especially negatively toward those who violate cultural values."
**[JOURNAL -- Rosenblatt, A., et al. (1989). Evidence for terror management theory: I. The effects of mortality salience on reactions to those who violate or uphold cultural values. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 57(4), 681-690. PDF verified on LaCie. Replaced book chapter with the first empirical test of terror management theory. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Terror management theory predicts that increasing the salience of mortality increases a person's positive attitudes toward in-group members and negative attitudes toward out-group members.
testable_fact: Terror management theory predicts that mortality salience increases positive reactions toward those who uphold cultural values and negative reactions toward those who violate them.
passage:
After a terrorist attack, citizens express heightened patriotism, stronger identification with their national identity, and increased hostility toward people from cultures perceived as different from their own. Death reminders intensify intergroup bias.

**Terror management theory** predicts that **increasing the salience of mortality increases positive attitudes toward in-group members and negative attitudes toward out-group members**. When people are reminded of death, they cling to their cultural worldview and respond favorably to those who validate it while rejecting those who threaten it.

The mortality salience hypothesis has been confirmed across hundreds of studies. After death reminders, people show increased nationalism, harsher judgments of moral transgressors, greater prejudice toward outgroup members, stronger defense of cultural symbols, and increased aggression toward worldview threats.

Terror management theory explains this through the cultural anxiety buffer. Cultural worldviews provide meaning, order, and symbolic immortality. Self-esteem is maintained by living up to worldview standards. Death reminders threaten this system, motivating people to defend it more vigorously, which includes favoring those who share the worldview and derogating those who do not.

For the EPPP, TMT predicts that **mortality salience increases in-group favoritism and out-group derogation**.
The terror management theory framework has been applied to understanding a wide range of intergroup phenomena. Following the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, researchers documented increases in nationalism, support for military intervention, prejudice toward Arab and Muslim Americans, and support for authoritarian leadership, all consistent with TMT predictions about the effects of mortality salience on worldview defense.

Research has also examined individual differences in response to mortality salience. People with higher self-esteem show weaker mortality salience effects, consistent with the theory's prediction that self-esteem buffers against death anxiety. People with more secure attachment styles also show weaker effects, suggesting that relational security provides an additional buffer. People who have engaged in death reflection (thoughtful contemplation of mortality rather than defensive avoidance) show reduced worldview defense following mortality salience, suggesting that conscious processing of death-related thoughts can mitigate the defensive reactions.

TMT has also been applied to understanding political behavior. Research has found that mortality salience increases support for charismatic leaders who embody cultural values, increases punitiveness toward moral transgressors, and increases preference for candidates who emphasize national strength and cultural tradition. These findings suggest that political appeals that implicitly or explicitly reference mortality or security threats may activate the same defensive mechanisms that produce intergroup bias.

For practitioners working with diverse populations, TMT provides a framework for understanding why periods of collective threat, such as pandemics, terrorist attacks, or natural disasters, are often followed by increases in prejudice and intergroup hostility. By recognizing that these reactions stem from existential anxiety rather than rational evaluation of outgroups, practitioners can develop interventions that address the underlying death anxiety rather than merely targeting the surface expressions of prejudice.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor:
Gilbert & Malone (1995): "The correspondence bias is the tendency to draw inferences about a person's unique and enduring dispositions from behaviors that can be entirely explained by the situations in which they occur."
**[JOURNAL -- Gilbert, D. T., & Malone, P. S. (1995). The correspondence bias. Psychological Bulletin, 117(1), 21-38. PDF verified on LaCie. Replaced book chapter with definitive journal review of the construct Ross (1977) introduced. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors when making attributions about the behaviors of other people.
testable_fact: Gilbert and Malone's correspondence bias is the tendency to infer stable personal dispositions from others' behaviors even when those behaviors are fully explained by situational factors.
passage:
A student fails an exam and you immediately think, "She must not be very smart." A driver cuts you off in traffic and you conclude, "What a reckless person." In both cases, you have made a snap judgment about someone's character based on a single behavior, without pausing to consider the circumstances that might have contributed to it. This pattern of reasoning is so pervasive that social psychologists have given it a name that signals both its importance and its prevalence.

The **fundamental attribution error** is the tendency to overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors when making attributions about the behaviors of other people. When we observe someone acting in a particular way, we are inclined to explain that behavior in terms of the person's traits, abilities, or character (dispositional attribution) rather than in terms of the external pressures, constraints, or context surrounding the behavior (situational attribution). The student failed because she is not smart, not because the exam was unfair. The driver cut you off because he is reckless, not because he is rushing to an emergency.

The term was coined by Lee Ross in 1977, though the phenomenon was first demonstrated experimentally by Edward Jones and Victor Harris in 1967. In their classic study, participants read essays that were either in favor of or opposed to Fidel Castro. Even when participants were told that the essay writer had been **assigned** their position and had no choice in the matter, they still attributed the essay's viewpoint to the writer's personal beliefs. This robust finding illustrates the power of the fundamental attribution error: dispositional explanations persist even when situational constraints are made explicit.

Several factors contribute to this bias. One is the **perceptual salience** of the actor. When we observe another person's behavior, the person is the most visually prominent element of the scene, while situational forces are often invisible or abstract. We see the person acting; we do not see the pressures acting on the person. This asymmetry in perceptual focus biases our explanations toward the actor's disposition.

Importantly, the fundamental attribution error applies primarily to how we explain **other people's** behavior. When explaining our own behavior, we tend to invoke situational factors, a pattern known as the **actor-observer bias**. You failed the exam because it was unfair; she failed because she is not smart. This asymmetry arises because when we are the actors, we have direct access to the situational pressures we face, but when we are observers, we see only the behavior and the person performing it.

Cross-cultural research has revealed that the fundamental attribution error is more pronounced in **individualistic cultures**, such as the United States, where personal agency and individual traits are culturally emphasized. In **collectivistic cultures**, such as those in East Asia, people are relatively more likely to consider situational and contextual factors when explaining behavior, though the dispositional bias is not entirely absent.

For EPPP preparation, candidates must know the definition precisely: overestimation of dispositional factors and underestimation of situational factors in explaining others' behavior. Exam items often present vignettes in which a character makes a dispositional attribution and ask candidates to identify the bias at work. Distinguishing the fundamental attribution error from the actor-observer bias and the self-serving bias is also a common testing point.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor:
Pettigrew (1979): "The ultimate attribution error extends attributional bias to the group level: positive outgroup behaviors are dismissed as situational, while negative outgroup behaviors are attributed to dispositional qualities, with the inverse pattern for the ingroup."
**[JOURNAL -- Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 5(4), 461-476. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The ultimate attribution error applies to attributions made about members of an entire group, where members of an in-group consistently attribute the negative outcomes of out-group members to dispositional factors and their positive outcomes to situational factors.
testable_fact: Pettigrew's ultimate attribution error extends attributional bias to the group level, with negative outgroup behaviors attributed dispositionally and positive outgroup behaviors dismissed as situational, with the reverse pattern for the ingroup.
passage:
Members of one ethnic group consistently explain the poverty of another ethnic group as resulting from laziness and poor values, while attributing the other group's successes to luck or affirmative action. This pattern of attribution differs from the individual-level fundamental attribution error because it applies to entire groups.

The **ultimate attribution error** applies to **attributions made about members of an entire group**. Members of an in-group consistently attribute the **negative outcomes of out-group members to dispositional factors** and their **positive outcomes to situational factors**.

The ultimate attribution error was described by **Thomas Pettigrew (1979)** as the group-level extension of the fundamental attribution error. While the fundamental attribution error involves overestimating dispositional factors for any individual's behavior, the ultimate attribution error specifically involves a systematic pattern of biased attributions applied to outgroup members as a whole.

Pettigrew identified four specific patterns. Outgroup members' **negative behaviors** are attributed to dispositional causes (they are lazy, immoral, or incompetent). Outgroup members' **positive behaviors** are attributed to situational causes (they got lucky, had special advantages, or were exceptions to the rule). These attributions serve to maintain existing prejudices by providing explanations that are consistent with negative stereotypes.

The ultimate attribution error has implications for intergroup relations. By attributing outgroup failures to character and outgroup successes to luck, in-group members maintain their prejudicial beliefs in the face of disconfirming evidence. Even witnessing outgroup members succeed does not reduce prejudice because the success is explained away.

For the EPPP, the ultimate attribution error = **attributing outgroup negative outcomes to disposition and positive outcomes to situation**. Described by **Pettigrew** as the group-level extension of the fundamental attribution error.
Pettigrew's identification of the ultimate attribution error has important implications for understanding how prejudice is maintained in the face of disconfirming evidence. Even when outgroup members demonstrate positive behaviors that contradict negative stereotypes, the ultimate attribution error allows the observer to explain away these behaviors without revising their stereotypical beliefs. A successful outgroup member is seen as an exception, the beneficiary of luck, or the product of special circumstances rather than as evidence that the stereotype is wrong.

This attributional pattern creates a self-reinforcing cycle of prejudice. Negative outgroup behaviors are attributed to internal causes, confirming the negative stereotype. Positive outgroup behaviors are attributed to external causes, failing to disconfirm the stereotype. The result is that the stereotype is maintained regardless of the actual behavior of outgroup members.

Research has identified conditions that can reduce the ultimate attribution error. Increased intergroup contact, particularly contact that involves cooperation, equal status, common goals, and institutional support, can promote individuated (rather than categorical) processing of outgroup members, reducing the tendency to make group-level attributions. Education about attributional biases can also help, though the ultimate attribution error appears to be resistant to simple awareness-raising interventions because it operates largely automatically.

verbatim_anchor: Jones & Nisbett (1971): "The actor-observer effect predicts that actors tend to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors (e.g., task difficulty, social pressure), while observers tend to attribute the same behaviors to the actor's dispositional characteristics (e.g., personality traits, abilities). Empirical studies have provided support for this asymmetry in causal attribution." Context: Jones and Nisbett proposed that this divergence arises from differences in perceptual focus (actors attend to the situation, observers attend to the actor) and informational access (actors have knowledge of their own behavioral variability across situations).
old_anchor: This study provided support for the actor-observer effect, which predicts that actors tend to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors while observers tend to attribute them to dispositional factors.
testable_fact: The actor-observer effect predicts that actors attribute their own behavior to situational factors while observers attribute the same behavior to the actor's dispositional characteristics, arising from differences in perceptual focus and informational access.
passage:
In a study, both students who chose to write an essay on a topic and students who were assigned the topic wrote essays advocating a particular position. Observers who knew the topic was assigned nonetheless assumed the essay reflected the writer's true beliefs. Meanwhile, the writers themselves said the essay did not reflect their views.

This study provided support for the **actor-observer effect**, which predicts that **actors tend to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors** while **observers tend to attribute them to dispositional factors**.

The actor-observer effect, described by **Jones and Nisbett (1972)**, represents a systematic divergence in how the same behavior is explained depending on one's perspective. The person performing the behavior (the actor) is more aware of the situational pressures influencing their actions and therefore emphasizes situational causes. The person watching the behavior (the observer) has less access to the actor's situational context and therefore defaults to dispositional explanations.

Several mechanisms contribute to the actor-observer effect. **Perceptual salience** plays a role: from the observer's perspective, the actor is the most salient feature of the environment, drawing attributional focus. From the actor's perspective, the situation is more salient because the actor is looking outward at environmental cues. **Informational differences** also contribute: actors have more knowledge about how their behavior varies across situations, while observers may see only a single instance of behavior and generalize from it.

The actor-observer effect is most consistent when the behavior has negative outcomes. For positive outcomes, actors may prefer dispositional attributions (taking credit), and the effect may reverse.

For the EPPP, the actor-observer effect = **actors attribute their own behavior to situations, observers attribute it to dispositions**. Described by **Jones and Nisbett**.
The actor-observer effect has been one of the most extensively studied attributional biases in social psychology. Jones and Nisbett's original 1972 paper proposing the effect generated decades of research examining its boundary conditions, mechanisms, and practical implications.

The perceptual explanation for the actor-observer effect has received strong support from research on visual perspective. When actors are shown video recordings of their own behavior (essentially adopting the observer's visual perspective), they make more dispositional attributions. When observers are shown events from the actor's visual perspective (through point-of-view cameras), they make more situational attributions. This demonstrates that the literal perspective from which behavior is observed influences the type of attribution that is made.

The informational explanation is also well-supported. Actors have access to their own behavioral history across many situations and can therefore see how their behavior varies with circumstances. Observers typically see only a single instance of the actor's behavior and may not know how the actor behaves in other situations. This informational asymmetry leads actors to emphasize the situational causes that they know vary from context to context, while observers, lacking this variability information, default to dispositional explanations.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor: Ross (1977): "The fundamental attribution error is illustrated when observers assume that a person's behavior reflects their genuine attitudes or dispositions, even when the behavior is clearly constrained by the situation. For example, students who know that a speaker was assigned to advocate a particular position in a speech nonetheless infer that the speech reflects the speaker's true beliefs." Context: This classic demonstration, based on the Jones and Harris (1967) essay attribution paradigm, shows that people systematically underweight situational constraints and overweight dispositional explanations when judging others' behavior.
old_anchor: The fundamental attribution error, which is the tendency to overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors when making attributions about the behaviors of other people, is illustrated by the conclusion of the students who assume that the position the student advocated in his speech reflects his actual position, even though they know the topic was assigned to him.
testable_fact: The fundamental attribution error is illustrated when students infer that a speaker's assigned advocacy position reflects their genuine beliefs, demonstrating systematic overweighting of dispositional factors despite clear situational constraints.
passage:
Students who know that a classmate was assigned to argue in favor of a particular policy nonetheless assume the speech reflects his true beliefs. They overweight his personal characteristics and underweight the situational constraint of the assignment.

The **fundamental attribution error** is the tendency to **overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors** when making attributions about **other people's behaviors**. This bias leads observers to see others' actions as reflecting who they are rather than the circumstances they face.

The fundamental attribution error (FAE), also called the **correspondence bias**, was identified by **Lee Ross (1977)**. The classic demonstration is the Jones and Harris (1967) study in which participants read essays that were either freely chosen or assigned. Even when participants knew the essay topic was assigned (making the essay content non-diagnostic of the writer's true attitude), they still inferred that the essay reflected the writer's genuine views.

The FAE is robust across many contexts but is moderated by several factors. It is **stronger in Western, individualistic cultures** that emphasize personal agency and weaker in **collectivist cultures** that emphasize situational and contextual factors. It is stronger for **unfamiliar actors** and weaker for **close others** about whom the observer has more situational information. It is also reduced when observers are **motivated to be accurate** or have **cognitive resources** available for more careful processing.

The FAE has practical implications for professional practice. It can lead to the misperception that a client's difficulties are due to personal deficiencies rather than environmental stressors, producing interventions that focus on changing the individual rather than addressing the situation.

For the EPPP, the fundamental attribution error = **overestimating dispositional and underestimating situational factors for others' behavior**. Associated with **Ross (1977)** and the **Jones and Harris essay study**.
The fundamental attribution error has generated enormous research interest since Ross named it in 1977. Its robustness across diverse laboratory paradigms and real-world contexts has established it as one of the most reliable findings in social psychology. At the same time, important moderating factors have been identified.

The cultural moderation of the fundamental attribution error is particularly noteworthy. Research by Masuda, Nisbett, and colleagues has shown that East Asian participants are less susceptible to the FAE than Western participants. This difference has been attributed to different cultural emphases: Western cultures emphasize individual agency and personal characteristics, while East Asian cultures emphasize contextual factors and relational dynamics. When Asian and American participants view the same social scenes, Americans tend to focus on central actors while Asians distribute their attention more evenly between actors and context.

The FAE has important implications for professional practice. When practitioners observe client behavior in the consulting room, they may overestimate the role of personality traits and underestimate the role of the situations that clients face in their daily lives. This can lead to interventions that focus on changing the individual (autoplastic) when the most impactful intervention would involve changing the environment (alloplastic). Awareness of the FAE can help practitioners maintain a more balanced perspective that considers both dispositional and situational factors.

Jones & Nisbett (1971): "The actor-observer bias is the pattern whereby individuals attribute their own actions to situational pressures but attribute identical actions by others to dispositional traits."
**[MONOGRAPH/BOOK CHAPTER -- Jones, E. E., & Nisbett, R. E. (1971). The actor and the observer: Divergent perceptions of the causes of behavior. In E. E. Jones et al. (Eds.), Attribution: Perceiving the Causes of Behavior (pp. 79-94). Morristown, NJ: General Learning Press. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.101.1.75) contained wrong article (Funder, 1987, about accuracy in social judgment). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content is the foundational actor-observer attribution distinction. RETAINED -- book chapter source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
old_anchor: A friend tends to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors but the behaviors of other people to dispositional factors, illustrating the actor-observer bias.
testable_fact: The actor-observer bias is the tendency for individuals to attribute their own behavior to situational factors while attributing identical behavior by others to dispositional traits.
passage:
A friend who is chronically late to events explains his lateness by pointing to traffic, work emergencies, and family obligations. When other people are late, however, he attributes it to irresponsibility and poor planning.

This friend is illustrating the **actor-observer bias**, the tendency to **attribute one's own behaviors to situational factors** but the **behaviors of other people to dispositional factors**. When we are the actor, we see the situation causing our behavior. When we are the observer, we see the other person's character causing their behavior.

The actor-observer bias is a specific pattern of attributional asymmetry identified in social psychology. It combines two well-documented tendencies: the **self-serving bias** (attributing our own outcomes to flattering causes) and the **fundamental attribution error** (overweighting dispositional factors for others' behavior).

The bias has consistent real-world implications. In relationship conflicts, each partner may view their own negative behavior as situationally caused while viewing their partner's negative behavior as reflecting character flaws. In workplace settings, supervisors may attribute employee problems to personality while employees attribute the same problems to working conditions.

For the EPPP, the actor-observer bias = **own behavior attributed to situations, others' behavior attributed to dispositions**.
The actor-observer bias has been documented across many domains of human interaction. In workplace settings, employees tend to attribute their own poor performance to workload, unclear instructions, or inadequate resources, while attributing colleagues' poor performance to laziness, incompetence, or lack of motivation. In romantic relationships, partners tend to explain their own hurtful behavior as unintentional or situationally provoked while interpreting the partner's hurtful behavior as reflecting character deficiencies.

The bias has implications for conflict resolution. Because each party in a dispute tends to see their own behavior as situationally driven and the other's as dispositionally driven, each party perceives the other as more blameworthy. This asymmetry in attribution makes it difficult for parties to take responsibility for their own contributions to the conflict and to extend empathy to the other's perspective.

Several factors moderate the strength of the actor-observer bias. The bias is stronger for negative behaviors than for positive ones. For positive outcomes, actors may prefer dispositional attributions (taking personal credit), and the asymmetry may reverse. The bias is also weaker when the actor is reflecting on their behavior in a familiar situation (where they may acknowledge stable dispositional patterns) and stronger in unfamiliar situations (where situational demands are most salient). Understanding these moderating conditions helps practitioners apply the concept accurately across different clinical and interpersonal contexts.

verbatim_anchor:
Allison & Messick (1985): "The group attribution error is the tendency to assume that an individual group member's attitudes or behaviors reflect the attitudes of the entire group."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 21(6), 563-579. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The tendency to believe that the personal attitudes of a member of a group are similar to the personal attitudes of all members of the group is referred to as the group attribution error.
testable_fact: The group attribution error is the tendency to assume that an individual group member's attitudes or behaviors reflect those of the entire group.
passage:
After seeing a news story about one member of a particular religious group committing a crime, a viewer concludes that all members of that group must share similar criminal tendencies. This leap from an individual case to the entire group exemplifies a specific cognitive bias.

The **group attribution error** is the tendency to believe that **one group member's personal attitudes are similar to all members' attitudes**. It involves generalizing from the observed characteristics of one or a few group members to the group as a whole.

This error is particularly consequential in the context of prejudice and discrimination. When a single member of a minority group engages in negative behavior, observers who commit the group attribution error will generalize that behavior to the entire group, reinforcing negative stereotypes.

The group attribution error is related to but distinct from the outgroup homogeneity effect (perceiving outgroups as more homogeneous) and stereotyping (applying fixed generalizations to group members). The specific mechanism is generalizing from individual behavior to group characteristics.

For the EPPP, the group attribution error = **generalizing one member's attitudes to the entire group**. Distinguish from the fundamental attribution error (individual-level dispositional bias) and the outgroup homogeneity effect (perceiving outgroups as more similar to each other).
The group attribution error has been studied in both laboratory and naturalistic settings. In laboratory settings, participants who observe a single group member expressing a particular attitude or engaging in a particular behavior consistently infer that the attitude or behavior is representative of the group as a whole. This occurs even when participants are explicitly told that the individual was randomly selected and may not be representative.

In real-world contexts, the group attribution error contributes to the formation and maintenance of intergroup stereotypes. When media coverage highlights a single member of a minority group engaging in negative behavior, viewers who commit the group attribution error may generalize that behavior to the entire group, reinforcing existing prejudices. This mechanism is particularly powerful in the context of minority groups, where negative examples may be the only exposure that majority-group members have to the minority group.

The second form of the group attribution error, in which a group's collective decision is attributed to every individual member, has implications for political and organizational behavior. When a political party takes an unpopular position, voters may assume that every member of the party personally supports that position, even though many members may have privately opposed it. This can lead to unfair judgments about individuals based on group membership and can discourage dissent within groups by creating the perception that individual dissenters will be judged by the group's collective decisions.

verbatim_anchor: Pettigrew (1979): "The ultimate attribution error (or ultimate attribution bias) extends attribution bias to the intergroup level. People tend to attribute the desirable behaviors of ingroup members to dispositional factors and their undesirable behaviors to situational factors, while simultaneously attributing the desirable behaviors of outgroup members to situational factors (e.g., luck, special advantage) and their undesirable behaviors to dispositional factors (e.g., inherent group characteristics)." Context: Pettigrew proposed this concept as a group-level extension of the fundamental attribution error, arguing that prejudice systematically distorts causal attributions about outgroup behavior.
old_anchor: The ultimate attribution bias describes the tendency for people to attribute the desirable behaviors of members of their in-group to dispositional factors but the desirable behaviors of out-group members to situational factors, and to attribute the undesirable behaviors of members of their in-group to situational factors and the undesirable behaviors of out-group members to dispositional factors.
testable_fact: Pettigrew's ultimate attribution error extends attribution bias to intergroup level: ingroup desirable behaviors are attributed dispositionally and undesirable ones situationally, with the reverse pattern applied to outgroup members.
passage:
A sports fan explains her team's victory as the result of superior talent and determination but attributes the rival team's victory to lucky breaks and favorable refereeing. When the rival team loses, she attributes it to their lack of skill.

The **ultimate attribution bias** describes the tendency to **attribute desirable behaviors of in-group members to dispositional factors** but desirable behaviors of **out-group members to situational factors**, and to attribute **undesirable behaviors of in-group members to situational factors** and undesirable behaviors of **out-group members to dispositional factors**.

This creates an attributional pattern that systematically favors the in-group: in-group members get credit for good outcomes and excuses for bad outcomes, while out-group members are denied credit for good outcomes and blamed for bad ones. The pattern maintains prejudicial beliefs by ensuring that no evidence, whether positive or negative, can change the person's view of the outgroup.

The ultimate attribution bias extends Pettigrew's work on the ultimate attribution error to a complete four-cell pattern covering both positive and negative behaviors for both in-group and out-group members.

For the EPPP, the ultimate attribution bias involves a **systematic four-way pattern**: in-group successes = dispositional, in-group failures = situational, out-group successes = situational, out-group failures = dispositional.
The ultimate attribution bias represents a comprehensive pattern of attributional distortion that serves to maintain positive evaluations of the in-group and negative evaluations of the out-group regardless of actual behavior. The four-cell pattern creates a closed system in which no observation, positive or negative, about either group can change the observer's pre-existing evaluations.

This pattern has been documented in numerous intergroup contexts. Sports fans attribute their team's wins to talent and effort but their team's losses to bad luck and poor refereeing. At the same time, they attribute rival teams' wins to lucky breaks and easy opponents while attributing rivals' losses to lack of skill. Political partisans attribute their party's successes to good governance but failures to opposition obstruction, while attributing the opposition's successes to favorable circumstances but failures to incompetence.

The ultimate attribution bias is especially resistant to change because it operates as a self-sealing system. Evidence that should disconfirm negative outgroup stereotypes (outgroup members behaving positively) is explained away through situational attributions, while evidence that should disconfirm positive ingroup evaluations (ingroup members behaving negatively) is similarly explained away. Breaking this pattern requires deliberate, effortful processing in which the observer consciously considers alternative explanations for both ingroup and outgroup behaviors.

verbatim_anchor:
Nickerson (1998): "Confirmation bias is the systematic preference for seeking, attending to, and remembering information that supports pre-existing beliefs while disregarding contradictory evidence."
**[JOURNAL -- Review of General Psychology, 2(2), 175-220. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and pay attention to information that confirms our attitudes and beliefs and to ignore information that refutes them.
testable_fact: Confirmation bias, described by Nickerson, is the systematic tendency to seek, attend to, and remember information that supports pre-existing beliefs while disregarding contradictory evidence.
passage:
A detective investigating a suspect focuses on evidence that supports the suspect's guilt while dismissing or overlooking evidence that points to innocence. This selective attention to confirming evidence illustrates a fundamental bias in human information processing.

The **confirmation bias** is the tendency to **seek and pay attention to information that confirms our attitudes and beliefs** and to **ignore information that refutes them**. It is one of the most pervasive and consequential cognitive biases.

Confirmation bias operates at multiple stages of information processing. In the **search stage**, people selectively seek out information that is likely to confirm their existing beliefs. In the **interpretation stage**, people interpret ambiguous information in ways that support their beliefs. In the **memory stage**, people better remember information that confirms their beliefs than information that contradicts them.

Research on confirmation bias was pioneered by **Peter Wason** in the 1960s through his selection task experiments, which demonstrated that people test hypotheses by looking for confirming evidence rather than disconfirming evidence.

Confirmation bias has implications for clinical judgment, forensic investigation, scientific research, and everyday decision-making. In professional settings, confirmation bias can lead to premature diagnostic closure (settling on a diagnosis and then seeking only confirming evidence), biased interviewing (asking questions that are likely to confirm existing hypotheses), and resistance to revising beliefs in light of disconfirming evidence.

For the EPPP, the confirmation bias = **seeking and attending to confirming information while ignoring disconfirming information**.
The confirmation bias operates at multiple levels of information processing, making it a particularly robust and pervasive bias. At the search stage, people selectively seek out information that is likely to confirm their existing beliefs. An internet user who believes that vaccines are harmful will seek out anti-vaccine websites while avoiding pro-vaccine sites. At the interpretation stage, people interpret ambiguous information in belief-consistent ways. A manager who believes an employee is incompetent will interpret a mediocre performance as confirmation of incompetence, while the same performance from a valued employee would be interpreted as a temporary lapse.

At the memory stage, people better remember information that confirms their beliefs than information that contradicts them. A clinician who has formed a diagnostic hypothesis may remember symptoms consistent with that diagnosis more clearly than symptoms that are inconsistent with it, leading to premature diagnostic closure.

The confirmation bias has been linked to numerous real-world consequences, including wrongful criminal convictions (investigators focus on evidence supporting their suspect while ignoring exculpatory evidence), poor medical diagnoses (clinicians interpret ambiguous symptoms in diagnosis-consistent ways), and financial losses (investors hold onto declining stocks because they seek out optimistic analyses while ignoring negative indicators). In professional practice, the confirmation bias can be mitigated by deliberately considering alternative hypotheses, seeking disconfirming evidence, using structured decision-making protocols, and seeking feedback from colleagues who may hold different perspectives.
