verbatim_anchor: Babinski (1914): Coined "anosognosia" to describe patients who were unaware of or denied their paralysis. Anosognosia is most commonly caused by damage to the right parietal lobe and is characterized by a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability. It is consistently associated with right hemisphere damage, particularly right parietal lesions.
old_anchor: Anosognosia is most commonly caused by damage to the right parietal lobe and is characterized by a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability.
testable_fact: Anosognosia, coined by Babinski (1914), is a lack of awareness of one's own physical disability most commonly caused by right parietal lobe damage.
passage:
A man suffers a severe stroke affecting the right side of his brain. When he regains consciousness, his left arm is completely paralyzed. Remarkably, when asked about his arm, he insists it is functioning normally. When the medical team demonstrates that he cannot move it, he becomes confused but continues to deny any disability. His wife reports that he tried to get out of bed and walk, seemingly unaware of his paralysis.

**Anosognosia** is a neurological condition characterized by a **lack of awareness of one's own physical disability**. It is most commonly caused by damage to the **right parietal lobe**, although lesions in the right frontal lobe, insula, and thalamus have also been implicated. The term, coined by Joseph Babinski in 1914, literally means "without knowledge of disease." Patients with anosognosia are not in denial in the psychological sense; they genuinely cannot perceive or comprehend their impairment due to disrupted neural mechanisms of self-monitoring and body awareness.

The neural basis of anosognosia involves disruption of the brain's self-monitoring and body representation systems. The right parietal lobe, particularly the **supramarginal gyrus** and **angular gyrus**, integrates proprioceptive, somatosensory, and motor feedback to maintain an online representation of the body's state and capabilities. When this region is damaged, the brain loses the ability to update its body model with information about the impairment. The **right insula** also plays a critical role in interoceptive awareness, the perception of the body's internal state, and damage to this structure has been linked to anosognosia for hemiplegia. Additionally, the **right prefrontal cortex** contributes to error monitoring and the detection of discrepancies between intended and actual motor output.

Anosognosia is distinct from but frequently co-occurs with **contralateral neglect** and **asomatognosia** (lack of recognition of part of one's own body). However, these conditions can be dissociated: a patient may show neglect without anosognosia, or anosognosia without neglect, suggesting that different components of the right hemisphere attention and body representation network subserve different functions.

The clinical significance of anosognosia is profound. Patients who are unaware of their deficits are at high risk for falls and injuries because they attempt activities beyond their current physical capabilities. They are also less likely to engage in rehabilitation, as they see no need for treatment. Anosognosia is most commonly seen following right middle cerebral artery stroke and is associated with larger lesion size, right hemisphere involvement, and acute presentation. It often improves somewhat over the weeks following stroke onset, though some patients show persistent unawareness.

Anosognosia has also been described in Alzheimer's disease, where patients may lack awareness of their cognitive decline. In this context, the condition is associated with right posterior parietal and frontal dysfunction and is correlated with disease severity.

On the EPPP, anosognosia is tested as unawareness of one's own disability, most commonly caused by right parietal damage. Distinguish from denial (a psychological defense mechanism) and from contralateral neglect (unawareness of one side of space). Questions typically describe a stroke patient who denies obvious paralysis.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Sperry (1968): "visual material projected to the right half of the field... could be described in speech and writing in an essentially normal manner. When the same visual material was projected into the left half of the field... the subject consistently denied having seen anything, or any flash of light." The left hand (right hemisphere) could retrieve the correct object by touch.
old_anchor: A split-brain patient will be able to say "knife" when the picture of a knife is projected to the right visual field, and although the patient can't say "fork," the patient will be able to pick out a fork with the left hand when the picture of a fork is briefly presented to the left visual field.
testable_fact: In split-brain patients, stimuli in the left visual field cannot be verbally reported (right hemisphere lacks speech output) but can be correctly identified by the left hand through touch, demonstrating right hemisphere nonverbal processing.
passage:
A patient who has undergone surgical severing of the corpus callosum for intractable epilepsy sits before a screen. A picture of a knife is briefly flashed to the right visual field, and the patient readily says "knife." Then a picture of a fork is flashed to the left visual field. The patient cannot say what was shown, but when asked to reach under a barrier and select the correct object with the left hand, she picks out the fork without hesitation.

This demonstration with a **split-brain patient** reveals the lateralized specialization of the two cerebral hemispheres and the critical role of the **corpus callosum** in interhemispheric communication. In the intact brain, visual information from the right visual field is processed by the left hemisphere, and information from the left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere. The corpus callosum, a massive bundle of approximately 200 million axons, allows the two hemispheres to share information. When this connection is severed, each hemisphere operates independently, and information presented to one hemisphere is inaccessible to the other.

The patient can say "knife" because the right visual field projects to the **left hemisphere**, which is dominant for language in most individuals and contains **Broca's area** and **Wernicke's area**. The left hemisphere can readily name objects it perceives. The fork, presented to the left visual field, is processed by the **right hemisphere**, which typically lacks the language production centers necessary for verbal naming. Thus, the patient cannot say "fork." However, the right hemisphere has its own perceptual and motor capabilities: it controls the **left hand** via contralateral motor pathways. The patient can use the left hand to select the fork by touch because the right hemisphere recognizes the object and can direct the contralateral hand to retrieve it.

The **split-brain research** of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, conducted beginning in the 1960s, provided foundational evidence for hemispheric specialization. Their work demonstrated that the left hemisphere is specialized for language, analytical reasoning, and sequential processing, while the right hemisphere excels at visuospatial processing, holistic perception, facial recognition, and emotional processing. Sperry received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1981 for this work.

Clinically, complete corpus callosum transection (corpus callosotomy) was historically performed as a last-resort treatment for medically intractable epilepsy. The procedure reduces the spread of seizure activity between hemispheres. Modern surgical approaches typically involve partial callosotomy, sectioning only the anterior portion, to preserve interhemispheric transfer while still reducing seizure generalization.

For the EPPP, split-brain questions follow a predictable pattern: right visual field stimuli can be named (left hemisphere processes and speaks), left visual field stimuli cannot be named but can be identified by touch with the left hand (right hemisphere processes and controls left hand). Know that the corpus callosum is the structure that was severed and that Sperry and Gazzaniga are the key researchers.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Bodamer (1947): "prosopagnosia" — patients lost the ability to recognize familiar faces, including their own reflection, while retaining the ability to recognize individuals by voice, gait, or other non-facial cues. The deficit is selective to face identity recognition.
old_anchor: Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize familiar faces.
testable_fact: Prosopagnosia, coined by Bodamer (1947), is a selective inability to recognize familiar faces, including one's own reflection, while recognition via voice, gait, or other non-facial cues remains intact.
passage:
A woman can see perfectly well. She can describe the color of someone's eyes, the shape of their nose, and the texture of their hair. Yet when her own daughter walks into the room, she does not recognize her until the daughter speaks. She can identify objects, read text, and navigate her environment without difficulty, but every face she encounters, no matter how familiar, appears as a stranger's face.

**Prosopagnosia** (also known as face blindness) is the inability to recognize **familiar faces** despite intact visual acuity and intact ability to recognize other objects. Individuals with prosopagnosia can perceive facial features, they can describe a face's components, but they cannot integrate these features into a holistic facial identity that matches a stored representation. The deficit is specific to facial recognition and does not typically extend to object recognition, reading, or other visual tasks.

The neural basis of prosopagnosia centers on the **fusiform face area** (FFA), located in the **fusiform gyrus** on the ventral surface of the **temporal lobe**, particularly in the right hemisphere. The FFA shows selective activation for faces compared to other object categories in neuroimaging studies. The **occipital face area** (OFA) in the inferior occipital gyrus provides earlier perceptual processing of facial features, while the FFA integrates these features into a holistic face representation. The **anterior temporal lobe** and **prefrontal cortex** link the perceived face to stored identity information (name, biographical details, emotional associations).

Prosopagnosia can be either **acquired** (resulting from brain damage, typically bilateral or right-sided lesions of the fusiform gyrus or its connections) or **developmental** (present from birth without any identifiable brain lesion, affecting approximately 2 percent of the population). Acquired prosopagnosia most commonly results from stroke or traumatic brain injury affecting the posterior cerebral artery territory. Developmental prosopagnosia is believed to involve disruption in the development of face-processing networks, possibly involving reduced connectivity between the FFA and other face-processing regions.

The mechanism of prosopagnosia involves a disruption in **configural processing**, the holistic perception of the spatial relationships among facial features (the distance between eyes, the relative position of nose to mouth). While individuals with prosopagnosia can process individual features (eyes, nose, mouth) through feature-based or analytic processing, they cannot combine these features into a unified facial gestalt. This is why they may use compensatory strategies such as recognizing people by voice, gait, hairstyle, or clothing rather than by face.

Clinically, prosopagnosia can cause significant psychosocial impairment, including social anxiety, difficulty in professional settings, and avoidance of social situations. It is often undiagnosed because individuals develop compensatory strategies and may not realize their experience differs from the norm.

For the EPPP, prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision. The key brain region is the fusiform gyrus (fusiform face area) of the temporal lobe. Do not confuse with visual agnosia (inability to recognize objects) or with Capgras syndrome (belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor).

chapter_title: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
verbatim_anchor: Miller & Cohen (2001): The prefrontal cortex plays "an important role in cognitive control, in the ability to orchestrate thought and action in accordance with internal goals." Specifically, lesions in the dorsolateral area of the prefrontal cortex are most likely to cause deficits in executive functions including insight, planning, judgment, abstract reasoning, set-shifting, and behavioral monitoring. The dorsolateral PFC provides bias signals that guide the flow of activity along neural pathways needed for goal-directed behavior.
old_anchor: Lesions in the dorsolateral area of the prefrontal cortex are most likely to cause deficits in insight, planning, judgment, and other executive functions.
testable_fact: Lesions in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex cause deficits in executive functions including insight, planning, judgment, abstract reasoning, set-shifting, and behavioral monitoring.
passage:
A 45-year-old executive sustains a traumatic brain injury in a motor vehicle accident. Although his IQ scores remain in the normal range after recovery, his colleagues notice dramatic changes in his work performance. He can no longer plan complex projects, struggles to shift strategies when his initial approach fails, makes impulsive decisions, and shows poor judgment in interpersonal situations. His memory and language abilities appear intact. Neuroimaging reveals damage to a specific region of the prefrontal cortex.

Lesions in the **dorsolateral** area of the **prefrontal cortex** (DLPFC) are most likely to cause deficits in insight, planning, judgment, and other **executive functions**. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, located on the lateral surface of the frontal lobe (Brodmann areas 9 and 46), is the neural substrate for the highest-order cognitive operations, collectively termed executive functions, that enable goal-directed behavior, flexible thinking, and adaptive decision-making.

Executive functions mediated by the DLPFC include **working memory** (the ability to hold and manipulate information online), **cognitive flexibility** (the ability to shift between mental sets or strategies), **planning** (the ability to formulate, evaluate, and execute multi-step sequences of actions), **abstract reasoning** (the ability to identify patterns and principles), and **judgment** (the ability to evaluate the consequences of potential actions). The DLPFC achieves these functions through its extensive reciprocal connections with posterior cortical association areas (parietal and temporal cortex), the cingulate cortex, the basal ganglia, and the thalamus.

The **Wisconsin Card Sorting Test** (WCST) is the classic neuropsychological measure of DLPFC function. In this task, participants must sort cards based on rules that change without warning. Patients with dorsolateral prefrontal damage show increased perseverative errors, continuing to sort by a previously correct rule even after the rule has changed. This perseveration reflects impaired cognitive flexibility. The **Tower of London** and **Tower of Hanoi** tests assess planning ability and are also sensitive to DLPFC damage.

The DLPFC is distinguished from other regions of the prefrontal cortex that serve different functions. The **orbitofrontal cortex** (ventral surface of the frontal lobe) is involved in emotional regulation, social behavior, and reward-based decision-making; damage here produces disinhibition, impulsivity, and personality change. The **ventromedial prefrontal cortex** integrates emotional signals with decision-making. The **anterior cingulate cortex** monitors for errors and conflicts. While all prefrontal regions contribute to adaptive behavior, the DLPFC is specifically associated with the cold, cognitive aspects of executive function.

Clinically, DLPFC dysfunction is implicated in schizophrenia (contributing to negative symptoms and cognitive deficits), major depression (reduced DLPFC activation), and ADHD (impaired executive control). The hallmark of DLPFC damage is a paradoxical pattern: relatively preserved intelligence on standard IQ tests combined with profound real-world functional impairment.

On the EPPP, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is the answer for deficits in planning, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and abstract reasoning. The orbitofrontal cortex is the answer for personality changes, disinhibition, and emotional dysregulation. Do not confuse these two prefrontal regions.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Gazzaniga, Bogen, & Sperry (1967): Patients had undergone complete surgical section of the corpus callosum as treatment for medically intractable epilepsy.
old_anchor: Sperry and Gazzaniga's (1967) "split-brain patients" had their corpus callosums severed as a treatment for severe epileptic seizures.
testable_fact: Split-brain patients studied by Gazzaniga, Bogen, and Sperry had undergone complete surgical section of the corpus callosum as treatment for medically intractable epilepsy.
passage:
In the 1960s, a radical surgical procedure was performed on a small number of patients with severe, medically intractable epilepsy. The surgeons cut the largest fiber bundle in the brain, the structure that connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres, in an attempt to prevent seizures from spreading from one hemisphere to the other. The patients who underwent this procedure became among the most famous subjects in neuroscience history.

Sperry and Gazzaniga's (1967) **split-brain patients** had their **corpus callosums** severed as a treatment for severe epileptic seizures. The **corpus callosum** is a thick bundle of approximately 200 million myelinated axons that forms the primary commissural pathway connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres. By cutting this structure, surgeons could prevent the generalization of seizure activity from one hemisphere to the other, dramatically reducing the frequency and severity of generalized seizures.

The split-brain procedure, known as **corpus callosotomy**, provided an unprecedented opportunity to study the independent functioning of each hemisphere. Roger Sperry and his graduate student Michael Gazzaniga developed ingenious experimental paradigms using tachistoscopic presentation (briefly flashing stimuli to one visual field) to study how each hemisphere processed information when it could not communicate with the other. Their research revealed that in everyday life, split-brain patients appeared remarkably normal because both hemispheres receive overlapping sensory input and because head and eye movements provide both hemispheres with access to environmental information. The dramatic disconnection effects emerged only under controlled laboratory conditions that restricted information to a single hemisphere.

Key findings from split-brain research established the principle of **hemispheric specialization**. The **left hemisphere** was found to be dominant for language production, speech, reading, writing, analytical reasoning, and mathematical calculation. The **right hemisphere** was found to be superior at visuospatial tasks, facial recognition, holistic processing, spatial reasoning, and processing emotional content of speech (prosody). Crucially, the research demonstrated that the right hemisphere possesses considerable cognitive ability despite its limited language capacity, it can understand simple words, recognize objects, and solve spatial problems, but it cannot produce speech.

The corpus callosum develops gradually throughout childhood and adolescence, with full myelination not complete until the mid-twenties. This protracted development has implications for interhemispheric cooperation during critical periods of cognitive development. Agenesis of the corpus callosum, a congenital condition in which the structure fails to develop, is associated with variable outcomes ranging from normal functioning to significant cognitive and social impairment.

Clinically, modern corpus callosotomy is still performed for intractable epilepsy, but the procedure is now typically partial (anterior two-thirds) rather than complete, preserving interhemispheric transfer through the splenium (posterior portion).

For the EPPP, know that split-brain studies were conducted by Sperry and Gazzaniga, that the corpus callosum was the structure severed, and that the procedure was performed to treat severe epilepsy. Questions focus on lateralized presentation paradigms and hemispheric specialization findings.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Gerstmann (1940): A tetrad of symptoms from lesions of the dominant (typically left) parietal lobe: (1) finger agnosia, (2) right-left disorientation, (3) agraphia, and (4) acalculia. Ataxia is not part of this syndrome; ataxia results from cerebellar pathology.
old_anchor: Damage to certain areas of the dominant parietal lobe can produce Gerstmann's syndrome, which involves four symptoms: finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia (difficulty writing), and acalculia (difficulty performing simple mathematical operations), but not ataxia (loss of muscle control), which is usually caused by damage to the cerebellum.
testable_fact: Gerstmann's syndrome, caused by lesions of the dominant (left) parietal lobe, consists of four symptoms: finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia; ataxia is not part of this syndrome and results from cerebellar damage.
passage:
A 52-year-old right-handed man presents to a neurology clinic after a stroke. During examination, he cannot identify which of his fingers the neurologist is touching (finger agnosia), he confuses left and right, he cannot write (agraphia), and he cannot perform simple arithmetic (acalculia). His speech, comprehension, memory, and motor strength are otherwise intact. This specific cluster of four deficits points to a well-defined neurological syndrome.

**Gerstmann's syndrome** is caused by damage to certain areas of the **dominant parietal lobe** (usually the left parietal lobe in right-handed individuals, specifically the angular gyrus region) and involves four characteristic symptoms: **finger agnosia** (inability to identify or distinguish one's own fingers), **left-right confusion** (inability to distinguish left from right), **agraphia** (difficulty writing), and **acalculia** (difficulty performing simple mathematical operations). Notably, **ataxia** (loss of muscle control and coordination) is NOT a symptom of Gerstmann's syndrome; ataxia is typically caused by damage to the **cerebellum**.

The **angular gyrus** (Brodmann area 39) in the left parietal lobe is the critical lesion site for Gerstmann's syndrome. This region sits at the junction of the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes and serves as a multimodal association area that integrates visual, auditory, and somatosensory information. It is critical for cross-modal mapping, the process of linking different representational systems, which underlies the ability to associate written symbols with spoken language (required for writing), to map numerical symbols onto quantity representations (required for calculation), to represent the spatial layout of the hand (required for finger identification), and to orient to left versus right spatial directions.

The four symptoms of Gerstmann's syndrome are believed to be related through their common dependence on the angular gyrus's role in **spatial and symbolic representation**. Finger recognition requires a spatial body schema that maps individual digits. Left-right discrimination requires a spatial reference frame for laterality. Writing requires the spatial sequencing and motor planning of letter forms. Calculation requires the spatial manipulation of numerical quantities. All four functions depend on the angular gyrus's capacity for cross-modal spatial representation.

The existence of Gerstmann's syndrome as a unified clinical entity has been debated. Some researchers argue that the four symptoms co-occur simply because the neural substrates are anatomically adjacent rather than functionally unified. Others maintain that the syndrome reflects damage to a common underlying cognitive process. Regardless of this debate, the clinical utility of recognizing the four-symptom cluster remains, as it localizes the lesion to the dominant parietal lobe with considerable specificity.

For the EPPP, Gerstmann's syndrome requires memorizing the four symptoms: finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia, and acalculia. The location is the dominant (usually left) parietal lobe, specifically the angular gyrus. The classic exam trap is including ataxia as a symptom, which is WRONG. Ataxia is a cerebellar symptom.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Wernicke (1874): Aphasia with severely impaired auditory and reading comprehension, fluent speech with paraphasias, neologisms, and semantic errors ("word salad"), and impaired repetition.
old_anchor: Individuals with Wernicke's aphasia have impaired comprehension of spoken and written language and fluent speech that's devoid of meaning.
testable_fact: Wernicke's aphasia, described by Wernicke (1874), is characterized by severely impaired auditory and reading comprehension, fluent but meaningless speech with paraphasias and neologisms, and impaired repetition.
passage:
A 70-year-old man suffers a stroke affecting the posterior region of his left temporal lobe. Afterward, he speaks fluently and at a normal rate, but his speech is largely meaningless. He uses real words but combines them in nonsensical ways, producing sentences like "The flinder was garting in the pluckish." He cannot understand what others say to him and does not seem aware that his own speech is incomprehensible.

Individuals with **Wernicke's aphasia** (also called receptive aphasia or fluent aphasia) have impaired comprehension of spoken and written language and produce **fluent speech that is devoid of meaning**. Wernicke's area is located in the **posterior portion of the left superior temporal gyrus** (Brodmann area 22) and is named after the German neurologist Carl Wernicke, who described this syndrome in 1874.

The speech output in Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by normal fluency, rate, prosody, and grammatical structure, but with severe content impairment. Patients produce **paraphasias** (word substitutions), including semantic paraphasias (substituting a related word, such as "chair" for "table"), phonemic paraphasias (substituting similar-sounding syllables), and neologisms (nonexistent words). In severe cases, speech degenerates into **jargon aphasia**, a stream of fluent but entirely meaningless output. Reading comprehension and writing are also impaired. A critical feature is **anosognosia for the language deficit**: patients are typically unaware that their speech is incomprehensible and may become frustrated or angry when others fail to understand them.

The comprehension deficit in Wernicke's aphasia reflects damage to the neural substrate for **phonological decoding** and **lexical-semantic processing**. Wernicke's area and the surrounding posterior temporal cortex are critical for mapping the sound patterns of speech onto their meanings. When this mapping is disrupted, the patient cannot extract meaning from incoming speech, even though auditory perception itself (the ability to hear sounds) remains intact. The comprehension deficit extends to written language because reading also requires the activation of phonological and semantic representations.

The distinction between Wernicke's and Broca's aphasia was foundational for the classical **Wernicke-Geschwind model** of language processing, which proposed that comprehension is mediated by Wernicke's area, production by Broca's area, and the connection between them by the **arcuate fasciculus**. While this model has been refined by modern network approaches, the basic dissociation between fluent/receptive and nonfluent/expressive aphasia remains clinically useful.

Clinically, Wernicke's aphasia carries a more guarded prognosis for language recovery than Broca's aphasia. Because patients are often unaware of their deficit, they may be less motivated to engage in language therapy. Recovery depends on lesion size, patient age, and the integrity of surrounding language areas.

On the EPPP, Wernicke's aphasia is fluent speech that lacks meaning plus impaired comprehension. The location is the left superior temporal gyrus. Contrast with Broca's (nonfluent speech, intact comprehension) and conduction aphasia (intact comprehension, fluent speech, impaired repetition). Remember: Wernicke's = Wordy but wrong.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Geschwind (1965): Conduction aphasia results from disconnection between Wernicke's area and Broca's area due to arcuate fasciculus damage. Hallmark is "a disproportionate impairment of repetition in the face of fluent, well-articulated speech and relatively preserved auditory comprehension."
old_anchor: Conduction aphasia, which is usually caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus, is characterized by fluent spontaneous speech, normal comprehension, and impaired repetition.
testable_fact: Conduction aphasia, caused by arcuate fasciculus damage disconnecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas, is hallmarked by disproportionately impaired repetition with fluent speech and relatively preserved auditory comprehension.
passage:
A patient can understand everything said to her and can speak fluently and spontaneously. However, when asked to repeat a phrase spoken by the examiner, such as "no ifs, ands, or buts," she fails badly, producing phonemic errors and struggling to reproduce the exact words. Her speech is fluent, her comprehension is normal, but her repetition is severely impaired. This dissociation points to a disruption of a specific white matter tract.

**Conduction aphasia** is usually caused by damage to the **arcuate fasciculus**, a major white matter tract that connects Wernicke's area in the posterior temporal lobe to Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus. It is characterized by **fluent spontaneous speech**, **normal comprehension**, and severely **impaired repetition**. The patient can understand language and can produce meaningful, grammatically correct speech, but cannot accurately repeat words, phrases, or sentences spoken by the examiner.

The arcuate fasciculus serves as the primary communication pathway in the classical Wernicke-Geschwind model of language. According to this model, repetition requires that auditory language input be processed in Wernicke's area, transmitted via the arcuate fasciculus to Broca's area, and then converted into motor speech output. When the arcuate fasciculus is damaged, this transmission is disrupted. Wernicke's area can still process incoming language (comprehension is intact), and Broca's area can still generate speech (spontaneous speech is fluent), but the direct connection between them is broken, making repetition impossible or error-prone.

A distinctive feature of conduction aphasia is the presence of frequent **phonemic paraphasias** during repetition attempts: the patient substitutes, transposes, or omits phonemes while attempting to repeat the target word. For example, when asked to repeat "catastrophe," the patient might say "catastophe" or "catrasaphe." Patients are typically aware of their errors and make repeated attempts to self-correct, a behavior called **conduit d'approche**. This self-correction behavior distinguishes conduction aphasia from Wernicke's aphasia, in which patients are usually unaware of their errors.

Modern neuroimaging research has expanded the anatomical understanding of conduction aphasia beyond the arcuate fasciculus alone. Damage to the left **supramarginal gyrus** in the inferior parietal lobe, which serves as a relay station in the dorsal language pathway, can also produce conduction aphasia. The condition may result from damage to either the white matter tract (the arcuate fasciculus) or the cortical area (the supramarginal gyrus) that the tract connects.

Clinically, conduction aphasia is less common than Broca's or Wernicke's aphasia and typically results from stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory. The prognosis for recovery is generally favorable because comprehension and spontaneous speech are preserved, and the repetition deficit may improve substantially with speech-language therapy.

For the EPPP, conduction aphasia has a classic triad: fluent speech, intact comprehension, impaired repetition. The damaged structure is the arcuate fasciculus. The distinguishing feature from Wernicke's aphasia is that comprehension is intact. The distinguishing feature from Broca's aphasia is that speech is fluent.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Goldenberg (2009): Apraxia is "a disorder of motor control which can be referred neither to 'elemental' motor deficits nor to general cognitive impairment." Three domains are susceptible: imitation of gestures, performance of meaningful gestures on command, and use of tools and objects. Most commonly associated with left parietal lobe lesions.
old_anchor: Ideomotor apraxia is usually caused by damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe.
testable_fact: Apraxia, a disorder of motor control not attributable to elemental motor deficits or general cognitive impairment, is most commonly associated with left parietal lobe lesions affecting gesture imitation, meaningful gesture performance, and tool use.
passage:
A neurologist asks a patient to demonstrate how to use a hammer. The patient stares at the examiner and makes vague, uncoordinated movements that bear no resemblance to the hammering action. Yet when handed an actual hammer and nail, the patient performs the task correctly. The ability to execute the movement automatically but not on command points to a specific type of motor programming deficit.

**Ideomotor apraxia** is usually caused by damage to the **left (dominant) parietal lobe** and is characterized by an inability to perform learned, skilled motor movements on verbal command or imitation, despite intact motor strength, sensation, and comprehension. The patient understands what is being asked, has the physical capacity to perform the movement, but cannot translate the verbal instruction or visual demonstration into the correct motor plan. Paradoxically, the patient may be able to perform the same action spontaneously in the appropriate context.

The **left parietal lobe**, particularly the **inferior parietal lobule** (supramarginal gyrus and angular gyrus), stores the **motor engrams** or representations of learned skilled movements. These representations specify the spatial and temporal parameters of complex actions: the trajectory, timing, force, and sequencing of movements required to use tools, make gestures, and perform skilled acts. When these representations are damaged, the patient cannot generate the correct motor plan when asked to pantomime or imitate the action, even though the primary motor pathways are intact.

The neuroanatomical model of praxis proposed by Geschwind and later elaborated by Heilman and Rothi identifies a network including the left inferior parietal lobule (where movement representations are stored), the left premotor cortex (where these representations are converted into motor programs), and the primary motor cortex (which executes the movement). Ideomotor apraxia can result from damage to any of these nodes or to the white matter connections between them, but left parietal lesions are the most common cause. The left hemisphere's dominance for praxis mirrors its dominance for language, and the two functions share the left inferior parietal lobule as a critical neural substrate.

The dissociation between impaired command performance and preserved automatic performance is a hallmark of ideomotor apraxia. This dissociation suggests that automatic, context-driven movements may be mediated by a separate neural pathway that does not require access to the left parietal motor engrams. When the correct tool is placed in the patient's hand, the tactile and contextual cues may activate a direct route from sensory input to motor output that bypasses the damaged parietal representations.

Clinically, ideomotor apraxia is common after left hemisphere stroke but is frequently underdiagnosed because it may be masked by coexisting aphasia or hemiparesis. Standard bedside testing involves asking the patient to pantomime tool use and imitate meaningless gestures.

On the EPPP, ideomotor apraxia is associated with the left (dominant) parietal lobe. The key feature is impaired pantomiming on command with preserved automatic performance. Distinguish from ideational apraxia (inability to sequence multi-step actions) and limb-kinetic apraxia (inability to make precise finger/hand movements).

chapter_title: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
verbatim_anchor: Sandson & Albert (1984): "Stuck-in-set perseveration, the inappropriate maintenance of a current category or framework, involves an underlying process deficit in executive functioning and is related neuroanatomically to frontal lobe damage." Patients repeat a previously correct response even after task demands have changed.
old_anchor: Damage to the frontal lobe causes perseveration, which involves repetition of the same response or action when it's inappropriate to do so in a variety of situations and on a variety of tasks.
testable_fact: Frontal lobe damage causes perseveration, specifically stuck-in-set perseveration, in which patients inappropriately repeat a previously correct response even after task demands have changed.
passage:
A patient who has suffered a traumatic brain injury to the frontal lobe is given a card-sorting task. He is told to sort cards by color, and he does so correctly. When the rule changes to sorting by shape, he continues sorting by color despite being told the rule has changed. He repeats the same incorrect response over and over, unable to shift to the new strategy.

Damage to the **frontal lobe** causes **perseveration**, which involves the repetition of the same response or action when it is inappropriate to do so, across a variety of situations and tasks. Perseveration reflects a fundamental failure of **cognitive flexibility**, the ability to adapt behavior in response to changing environmental demands. The patient becomes "stuck" on a previously correct or habitual response and cannot inhibit it in favor of a new, appropriate response.

The frontal lobes, particularly the **prefrontal cortex**, are the neural substrate of executive control, the set of higher-order cognitive processes that regulate and direct behavior. Executive control includes the ability to inhibit prepotent responses, shift between mental sets, update working memory, monitor performance, and detect errors. Perseveration results from impairment in **response inhibition** (the inability to suppress the previous response) and **set shifting** (the inability to adopt a new behavioral rule), both of which depend on the integrity of the prefrontal cortex.

There are several types of perseveration. **Stuck-in-set perseveration** (also called set-level perseveration), as seen in the card-sorting example, involves continued application of a previously correct rule or strategy. **Recurrent perseveration** involves the unintentional repetition of a previous response to a new stimulus (for example, naming every object shown as "fork" after having correctly named a fork earlier). **Continuous perseveration** involves the inappropriate repetition or prolongation of an ongoing behavior (for example, drawing extra loops when asked to draw a circle).

The **Wisconsin Card Sorting Test** (WCST) is the gold standard neuropsychological measure of set-level perseveration. In this task, perseverative errors, continuing to sort by a previously correct rule after the rule has changed, are the hallmark indicator of frontal lobe dysfunction. The **Luria hand sequencing test**, in which the patient must reproduce a series of three hand positions, is sensitive to motor perseveration.

Clinically, perseveration is seen in a wide range of conditions affecting the frontal lobes, including traumatic brain injury, frontal lobe stroke, frontotemporal dementia, and schizophrenia. In everyday life, perseveration manifests as difficulty switching topics in conversation, repetitive speech, inability to change plans when circumstances shift, and difficulty stopping an activity once started.

For the EPPP, perseveration is the key behavioral sign of frontal lobe damage. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test is the classic assessment. Know that perseveration involves repeating responses that are no longer appropriate and that it reflects impaired executive function, not a memory or language deficit.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Gazzaniga (1967): In split-brain patients with a severed corpus callosum, when a compound word such as "COPYCAT" is presented so that "COPY" falls in the left visual field (right hemisphere) and "CAT" in the right visual field (left hemisphere), the patient will verbally report "CAT" (left hemisphere language production) but will point to "COPY" with the left hand (right hemisphere motor control). The two hemispheres process their respective visual fields independently and cannot share information across the severed callosum.
old_anchor: A split-brain patient presented with the word "COPYCAT" will say "CAT" and point to "COPY" with their left hand, as the left visual field and right hemisphere cannot communicate with the right visual field and left hemisphere.
testable_fact: In split-brain patients, presenting "COPYCAT" across the visual midline causes the patient to verbally report "CAT" (left hemisphere) while pointing to "COPY" with the left hand (right hemisphere), demonstrating independent hemispheric processing after corpus callosum severance.
passage:
A split-brain patient sits before a screen with a fixation point in the center. The word "COPYCAT" is flashed briefly, with "COPY" appearing in the left visual field and "CAT" in the right visual field. When asked what she saw, the patient says "CAT." When asked to point to what she saw with her left hand, she points to the word "COPY." This fascinating demonstration reveals the independent processing of the two disconnected hemispheres.

When a split-brain patient is presented with the word "COPYCAT," she will say "CAT" and point to "COPY" with her left hand because the **left visual field** and **right hemisphere** cannot communicate with the **right visual field** and **left hemisphere** after the corpus callosum has been severed. This demonstrates the fundamental principle of **contralateral visual processing** combined with hemispheric specialization for language.

The explanation depends on two established neuroanatomical facts. First, visual information from the **right visual field** is processed by the **left hemisphere**, and visual information from the **left visual field** is processed by the **right hemisphere**. This contralateral organization occurs because the nasal fibers of each optic nerve cross at the optic chiasm, ensuring that each hemisphere receives input from the opposite visual field. Second, language production (speech) is typically mediated by the **left hemisphere**, specifically Broca's area and associated left-lateralized language networks.

In the intact brain, the corpus callosum would allow both hemispheres to access all the visual information, so the person would perceive the complete word "COPYCAT." In the split-brain patient, however, the severed corpus callosum prevents interhemispheric transfer. The left hemisphere receives "CAT" from the right visual field and can produce a verbal response: the patient says "CAT." The right hemisphere receives "COPY" from the left visual field but cannot produce speech because it lacks access to the left hemisphere's language production centers. However, the right hemisphere controls the **left hand** via contralateral motor pathways. When instructed to point with the left hand, the right hemisphere directs the left hand to indicate "COPY," the word it perceived.

This demonstration also reveals a phenomenon that Gazzaniga called the **left hemisphere interpreter**: when asked to explain the left-hand response, the patient's left hemisphere, which has no access to the information that drove the right hemisphere's response, will often confabulate a plausible explanation rather than acknowledging ignorance. This finding has profound implications for understanding consciousness, self-awareness, and the narrative construction of experience.

Clinically, these split-brain findings have been essential for presurgical planning in epilepsy patients being considered for callosotomy, helping surgeons and neuropsychologists anticipate and counsel patients about the potential consequences of disconnecting the hemispheres.

On the EPPP, split-brain COPYCAT-type questions test the combination of contralateral visual processing and hemispheric language lateralization. The key formula: right visual field = left hemisphere = verbal naming; left visual field = right hemisphere = left-hand pointing. Practice applying this logic to various word combinations.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Kimura (1967): Dichotic listening — when different auditory stimuli are simultaneously presented to each ear, most individuals show a right-ear advantage for verbal material (left hemisphere language dominance) and a left-ear advantage for nonverbal stimuli (right hemisphere specialization).
old_anchor: The dichotic listening task is used to obtain information about hemispheric specialization.
testable_fact: In dichotic listening, simultaneous presentation of different stimuli to each ear reveals a right-ear advantage for verbal material and a left-ear advantage for nonverbal stimuli, reflecting hemispheric specialization.
passage:
A research participant wears headphones that simultaneously deliver different auditory stimuli to each ear, a series of digits to the left ear and a series of letters to the right ear. The participant is instructed to attend to one ear and report what was heard. Researchers then analyze the accuracy of report for each ear to determine which hemisphere processes linguistic information more efficiently.

The **dichotic listening task** is used to obtain information about **hemispheric specialization** for various cognitive functions, most commonly language processing. In this paradigm, two different auditory stimuli are presented simultaneously, one to each ear, and the participant's performance in reporting stimuli from each ear reveals the relative contribution of each hemisphere to the processing of that type of stimulus.

The dichotic listening task exploits the organization of the **auditory pathways**. While each ear sends projections to both hemispheres, the **contralateral pathways** (ear to opposite hemisphere) are stronger and more numerous than the ipsilateral pathways (ear to same hemisphere). During dichotic presentation, when different stimuli compete at each ear, the contralateral pathways dominate, and the ipsilateral pathways are functionally suppressed. This means that stimuli presented to the right ear are preferentially processed by the left hemisphere, and stimuli presented to the left ear are preferentially processed by the right hemisphere.

For verbal stimuli such as words, digits, or consonant-vowel syllables, most right-handed individuals show a **right ear advantage** (REA), meaning they report more items accurately from the right ear. This REA reflects the left hemisphere's dominance for language processing: right ear stimuli travel primarily to the left hemisphere, where they are processed more efficiently by left-lateralized language areas. Conversely, for nonverbal stimuli such as melodies, environmental sounds, or emotional prosody, most individuals show a **left ear advantage** (LEA), reflecting right hemisphere specialization for these types of processing.

The dichotic listening paradigm was introduced by Doreen Kimura in the 1960s and has become one of the most widely used behavioral methods for assessing hemispheric lateralization. It provides a noninvasive alternative to more invasive procedures such as the Wada test (intracarotid injection of an anesthetic agent), which directly anesthetizes one hemisphere to determine language lateralization before neurosurgery. While the dichotic listening task provides less definitive lateralization information than the Wada test, it has the advantage of being safe, easily administered, and repeatable.

Clinically, dichotic listening performance is used in neuropsychological assessment to evaluate hemispheric function, detect lateralized processing deficits, and identify atypical language lateralization. Patients with left hemisphere lesions often show a reduced or reversed right ear advantage, while patients with corpus callosum damage may show an exaggerated right ear advantage due to impaired left ear to left hemisphere transfer.

For the EPPP, know that the dichotic listening task assesses hemispheric specialization. The right ear advantage for verbal stimuli reflects left hemisphere language dominance. The left ear advantage for nonverbal stimuli reflects right hemisphere specialization. The key researcher is Kimura.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Reed, Caselli, & Farah (1996): Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) is "a modality-specific impairment in object recognition through touch, in which basic somatosensory functions such as tactile acuity, pressure sensitivity, and proprioception remain intact." Tactile agnosia is caused by lesions in the parietal lobe, resulting in an inability to recognize familiar objects by touch despite intact somatosensory functions.
old_anchor: Lesions in the parietal lobe cause the condition of tactile agnosia, in which a person is unable to recognize familiar objects by touch following a closed head injury.
testable_fact: Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) is a modality-specific inability to recognize objects by touch despite intact basic somatosensory functions, caused by parietal lobe lesions.
passage:
Following a closed head injury from a fall, a 40-year-old woman can see and describe objects placed in front of her but cannot identify familiar objects by touch alone. When a key is placed in her hand while her eyes are closed, she can describe its shape, temperature, and weight, but she cannot name it as a key. The moment she opens her eyes, she instantly recognizes the object.

Lesions in the **parietal lobe** cause the condition of **tactile agnosia** (also called astereognosis), in which a person is unable to recognize familiar objects by touch despite intact basic somatosensory function. The patient can perceive the elementary sensory qualities of an object, such as its texture, temperature, weight, and shape, but cannot integrate these features into a unified percept that matches a stored object representation. The deficit is modality-specific: the patient can recognize the object immediately through another sensory channel, such as vision.

The **somatosensory association cortex** in the parietal lobe, particularly the **anterior intraparietal area** and the **secondary somatosensory cortex** (SII) in the parietal operculum, is responsible for the higher-order tactile processing required for object recognition by touch. Primary somatosensory cortex (S1, in the postcentral gyrus) processes basic tactile features, but the integration of these features into a coherent object representation requires the association areas of the parietal lobe. Tactile agnosia results when these association areas are damaged while S1 remains intact.

The process of recognizing an object by touch, called **haptic object recognition** or **stereognosis**, involves several stages: extraction of basic sensory features (texture, temperature, compliance), integration of these features into a three-dimensional shape representation, and matching this representation against stored object representations in semantic memory. The parietal association cortex performs the intermediate integration stage, while the matching stage involves interaction with temporal lobe semantic networks. Tactile agnosia reflects a breakdown at the integration stage.

Tactile agnosia is distinct from several related conditions. **Peripheral neuropathy** affects basic sensory transmission and would impair the perception of texture and temperature. **Anomia** (naming difficulty) would impair the patient's ability to name objects regardless of sensory modality. In tactile agnosia, the deficit is specifically in the integration of tactile features into a recognizable object percept, not in basic sensation or naming ability.

Clinically, tactile agnosia is tested by asking the patient to identify common objects placed in the hand while blindfolded. This bedside test of stereognosis is a standard component of the neurological examination and is particularly useful for detecting parietal lobe lesions. Bilateral parietal lesions can produce bilateral tactile agnosia, while unilateral lesions typically produce contralateral tactile agnosia.

For the EPPP, tactile agnosia (astereognosis) results from parietal lobe lesions and involves the inability to recognize objects by touch with intact basic sensation. Distinguish from visual agnosia (temporal lobe) and from peripheral sensory loss. The parietal lobe's role in somatosensory integration is the key concept.

chapter_title: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
verbatim_anchor: Ross (1981): The right hemisphere organizes affective components of language (prosody). Right hemisphere damage produces "aprosodias" -- impairments in production and/or comprehension of melodic, tonal, and rhythmic aspects of speech conveying emotion. Right hemisphere damage is also associated with impairments in pragmatics -- the ability to use language appropriately in social contexts, including understanding humor, sarcasm, indirect requests, and conversational inference.
old_anchor: Right hemisphere damage is associated with impairments in both emotional prosody and pragmatics.
testable_fact: The right hemisphere organizes affective prosody, and right hemisphere damage produces aprosodias (impaired production/comprehension of emotional speech melody) and pragmatic language deficits including impaired understanding of humor, sarcasm, and indirect requests.
passage:
A man who has suffered a right hemisphere stroke speaks in a flat, monotone voice with no emotional inflection. When his wife tells him exciting news, his verbal response is appropriate ("That's wonderful"), but his tone of voice conveys no enthusiasm whatsoever. He also has difficulty understanding when others are being sarcastic, joking, or speaking figuratively. He takes everything literally and misses the social subtleties of conversation.

**Right hemisphere damage** is associated with impairments in both **emotional prosody** and **pragmatics**, the aspects of language that convey meaning beyond the literal content of words. While the left hemisphere processes the linguistic content of speech (phonology, syntax, semantics), the right hemisphere processes the emotional and social dimensions of communication, including the tone of voice used to convey emotions and the contextual, nonliteral aspects of language use.

**Emotional prosody** refers to the patterns of pitch, rhythm, stress, and intonation that convey emotional meaning in speech. The right hemisphere contains regions analogous to Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the left hemisphere that are specialized for prosodic processing. The **right inferior frontal gyrus** is involved in the production of emotional prosody (generating appropriate tone of voice), while the **right superior temporal gyrus** is involved in the comprehension of emotional prosody (understanding others' emotional tone). Damage to these right hemisphere areas produces **aprosodia**, which can be expressive (flat, monotone speech), receptive (inability to interpret others' emotional tone), or both.

**Pragmatics** encompasses the social and contextual rules governing language use, including the ability to understand sarcasm, irony, humor, indirect requests, metaphor, and conversational implicature. The right hemisphere, particularly the **right prefrontal cortex** and **right temporoparietal junction**, is critical for pragmatic processing because these functions require the integration of linguistic content with contextual information, speaker intent, social norms, and theory of mind, all of which are right hemisphere-dominant processes. Patients with right hemisphere damage often show literal interpretation of figurative language, difficulty understanding jokes, inability to detect sarcasm, and reduced appreciation of the conversational context.

The combination of prosodic and pragmatic deficits following right hemisphere damage can produce significant social communication impairment even when the patient's basic language abilities (vocabulary, grammar, naming, repetition) are fully intact. This has led to the recognition of **right hemisphere communication disorder** as a clinical entity distinct from the aphasias, which are primarily left hemisphere phenomena.

Clinically, right hemisphere communication disorder is underdiagnosed because standard aphasia batteries focus on left hemisphere language functions and may not detect prosodic or pragmatic deficits. Specialized assessments such as the Right Hemisphere Language Battery and tests of prosody comprehension and production are needed.

For the EPPP, right hemisphere damage produces deficits in emotional prosody and pragmatics, not in basic language production or comprehension. The classic exam scenario describes a patient with flat emotional tone and literal interpretation of figurative language. Do not confuse with left hemisphere aphasias, which affect the linguistic content of speech.

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Rasmussen & Milner (1977): Left-hemisphere language dominance occurred in approximately 96% of right-handed individuals and approximately 70% of left-handed individuals.
old_anchor: Left-hemisphere dominance for language is found in about 95% of right-handed people and 70% of left-handed people.
testable_fact: Left-hemisphere language dominance occurs in approximately 96% of right-handed individuals and approximately 70% of left-handed individuals.
passage:
A neurosurgeon preparing to operate on a patient's left hemisphere must first determine whether the patient's language functions are located in the left hemisphere, as is typical, or in the right hemisphere, which is possible in some individuals. This determination is essential because operating on the language-dominant hemisphere without appropriate precautions could result in devastating aphasia.

**Left-hemisphere dominance for language** is found in approximately **95 percent of right-handed people** and **70 percent of left-handed people**. This statistic, established through decades of research using the Wada test, cortical stimulation mapping, and more recently functional neuroimaging, represents one of the most robust findings in neuropsychology regarding the lateralization of cognitive function.

The evidence for these lateralization statistics comes from multiple converging methodologies. The **Wada test** (intracarotid anesthetic procedure), developed by Juhn Wada in 1949, involves temporarily anesthetizing one hemisphere by injecting a short-acting anesthetic into the carotid artery and then testing the patient's language ability while that hemisphere is inactive. If language is disrupted when the left hemisphere is anesthetized, the patient is left-hemisphere dominant for language. Studies using the Wada test on hundreds of patients consistently show left-hemisphere language dominance in about 95 percent of right-handers. Among left-handers, approximately 70 percent show left-hemisphere dominance, 15 percent show right-hemisphere dominance, and 15 percent show bilateral language representation.

The neural basis for the association between handedness and language lateralization involves the **planum temporale**, an auditory association area on the superior surface of the temporal lobe that is part of Wernicke's area. In most individuals, the planum temporale is larger in the left hemisphere than in the right, and this asymmetry is correlated with left-hemisphere language dominance. The asymmetry is present at birth and is influenced by genetic factors, including variations in genes involved in brain lateralization.

The minority of left-handers who show right-hemisphere or bilateral language representation are of particular clinical significance. Bilateral language representation may provide some protection against aphasia following unilateral brain damage, as the intact hemisphere retains some language capacity. However, bilateral representation may also mean that damage to either hemisphere can produce some degree of language impairment.

Clinically, determining language lateralization is critical for presurgical planning in neurosurgery, particularly for temporal lobe resections in epilepsy surgery and for tumor resections near language-relevant cortex. Functional MRI has increasingly replaced the Wada test as a less invasive method for determining language lateralization.

On the EPPP, the key statistics are 95 percent left-hemisphere dominance in right-handers and 70 percent in left-handers. Know that left-handedness does NOT mean right-hemisphere language dominance; the majority of left-handers are still left-hemisphere dominant for language. This is a high-frequency exam question.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Vallar & Ronchi (2009): Asomatognosia is the lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, most commonly the left hemiplegic limb following right parietal lobe damage. Frequently co-occurs with anosognosia — a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness or disability — and is associated with lesions in the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction.
old_anchor: Following a stroke that caused left-sided hemiplegia, a woman exhibiting asomatognosia, which is a lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, often involving the left hemiplegic arm and accompanied by anosognosia, a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness, due to damage to certain areas of the right parietal lobe.
testable_fact: Asomatognosia, a lack of recognition of part of one's own body (most commonly the left hemiplegic limb), results from right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction damage and frequently co-occurs with anosognosia.
passage:
Following a stroke that damaged the right side of her brain, a woman develops complete paralysis of her left arm. During a hospital visit, the neuropsychologist asks her about her left arm. She looks at it blankly and says, "That's not my arm. It must belong to someone else." When shown that the arm is attached to her body, she appears confused but unpersuaded. She also denies having any physical disability whatsoever.

This woman is exhibiting **asomatognosia**, which is a lack of recognition or awareness of part of one's own body, often involving the left side following right hemisphere damage. Her denial of the paralysis itself represents **anosognosia**, a lack of awareness or denial of one's illness. Both conditions are commonly caused by damage to certain areas of the **right parietal lobe** and frequently co-occur with left-sided hemiplegia (paralysis of one side of the body).

**Asomatognosia** (literally "lack of body knowledge") specifically involves a failure to recognize or acknowledge ownership of a body part. The patient may deny that a paralyzed limb belongs to them, may attribute it to another person, or may show complete indifference toward it. In extreme cases, the patient may become hostile toward the affected limb or try to push it out of the bed. This disorder reflects damage to the brain's **body schema**, the internal neural representation of the body's structure, boundaries, and spatial configuration.

The right parietal lobe, particularly the **right inferior parietal lobule** and the **right insula**, maintains the body schema by integrating proprioceptive, somatosensory, vestibular, and visual information about the body. The **right posterior parietal cortex** processes the spatial relationships between body parts and between the body and the external environment. The **right insula** provides interoceptive awareness, the sense of the body's internal state. When these structures are damaged, the brain can no longer update or maintain an accurate representation of the contralateral body, leading to the dissociative experience of asomatognosia.

The co-occurrence of asomatognosia and anosognosia is common because both depend on the right hemisphere's role in self-monitoring and body awareness. However, the two conditions can be dissociated: some patients acknowledge their paralysis but deny ownership of the limb (asomatognosia without anosognosia), while others acknowledge the limb as their own but deny the paralysis (anosognosia without asomatognosia). These dissociations suggest that body ownership and illness awareness, while both right-hemisphere functions, are mediated by partially distinct neural circuits.

Clinically, asomatognosia and anosognosia together create a particularly challenging rehabilitation scenario. Patients who neither recognize their affected limb nor acknowledge their disability are resistant to rehabilitation efforts and at high risk for falls and injuries.

For the EPPP, know that asomatognosia is failure to recognize one's own body part and anosognosia is unawareness of one's disability. Both are associated with right parietal damage. The classic scenario involves left-sided hemiplegia with denial of both the limb and the paralysis. Do not confuse with somatoparaphrenia (delusional misidentification of a body part).

chapter_title: Language, Lateralization, and the Split Brain
verbatim_anchor: Geschwind (1965): Conduction aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, disconnecting Wernicke's area from Broca's area. Cardinal features include relatively intact auditory comprehension, fluent but paraphasic speech, anomia (impaired naming), and disproportionately impaired repetition — the hallmark deficit.
old_anchor: Conduction aphasia is characterized by relatively intact comprehension, fluent aphasia, anomia, and impaired repetition, and is caused by damage to the arcuate fasciculus.
testable_fact: Conduction aphasia, caused by arcuate fasciculus damage, is characterized by fluent but paraphasic speech, relatively intact comprehension, anomia, and disproportionately impaired repetition as the hallmark deficit.
passage:
A patient with damage to a major white matter tract connecting posterior and anterior language areas shows relatively intact comprehension and fluent speech but is severely impaired when asked to repeat words or sentences. She also has difficulty naming objects, often approximating the correct word with phonemic substitutions. This distinct pattern of preserved and impaired language abilities points to a disconnection syndrome.

**Conduction aphasia** is characterized by relatively intact comprehension, fluent speech, **anomia** (difficulty finding words), and severely **impaired repetition**. It is caused by damage to the **arcuate fasciculus**, the primary white matter fiber bundle connecting Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) to Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus). The syndrome represents a classic **disconnection syndrome** in which the language comprehension and production systems are individually intact but cannot communicate effectively with each other.

The hallmark feature of conduction aphasia is the disproportionate impairment of repetition relative to comprehension and spontaneous speech. While the patient can understand spoken language (Wernicke's area is intact) and can generate fluent, meaningful speech (Broca's area is intact), the direct transmission of auditory verbal information from Wernicke's area to Broca's area for reproduction is disrupted. Repetition requires this direct transmission because the patient must accurately reproduce the phonological form of the examiner's utterance, which requires precise transfer of the auditory representation to the speech production system.

The anomia in conduction aphasia is typically characterized by frequent **phonemic paraphasias** (sound-based errors) during naming attempts. The patient may approximate the target word through multiple attempts, progressively getting closer to the correct pronunciation, a phenomenon called **conduit d'approche**. For example, when trying to say "pencil," the patient might say "pekil...pensal...pencal...pencil." This self-correction behavior indicates that the patient has access to the semantic representation of the word (knows what it is) and can monitor their output (knows when it sounds wrong), but has difficulty translating the phonological representation into the correct motor plan for articulation.

The arcuate fasciculus is not the only white matter tract involved in language. The **extreme capsule fiber system** and the **uncinate fasciculus** provide alternative ventral pathways connecting temporal and frontal language areas. These ventral pathways may support semantic processing during language tasks, while the dorsal pathway (arcuate fasciculus) supports phonological processing. This dual-stream model explains why comprehension and semantic processing are relatively preserved in conduction aphasia while phonological repetition is impaired.

For the EPPP, conduction aphasia equals fluent speech plus intact comprehension plus impaired repetition. The damaged structure is the arcuate fasciculus. The signature behavior is phonemic paraphasias with self-correction attempts. The key distinction from Wernicke's aphasia: in conduction aphasia, the patient knows their speech is wrong and tries to fix it.

chapter_title: Parietal and Temporal Lobes: Sensation, Language Areas, and the Agnosias
verbatim_anchor: Geschwind (1975): Ideomotor apraxia is "an inability to carry out learned, purposeful movements on verbal command or imitation, despite having the physical ability and desire to perform them." Most commonly results from damage to the left (dominant) parietal lobe, particularly the supramarginal gyrus, which stores motor representations (praxicons) for learned skilled actions.
old_anchor: Damage to the left parietal lobe can result in ideomotor apraxia, an inability to perform purposeful motor movements when asked to do so.
testable_fact: Ideomotor apraxia, the inability to perform learned purposeful movements on command despite intact motor ability, most commonly results from damage to the left parietal lobe's supramarginal gyrus, which stores motor representations (praxicons).
passage:
A neurologist instructs a patient to demonstrate how to wave goodbye. The patient looks at the neurologist, clearly understands the instruction, but produces an awkward, clumsy approximation of the gesture that does not resemble a normal wave. Yet when a friend unexpectedly leaves the room, the patient spontaneously waves goodbye correctly. This dissociation between impaired voluntary and preserved automatic movement defines a specific form of motor planning deficit.

Damage to the **left parietal lobe** can result in **ideomotor apraxia**, an inability to perform **purposeful motor movements** when asked to do so. The patient cannot pantomime skilled actions on command or imitate gestures demonstrated by the examiner, despite having normal motor strength, coordination, and comprehension. The critical feature is the dissociation between impaired performance on command and preserved automatic or spontaneous performance of the same movements in naturalistic contexts.

The left parietal lobe, specifically the **inferior parietal lobule** encompassing the supramarginal gyrus (Brodmann area 40) and angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39), serves as the repository for **praxicons**, the stored representations of skilled motor actions. These praxicons encode the spatial trajectories, timing patterns, and force parameters of learned movements such as tool use, communicative gestures, and skilled manual actions. When the parietal lobe is damaged, these stored representations are degraded or inaccessible, and the patient cannot generate the appropriate motor plan when verbally instructed to perform the action.

The left hemisphere's dominance for praxis (skilled motor programming) parallels its dominance for language. Both functions rely on the left inferior parietal lobule, and ideomotor apraxia most commonly co-occurs with aphasia following left hemisphere stroke. However, the two deficits can be dissociated: patients with Broca's aphasia may not have apraxia, and patients with apraxia may not have aphasia, depending on the precise location and extent of the lesion.

The distinction between ideomotor apraxia and other forms of apraxia is clinically important. **Ideational apraxia** (also called conceptual apraxia) involves a loss of the conceptual knowledge of how to use objects, the patient no longer knows what a hammer is for. **Limb-kinetic apraxia** involves a loss of fine motor dexterity due to damage to the premotor or motor cortex. In ideomotor apraxia, the patient retains the conceptual knowledge and the motor capacity but cannot translate the concept into action on command.

Clinically, ideomotor apraxia is assessed by asking the patient to pantomime actions (show how to use a comb, wave goodbye, salute), imitate meaningless gestures, and perform actions with actual objects. The discrepancy between impaired pantomime and preserved object use is the diagnostic hallmark.

On the EPPP, ideomotor apraxia equals impaired voluntary movement on command with preserved automatic movement. The lesion is the left parietal lobe. Distinguish from ideational apraxia (conceptual loss) and limb-kinetic apraxia (fine motor loss). The left parietal lobe stores the motor programs for skilled actions.

chapter_title: The Frontal Lobe: Executive Function, Motor Control, and Prefrontal Syndromes
verbatim_anchor: Heilman, Watson, & Valenstein (1993): Contralateral neglect (hemispatial neglect) is a failure to attend to, respond to, or orient toward stimuli in the contralesional hemispace. It is most commonly and most severely produced by damage to the right parietal lobe, particularly the inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction. Patients may bump into objects on the neglected side, fail to eat food on one side of the plate, or draw only one half of objects.
old_anchor: Carl's symptoms of contralateral neglect, including bumping into things on the left side and drawing only the right side of a house, indicate an injury to his parietal lobe.
testable_fact: Contralateral (hemispatial) neglect, a failure to attend to stimuli in the contralesional hemispace, is most commonly and severely produced by damage to the right inferior parietal lobule and temporoparietal junction.
passage:
Carl, a 55-year-old construction worker, was involved in a scaffolding accident that resulted in a head injury. Since the accident, he consistently bumps into doorframes and furniture on his left side. When asked to draw a picture of his house, he draws only the right half, leaving the left side of the page completely blank. He eats only the food on the right side of his plate and shaves only the right side of his face.

Carl's symptoms of **contralateral neglect**, including bumping into things on the left side and drawing only the right side of objects, indicate an injury to his **parietal lobe**, specifically the **right parietal lobe**. Contralateral neglect (hemispatial neglect) involves a failure to attend to, perceive, or respond to stimuli on the side of space opposite to the brain lesion. Because the right hemisphere is dominant for spatial attention, right parietal damage produces a more severe and persistent left-sided neglect than left parietal damage produces of the right side.

Carl's specific symptoms each illustrate different manifestations of neglect. Bumping into objects on the left reflects **navigational neglect**, an inability to attend to obstacles in the left hemispace during locomotion. Drawing only the right half of the house reflects **constructional neglect**, a failure to represent the left side of space in drawing and copying tasks. Eating only from the right side of the plate reflects **personal/peripersonal neglect**, an inability to attend to the left side of near space. Together, these symptoms confirm a comprehensive left-sided spatial attention deficit.

The parietal lobe's role in spatial attention is understood through the **Heilman-Valenstein model**, which proposes that each hemisphere directs attention to the contralateral side of space, but the right hemisphere also directs some attention to the ipsilateral (right) side. This asymmetry means that when the left parietal lobe is damaged, the right hemisphere can partially compensate by directing attention to both visual fields. When the right parietal lobe is damaged, however, the left hemisphere can only attend to the right side, leaving the left side unattended.

The assessment of contralateral neglect includes line bisection (the patient marks the midpoint of a horizontal line, typically displacing rightward), cancellation tasks (the patient crosses out targets distributed across a page, omitting left-side targets), drawing tasks (copying or drawing from memory, omitting left-side details), and functional observation (eating, grooming, navigation behaviors).

Clinically, neglect is one of the strongest predictors of poor functional outcome after stroke. Patients with neglect have longer hospital stays, slower rehabilitation progress, and greater disability at discharge than patients without neglect.

On the EPPP, contralateral neglect following right parietal damage is a high-frequency topic. The symptoms described (bumping into things on the left, drawing only the right side, eating from one side of the plate) are classic indicators.
